topics.ch: Human: Human Geography: Nature and Scope
topics.h: Why does a mango orchard in Ratnagiri look so different from a tea garden in Darjeeling? Answering that needs both nature and people — and that is exactly what geography does.
p: Geography as a field of study is integrative, empirical and practical: it pulls together knowledge from many fields, rests on observation, and is used to solve real problems.
Geography studies phenomena that vary over space and time — the 'where' and 'when' of things on the earth's surface.
Dualism: geography has two main branches — physical geography (geomorphology, climatology, hydrology, soil geography, biogeography) and human geography.
Human geography studies the interrelationship between the physical environment and the socio-cultural environment created by human beings through mutual interaction.
Physical and human phenomena are closely tied: geographers describe nature with human terms (the 'face' of the earth, the 'eye' of a storm) and human features with natural ones.

ex.q: Classify the study of a cyclone's track over the Bay of Bengal and the study of fishermen's migration after the cyclone into the two branches of geography.
st: Cyclone track: an atmospheric process — climatology, a part of physical geography.
Fishermen's migration: a movement of people responding to the event — human geography.
Together they show the interrelationship between the physical and the socio-cultural environment.
ex.a: Cyclone track → physical geography; fishermen's migration → human geography

topics.rl: IMD tracks cyclones (physical geography), while state disaster authorities in Odisha plan evacuation of coastal villages (human geography) — the two branches work as one system.

rv.summary: Geography is an integrative, empirical and practical discipline that studies how phenomena vary over space and time. It has two branches, physical and human geography, which are closely interlinked.
focus: Describing geography as integrative, empirical and practical
The dualism of physical and human geography and the sub-branches of each
The definition of human geography as the study of the physical and socio-cultural environment interacting
How human terms describe nature ('foot' of a mountain, 'eye' of a storm) and why that shows the human–nature link
remember: Physical geography: geomorphology, climatology, hydrology, soil geography, biogeography
Human geography: interrelationship between the physical environment and the socio-cultural environment created by humans
Geography studies phenomena that vary over space and time
traps: Don't put soil geography or geomorphology in the human branch — they are physical
Human geography does not ignore the physical environment; it studies the two together

topics.ch: Human: Human Geography: Nature and Scope
topics.h: Three famous scholars, three definitions — and examiners love asking which one said what!
p: Friedrich Ratzel: human geography is the synthetic study of the relationship between human societies and the earth's surface.
Ellen C. Semple: human geography is the study of 'the changing relationship between the unresting man and the unstable earth'.
Paul Vidal de la Blache: a conception resulting from a more synthetic knowledge of the physical laws governing our earth and of the relations between the living beings which inhabit it.
Ratzel stresses synthesis; Semple stresses dynamism (both humans and earth keep changing); Vidal de la Blache stresses natural laws and living beings.
Common theme: the relationship between humans and the environment is not fixed — it is dynamic.

ex.q: Which definition uses the words 'unresting man' and 'unstable earth', and what idea does it highlight?
st: Recall the three definitions: Ratzel (synthetic study), Semple (changing relationship), Vidal de la Blache (physical laws and living beings).
'Unresting man and unstable earth' belongs to Ellen C. Semple.
It highlights that both humans and the earth are always changing, so their relationship is dynamic.
ex.a: Ellen C. Semple; it shows the human–environment relationship is dynamic

topics.rl: Think of Mumbai reclaiming land from the sea and then facing flooding during heavy monsoon rains — an 'unresting man' meeting an 'unstable earth', exactly as Semple described.

rv.summary: Three scholars defined human geography: Ratzel called it a synthetic study, Semple stressed the changing relationship between 'unresting man and unstable earth', and Vidal de la Blache linked physical laws with living beings. All see the human–environment relationship as dynamic.
focus: Matching each definition to Ratzel, Semple or Vidal de la Blache
Key words: 'synthetic' (Ratzel), 'unresting man and unstable earth' (Semple), 'physical laws' and 'living beings' (Vidal de la Blache)
The common idea: the human–environment relationship is dynamic
remember: Ratzel: synthetic study of the relationship between human societies and the earth's surface
Semple: the changing relationship between the unresting man and the unstable earth
Vidal de la Blache (France): synthetic knowledge of the physical laws governing the earth and relations between living beings on it
traps: Don't mix Semple's 'changing relationship' with Vidal de la Blache's 'physical laws'
Don't assign every definition to Ratzel

topics.ch: Human: Human Geography: Nature and Scope
topics.t: Nature of human geography: physical and cultural landscapes
topics.h: Look out of your window. Every road, roof and electric pole is a human mark painted on a natural canvas.
p: Physical environment: landforms, soils, climate, water, natural vegetation and diverse flora and fauna.
Cultural landscape: elements humans create using the stage provided by nature — houses, villages, cities, road and rail networks, industries, farms, ports and items of daily use.
Humans interact with the environment through technology; technology indicates the level of cultural development of a society.
Technology grew from understanding natural laws: knowing friction and heat led to fire; knowing DNA helped fight diseases; aerodynamics gave faster planes.
Human activities keep reshaping the cultural landscape on top of the physical environment.

ex.q: Sort these into physical environment or cultural landscape: Western Ghats, Konkan Railway, black soil, Jawaharlal Nehru Port.
st: Physical environment = elements given by nature.
Western Ghats (landform) and black soil → physical.
Konkan Railway and Jawaharlal Nehru Port were built by humans → cultural landscape.
ex.a: Physical: Western Ghats, black soil; Cultural: Konkan Railway, JNPT

topics.rl: The Konkan Railway cut tunnels through the Western Ghats — technology helped people lay a cultural landscape over a tough physical one.

rv.summary: The physical environment (landforms, soils, climate, water, vegetation, flora and fauna) is the stage on which humans build a cultural landscape of houses, roads, farms, ports and cities. The technology a society uses shows its level of cultural development.
focus: Sorting features into physical environment vs cultural landscape
Technology as an indicator of a society's cultural development
Which natural law led to which technology (fire, DNA, aerodynamics)
remember: Physical environment: landforms, soils, climate, water, natural vegetation, flora and fauna
Cultural landscape: elements humans create on the stage provided by nature — houses, villages, cities, roads, rail, industries, farms, ports
Friction and heat → fire; DNA → fighting diseases; aerodynamics → faster planes
traps: Don't treat farms or terraced fields as natural just because crops are plants — they are human-made
Don't think culture is built independently of nature; nature provides the stage

topics.ch: Human: Human Geography: Nature and Scope
topics.h: Imagine a world with no shops, no electricity — only the forest deciding what you eat and wear. That was life for early societies.
p: In early stages, humans were greatly influenced by nature and adapted to its dictates; technology was very low.
Such interaction is called environmental determinism: nature determines human life and activities.
Primitive societies saw nature as a powerful force — feared, worshipped and revered as 'Mother Nature'.
Direct dependence on nature for resources is called the naturalisation of humans.
NCERT example: Benda, living in the forests of Abujh Marh in central India, depends on the forest for food, shelter, medicines and livelihood; his community moves through shifting cultivation.

ex.q: Benda's family hunts, gathers forest produce and treats illness with forest herbs. Which concept does this illustrate and why?
st: Their food, shelter and medicine come directly from the forest.
Technology is minimal, so nature dictates their way of life.
This direct dependence is the naturalisation of humans, under environmental determinism.
ex.a: Naturalisation of humans (environmental determinism)

topics.rl: Some forest communities in Chhattisgarh's Abujhmarh region still depend heavily on forests — mahua flowers, tendu leaves and forest herbs form part of their livelihood.

rv.summary: In early stages, with very low technology, humans adapted to the dictates of nature and depended on it directly — this is environmental determinism, or the naturalisation of humans. NCERT's example is Benda in the Abujh Marh forests of central India.
focus: Defining environmental determinism and naturalisation of humans
The NCERT example of Benda in Abujh Marh and what it shows
Why low technology caused direct dependence on nature
remember: Environmental determinism: nature determines human life and activities
Naturalisation of humans: direct dependence on nature for resources
Benda lives in Abujh Marh, central India; depends on the forest; his community practises shifting cultivation
traps: Don't swap naturalisation of humans with humanisation of nature
Don't confuse Benda (Abujh Marh, determinism) with Kari (Trondheim, possibilism)

topics.ch: Human: Human Geography: Nature and Scope
topics.t: Humanisation of nature, possibilism and neo-determinism
topics.h: A Norwegian city in deep winter: fierce winds, heavy snow, barely any daylight — and yet people work, drive and stay warm. How?
p: With time, people understood their environment and developed technology; they moved from necessity to freedom and created possibilities — this is possibilism.

Nature provides opportunities; humans use them, and nature gets humanised, bearing imprints of human effort. NCERT example: Kari in Trondheim, Norway, lives through harsh winters with heated homes, technology and imported food.
Imprints of humans on nature: health resorts on highlands, huge urban sprawls, fields, orchards and pastures, ports on coasts, oceanic routes, and satellites in space.
Neo-determinism (stop and go determinism), given by Griffith Taylor, is a middle path: humans can conquer nature by obeying it, like obeying traffic lights.

Determinism = nature controls; possibilism = humans create possibilities; neo-determinism = humans develop within limits set by nature — a free run has caused global warming, ozone depletion and degraded lands.

ex.q: A town in Himachal builds roads but stops building on landslide-prone slopes after warnings from geologists. Which concept is this?
st: Humans are developing (building roads), so it is not pure determinism.
They respect limits set by nature (avoid unsafe slopes), so it is not unlimited possibilism.
Developing while obeying nature's 'red signals' is neo-determinism.
ex.a: Neo-determinism (stop and go determinism)

topics.rl: After repeated floods and landslides, Uttarakhand and Himachal have tightened rules for hill construction — a real-life application of Griffith Taylor's 'stop and go' idea.

rv.summary: With better technology humans moved from necessity to freedom and used nature's opportunities — possibilism, or humanisation of nature (Kari in Trondheim). Griffith Taylor's neo-determinism ('stop and go') is a middle path: develop, but obey nature's limits.
focus: Distinguishing determinism, possibilism and neo-determinism
Griffith Taylor and the traffic-light analogy
Imprints of humans on nature and the Trondheim example
remember: Possibilism: nature provides opportunities and humans use them; nature gets humanised
Neo-determinism = stop and go determinism, given by Griffith Taylor: conquer nature by obeying it
Human imprints: health resorts on highlands, urban sprawls, fields, orchards, pastures, ports, oceanic routes, satellites
traps: Don't link neo-determinism to Ratzel — it is Griffith Taylor's idea
A 'red signal' does not mean ending development forever; it means respecting nature's limit

topics.ch: Human: Human Geography: Nature and Scope
topics.t: Human geography through time: from exploration to spatial organisation
topics.h: From sailors' diaries to supercomputer maps — human geography changed its focus again and again over 500 years.
p: Early colonial period — exploration and description: imperial and trade interests drove discovery of new areas; geographers wrote encyclopaedic descriptions and travel accounts.
Later colonial period — regional analysis: elaborate description of all aspects of a region; regions are parts of a whole (the earth), so studying parts leads to understanding the whole.
1930s, inter-war period — areal differentiation: identifying the uniqueness of a region and why and how it differs from others (associated with Richard Hartshorne).
Late 1950s to late 1960s — spatial organisation: use of computers and sophisticated statistical tools; laws of physics applied to map and analyse human phenomena — the quantitative revolution.
Then came the 1970s schools (humanistic, radical, behavioural) and 1990s post-modernism.

ex.q: A 1960s study uses a gravity-model equation and a computer to predict how many people migrate between two cities. Which stage does it belong to?
st: Computers + statistical tools + physics-like laws are clues.
That describes spatial organisation, late 1950s to late 1960s.
This phase is called the quantitative revolution.
ex.a: Spatial organisation (quantitative revolution), late 1950s–late 1960s

topics.rl: Today's Census and ISRO Bhuvan maps rely on computers and statistics — a legacy of the quantitative revolution of the 1960s.

rv.summary: Human geography's focus changed over time: exploration and description (early colonial), regional analysis (later colonial), areal differentiation (1930s), and spatial organisation or the quantitative revolution (late 1950s–late 1960s), followed by 1970s schools and 1990s post-modernism.
focus: The correct order of stages and their periods
The main thrust of each stage
Tools of the quantitative revolution: computers, statistics, laws of physics
remember: Early colonial: exploration and description, driven by imperial and trade interests
Later colonial: regional analysis — regions as parts of a whole
1930s inter-war: areal differentiation — uniqueness of a region
Late 1950s–late 1960s: spatial organisation — the quantitative revolution
traps: Don't confuse areal differentiation (uniqueness) with regional analysis (parts of a whole)
Don't place the quantitative revolution in the 1930s or 1990s

topics.ch: Human: Human Geography: Nature and Scope
topics.h: By the 1970s, geographers asked: can equations explain poverty, feelings or culture? Three new schools said 'not alone!'
p: Dissatisfaction with the quantitative revolution's dehumanised approach led to humanistic, radical and behavioural schools in the 1970s.

Humanistic geography: stresses the central and active role of human awareness, human agency, human consciousness and creativity. (NCERT also notes a welfare/humanistic concern with social well-being — housing, health, education.)
Radical school: uses Marxian theory to explain the basic causes of poverty, deprivation and social inequality, linking them to the development of capitalism.
Behavioural school: emphasises lived experience and the perception of space by social categories based on ethnicity, race, religion and so on.
1990s post-modernism: questions grand generalisations and universal theories; stresses understanding each local context.

ex.q: A researcher interviews migrant workers in Surat to learn how safe or unsafe different neighbourhoods feel to them. Which school does this reflect?
st: Focus is on lived experience and perception of space.
Perceptions differ by social group.
This is the behavioural school.
ex.a: Behavioural school

topics.rl: Studies of how women perceive safety in Delhi's metro and streets use a behavioural approach — mapping feelings, not just distances.

rv.summary: Dissatisfied with the dehumanised quantitative approach, geographers formed humanistic, radical and behavioural schools in the 1970s. Post-modernism in the 1990s questioned grand generalisations and stressed local context.
focus: Matching each school to its focus
Why the 1970s schools emerged
What post-modernism rejects and stresses
remember: Humanistic: human awareness, agency, consciousness and creativity (welfare concern: housing, health, education)
Radical: Marxian theory to explain poverty, deprivation and inequality, linked to capitalism
Behavioural: lived experience and perception of space by ethnicity, race, religion
Post-modernism (1990s): questions universal theories; stresses local context
traps: Don't swap the radical school (Marxian) with the humanistic school (human agency)
The word 'model' does not make a study quantitative — rejecting universal models is post-modern

topics.ch: Human: Human Geography: Nature and Scope
topics.t: Fields of human geography: social, urban and political
topics.h: Psephologists predicting election results on TV are borrowing from a branch of geography. Which one?
p: Human geography is interdisciplinary: it has close links with sister disciplines in the social sciences.

Social geography sub-fields and sisters: behavioural geography (psychology), geography of social well-being (welfare economics), geography of leisure (sociology), cultural geography (anthropology), gender geography (sociology, anthropology, women's studies), historical geography (history), medical geography (epidemiology).
Urban geography is linked with urban studies and planning.
Political geography is linked with political science; its sub-fields are electoral geography (psephology) and military geography (military science).

ex.q: Which sister discipline is linked to electoral geography, and to medical geography?
st: Electoral geography is a sub-field of political geography.
It is linked with psephology (study of elections).
Medical geography (social geography) is linked with epidemiology.
ex.a: Electoral geography → psephology; medical geography → epidemiology

topics.rl: During COVID-19, district-wise hotspot maps by ICMR and state governments were medical geography in action, drawing on epidemiology.

rv.summary: Human geography is interdisciplinary. Social geography sub-fields link with psychology, welfare economics, sociology, anthropology, history and epidemiology; urban geography with urban studies; political geography (electoral, military) with political science, psephology and military science.
focus: Matching each sub-field to its sister discipline
Sub-fields of political geography
Why human geography is called interdisciplinary
remember: Behavioural → psychology; social well-being → welfare economics; leisure → sociology; cultural → anthropology
Gender → sociology, anthropology, women's studies; historical → history; medical → epidemiology
Electoral geography → psephology; military geography → military science (both under political geography)
traps: Don't confuse psephology (elections) with demography (population)
Don't link medical geography with welfare economics — its sister is epidemiology

topics.ch: Human: Human Geography: Nature and Scope
topics.t: Fields of human geography: population, settlement and economic
topics.h: Why is the government planning new smart cities and dedicated freight corridors? Settlement and economic geographers have the answers.
p: Population geography is linked with demography; settlement geography with urban and rural planning.

Economic geography is linked with economics. Sub-fields: geography of resources (resource economics), geography of agriculture (agricultural sciences), geography of industries (industrial economics), geography of marketing (business studies, economics, commerce), geography of tourism (tourism and travel management), geography of international trade (international trade).
Exam tip: learn the table 'fields — sub-fields — sister disciplines' by heart; one-mark questions pick a single row.
Long answers often ask: distinguish naturalisation of humans and humanisation of nature; explain neo-determinism; describe the nature and scope, and fields and sub-fields, of human geography.

ex.q: A student must answer: 'Geography of marketing is linked with which disciplines?' Work it out.
st: Marketing belongs to economic geography.
It deals with buying, selling and distribution.
Its sisters are business studies, economics and commerce.
ex.a: Business studies, economics and commerce

topics.rl: Planning Kerala's tourism circuits draws on the geography of tourism and travel management; the Census of India is the raw material of population geography.

rv.summary: Population geography links with demography and settlement geography with urban and rural planning. Economic geography's sub-fields — resources, agriculture, industries, marketing, tourism and international trade — each have a sister discipline.
focus: Sister disciplines of population, settlement and economic geography
The six sub-fields of economic geography and their sisters
Telling naturalisation of humans from humanisation of nature
remember: Population geography → demography; settlement geography → urban and rural planning
Resources → resource economics; agriculture → agricultural sciences; industries → industrial economics
Marketing → business studies, economics, commerce; tourism → tourism and travel management; trade → international trade
traps: Electoral geography is not part of economic geography — it is political geography
Don't reverse the terms: adapting to nature = naturalisation of humans; modifying nature = humanisation of nature

topics.ch: Human: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
topics.t: People as wealth and the idea of distribution
topics.h: India's biggest resource isn't coal or iron — it's 140 crore people. Geography starts by asking where they live.
p: The people of a country are its real wealth: they use its resources and decide its policies; a country is ultimately known by its people.
World population has crossed 8 billion (the UN marked this in November 2022), after growing slowly for most of history and very fast in the last few centuries.
Geographers study population under four heads: distribution, density, growth and composition.
Distribution means the way people are spaced over the earth's surface — some areas are crowded, others nearly empty.

ex.q: A teacher asks: 'Name the four aspects in which population is studied, and define the first one.'
st: The four aspects are distribution, density, growth and composition.
Distribution is the first.
It refers to the way people are spaced over the earth's surface.
ex.a: Distribution, density, growth, composition; distribution = spacing of people over the earth's surface

topics.rl: India's demographic dividend — a huge young workforce powering IT services in Bengaluru and factories in Tamil Nadu — shows why people are called a nation's real wealth.

rv.summary: A country's people are its real wealth because they use its resources and make its policies. World population crossed 8 billion in November 2022, and geographers study it by distribution, density, growth and composition.
focus: The four aspects: distribution, density, growth and composition
Telling distribution (spacing of people) from density (people per unit area)
Why people are called the real wealth of a country
remember: Population is studied by distribution, density, growth and composition
Distribution = the way people are spaced over the earth's surface
World population crossed 8 billion in November 2022 (UN)
traps: Don't swap distribution and density — density is a ratio of people to area
Don't think world population always grew fast — it was slow for most of history

topics.ch: Human: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
topics.h: Nine out of ten people on Earth squeeze into just one-tenth of its land. Where are they all?
p: About 90 per cent of the world's population lives in about 10 per cent of its land area.
The 10 most populous countries contribute about 60 per cent of world population; 6 of these 10 are in Asia.
India and China together hold over a third of humanity; India became the most populous country in 2023 (UN estimate).
On a world map, densely populated belts lie in East, South and South-east Asia, north-western Europe and north-eastern USA; sparse areas lie near the poles, in deserts and in equatorial rainforests.

ex.q: If world population is 8 billion, about how many people live on 10 per cent of the land?
st: About 90% of people live on 10% of land.
90% of 8 billion = 0.9 × 8 = 7.2 billion.
ex.a: About 7.2 billion

topics.rl: India's population is about 18 per cent of the world but on only about 2.4 per cent of world land — a classic example of uneven distribution.

rv.summary: World population is very unevenly spread: about 90% of people live on about 10% of the land. The 10 most populous countries hold about 60% of people, 6 of them in Asia, and India became the most populous country in 2023.
focus: The 90% on 10% of land figure and the 60% top-10 figure
Dense belts vs sparse areas on a world map
Asia's share of the most populous countries
remember: About 90% of people live on about 10% of the land
10 most populous countries ≈ 60% of world population; 6 of the 10 are in Asia
India became the most populous country in 2023 (UN estimate)
traps: Don't mix the 90% (land concentration) with the 60% (top 10 countries)
Sparse areas are near the poles, in deserts and in equatorial rainforests — not north-eastern USA

topics.ch: Human: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
topics.h: Bihar packs over 1,100 people into each square kilometre; Arunachal Pradesh, about 17. Same country, very different crowding!
p: Density of population = number of people ÷ area of land; expressed as persons per sq km.
Example: a region of 100 sq km with 1,50,000 people has density 1,50,000 ÷ 100 = 1,500 persons per sq km.
Densely populated regions: north-eastern USA, north-western Europe, and South, South-east and East Asia.
Sparsely populated regions: areas near the North and South Poles, hot and cold deserts, and high rainfall zones near the equator.
Medium density regions: western China, southern India, Norway and Sweden.

ex.q: District A has 24,00,000 people on 1,200 sq km. District B has 9,00,000 people on 300 sq km. Which is denser?
st: Density B = 9,00,000 ÷ 300 = 3,000 per sq km.
B is denser even though it has fewer people.
ex.a: District B (3,000 per sq km)

topics.rl: Census 2011 recorded India's density as 382 persons per sq km — Delhi topped among states/UTs, while Arunachal Pradesh was the lowest.

rv.summary: Density of population = number of people ÷ area, in persons per sq km. Dense regions include north-eastern USA, north-western Europe and South, South-east and East Asia; sparse regions are polar areas, deserts and equatorial rainforests.
focus: Calculating density, and population from density × area
Classifying regions as dense, medium or sparse
Comparing densities rather than total populations
remember: Density = population ÷ area (persons per sq km)
Dense: north-eastern USA, north-western Europe, South, South-east and East Asia
Medium: western China, southern India, Norway, Sweden
Sparse: near the poles, hot and cold deserts, high rainfall zones near the equator
traps: Don't multiply population by area to get density — divide
A place with more people is not always denser; compare people per sq km

topics.ch: Human: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
topics.h: Why did the great civilisations grow along the Nile, the Indus and the Hwang He? Follow the water.
p: Availability of water: people prefer areas where fresh water is easily available; river valleys are among the most densely populated areas.
Landforms: people prefer flat plains and gentle slopes, which suit farming, roads and industry. Ganga plains are densely populated; mountains like the Andes, Alps and Himalayas are sparse.
Climate: extreme climates such as very hot or cold deserts are uncomfortable; areas with a comfortable climate with little seasonal variation, like Mediterranean regions, attract people.
Soils: fertile loamy soils support intensive agriculture, so plains of the Nile, Ganga, Hwang-He and Chang Jiang (in China) are densely populated.

ex.q: Explain why the Ganga plains are far more crowded than Ladakh.
st: Water: perennial Ganga and tributaries vs scarce water in Ladakh.
Landform: flat plain vs high mountains.
Climate and soil: moderate climate and fertile alluvium vs cold desert and thin soils.
ex.a: Water, flat land, fertile soil and moderate climate make the Ganga plains densely populated

topics.rl: The Indo-Gangetic plain supports some of the world's highest rural densities thanks to rivers, alluvial soil and canal irrigation.

rv.summary: Geographical factors shape where people live: fresh water, flat plains, a comfortable climate and fertile soils attract people, so river valleys and plains like the Ganga are crowded, while mountains, deserts and polar areas are sparse.
focus: The four geographical factors: water, landforms, climate, soils
Using factors to explain dense vs sparse areas
Finding the limiting factor in a case
remember: River valleys are among the most densely populated areas because of fresh water
Plains and gentle slopes suit farming, roads and industry; mountains (Andes, Alps, Himalayas) are sparse
Fertile loamy soils: plains of the Nile, Ganga, Hwang-He and Chang Jiang are dense
traps: Urbanisation and industrialisation are economic factors, not geographical
Don't say mountains are empty for lack of water — rugged terrain is the reason

topics.ch: Human: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
topics.h: Jamshedpur grew from a forest village to a steel city in a few decades. What pulled people there?
p: Minerals: areas with mineral deposits attract industries, and mining and industrial activity create jobs; e.g. the Katanga-Zambia copper belt in Africa.
Urbanisation: cities offer better civic amenities, employment, education, medical facilities and transport, so they attract rural-urban migrants and grow large.
Industrialisation: industrial belts provide jobs for factory workers and also transport operators, shopkeepers, bank staff, doctors and teachers; e.g. Kobe-Osaka region of Japan.

Social and cultural factors: places of religious or cultural significance attract people (Varanasi, Jerusalem, Vatican City); social and political unrest pushes people out; governments sometimes offer incentives to settle sparse areas.

ex.q: Classify: (i) Jharia coalfield town grows; (ii) pilgrims settle in Varanasi; (iii) people leave a conflict-hit region; (iv) Gurugram's offices draw graduates.
st: (i) Minerals → economic.
(ii) Religious significance → social/cultural.
(iii) Unrest → social/political push.
(iv) Urban jobs and amenities → economic (urbanisation).
ex.a: (i) economic, (ii) cultural, (iii) social-political, (iv) economic (urbanisation)

topics.rl: Migrants from Bihar and UP to Mumbai, Surat and Delhi follow jobs created by industrialisation and urbanisation.

rv.summary: Economic factors (minerals, urbanisation, industrialisation) and social-cultural factors (religious centres, unrest, government incentives) also shape population distribution. Jobs and amenities pull people in; unrest pushes them out.
focus: Examples: Katanga-Zambia copper belt, Kobe-Osaka, Varanasi, Jerusalem, Vatican City
Classifying a case as economic or social-cultural
How industrial belts create service jobs too
remember: Economic factors: minerals, urbanisation, industrialisation
Katanga-Zambia copper belt = minerals; Kobe-Osaka region of Japan = industrialisation
Religious/cultural centres: Varanasi, Jerusalem, Vatican City; social and political unrest pushes people out
traps: Don't treat climate or landforms as economic factors
Industries do not employ only factory workers — they also draw shopkeepers, bank staff, doctors and teachers

topics.ch: Human: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
topics.h: India added about 18 crore people between Census 2001 and 2011. How do geographers measure change on that scale?
p: Population growth (population change) is the change in the number of inhabitants of a territory over a period of time; it may be positive or negative.
Growth of population: change between two points of time in absolute numbers = later population − earlier population.
Growth rate of population: the change expressed as a percentage = (change ÷ earlier population) × 100.
Growth rate lets us compare places of very different sizes fairly.

ex.q: A town had 50,000 people in 2011 and 60,000 in 2021. Find the growth and the growth rate.
ex.a: Growth = 10,000; growth rate = 20%

topics.rl: Census 2011 showed India's decadal growth rate as 17.7% for 2001–2011, the lowest decadal growth recorded after Independence.

rv.summary: Population growth is the change in the number of people between two points of time. Growth = later − earlier population; growth rate = (change ÷ earlier population) × 100, which lets us compare places of different sizes fairly.
focus: Calculating growth (absolute) and growth rate (%)
Dividing by the earlier (base) population
Handling negative growth with a minus sign
remember: Growth = later population − earlier population
Growth rate = (change ÷ earlier population) × 100
Growth can be positive or negative
traps: Don't divide by the later population when finding the growth rate
A bigger absolute increase does not mean a faster growth rate

topics.ch: Human: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
topics.t: Natural growth, actual growth, positive and negative growth
topics.h: Kerala has low birth rates, yet its villages fill with new houses built by Gulf migrants. Births alone don't tell the whole story.
p: Natural growth of population = births − deaths in a region between two points of time.
Actual growth of population = births − deaths + in-migration − out-migration.
Positive growth: when births exceed deaths between two points of time, or when people from other countries migrate in permanently.
Negative growth: when the population decreases between two points of time — births fall below deaths or people emigrate.

ex.q: A city records 30,000 births, 10,000 deaths, 15,000 in-migrants and 5,000 out-migrants in a year. Find natural and actual growth.
ex.a: Natural growth = 20,000; actual growth = 30,000

topics.rl: Several countries such as Japan and some in eastern Europe have recorded negative population growth as deaths outnumber births.

rv.summary: Natural growth = births − deaths. Actual growth = births − deaths + in-migration − out-migration. Growth is positive when population rises (more births or permanent immigration) and negative when it falls.
focus: Computing natural and actual growth with correct signs
Positive vs negative growth
How migration can make actual growth differ from natural growth
remember: Natural growth = Births − Deaths
Actual growth = Births − Deaths + In-migration − Out-migration
Negative growth: population decreases between two points of time
traps: Don't include migration in natural growth
Natural growth and actual growth need not have the same sign

topics.ch: Human: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
topics.t: Births and deaths: CBR, CDR and mortality
topics.h: Every year the Sample Registration System tells India how many babies were born per 1,000 people. That single number shapes school and hospital budgets.
p: The three components of population change are births, deaths and migration.
Crude Birth Rate (CBR) = number of live births in a year per thousand of population: CBR = (Bi ÷ P) × 1000, where Bi = live births in the year and P = mid-year population.
Crude Death Rate (CDR) = number of deaths in a year per thousand of population: CDR = (D ÷ P) × 1000.
Mortality is affected by the region's demographic structure, social advancement and levels of economic development.
Natural growth rate (per thousand) = CBR − CDR.

ex.q: A town has a mid-year population of 2,00,000. In the year, 4,000 babies are born and 1,600 people die. Find CBR and CDR.
st: Natural growth rate = 20 − 8 = 12 per thousand.
ex.a: CBR = 20, CDR = 8 per thousand

topics.rl: India's SRS data show CBR falling to about 19.5 per thousand and CDR to about 6 per thousand in recent years — signs of demographic transition.

rv.summary: Births, deaths and migration change population. CBR = (live births in a year ÷ mid-year population) × 1000 and CDR = (deaths ÷ P) × 1000, both per thousand; natural growth rate = CBR − CDR.
focus: CBR and CDR numericals with the ×1000 step
Natural growth rate = CBR − CDR
Factors affecting mortality
remember: CBR = (Bi ÷ P) × 1000; P = mid-year population
Natural growth rate (per thousand) = CBR − CDR
Mortality depends on demographic structure, social advancement, economic development
traps: Don't forget to multiply by 1000 — rates are per thousand
Compare rates, not raw numbers of births

topics.ch: Human: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
topics.t: Migration: types, push and pull factors
topics.h: Every Diwali, trains from Mumbai to Patna overflow. Every harvest, Punjab's fields welcome workers from Bihar. Migration moves India.
p: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another; the place they leave is the place of origin (population falls) and the place they move to is the place of destination (population rises).
Immigrants are migrants who move into a new place; emigrants are migrants who move out of a place.
Migration may be permanent, temporary or seasonal; and rural-rural, rural-urban, urban-urban or urban-rural.
Push factors make the place of origin less attractive: unemployment, poor living conditions, political turmoil, unpleasant climate, natural disasters, epidemics and socio-economic backwardness.
Pull factors make the destination more attractive: better job opportunities and living conditions, peace and stability, security of life and property, and pleasant climate.

ex.q: A farmer from drought-hit Marathwada moves to Pune for a factory job. Identify origin, destination, a push and a pull factor.
st: Origin: Marathwada (population falls).
Destination: Pune (population rises).
Push: drought (natural disaster) and unemployment.
Pull: better job opportunities.
ex.a: Origin Marathwada, destination Pune; push = drought/unemployment; pull = jobs

topics.rl: Seasonal migration of sugarcane cutters from Beed to western Maharashtra and Karnataka every winter is a well-known Indian case.

rv.summary: Migration moves people from a place of origin (population falls) to a destination (population rises). Push factors like unemployment, disasters and turmoil drive people out; pull factors like jobs, peace, security and pleasant climate draw them in.
focus: Sorting factors into push and pull
Immigrants vs emigrants; origin vs destination
Types: permanent, temporary, seasonal; rural-urban and other streams
remember: Immigrants move into a place; emigrants move out of a place
Push: unemployment, poor living conditions, political turmoil, unpleasant climate, disasters, epidemics, backwardness
Pull: better jobs and living conditions, peace and stability, security of life and property, pleasant climate
traps: Don't swap push and pull — push acts at the origin, pull at the destination
Not all migration is rural-urban; city to city is urban-urban

topics.ch: Human: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
topics.t: Trends in world population growth and doubling time
topics.h: It took more than a million years for humanity to reach 1 billion — yet only 12 years to go from 5 billion to 6 billion!
p: For most of history population grew very slowly; it was below 300 million in the first century AD.
Growth speeded up sharply after the Industrial Revolution (around 1750).
Technological advancement, expansion of world trade, better food supply and medical facilities reduced death rates, so population grew rapidly.

Doubling time — the years a population takes to double — kept shrinking: about 200 years from 1650 to 1850 (500 to 1,000 million), 80 years to 1930 (2,000 million) and 45 years to 1975 (4,000 million).
On a graph, world population looks like a 'J' curve: flat for centuries, then shooting up.

ex.q: World population was 2,000 million in 1930 and 4,000 million in 1975. What was the doubling time?
st: Doubling time = later year − earlier year when population doubled.
ex.a: 45 years

topics.rl: Better food (Green Revolution), vaccines and clean water reduced deaths in India after 1951, causing a population 'explosion' between 1951 and 1981.

rv.summary: World population grew very slowly for most of history (below 300 million in the first century AD) and sped up after the Industrial Revolution around 1750 as death rates fell. Doubling time shrank from about 200 to 80 to 45 years, giving a J-shaped curve.
focus: Doubling time calculations from year pairs
Why growth sped up after 1750
The shrinking doubling time and the J curve
remember: First century AD: below 300 million
5 billion to 6 billion took only 12 years
traps: Faster growth means a shorter doubling time, not a longer one
Death rates fell after 1750; rising deaths would slow growth

topics.ch: Human: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
topics.t: Spatial pattern and impact of population change
topics.h: Japan's villages have schools with no children; Niger's schools burst at the seams. Two very different population problems.
p: Spatial pattern: developed countries generally have slow (or even negative) growth; developing countries generally grow faster. Growth is negatively correlated with economic development.
A small increase in population is desirable in a growing economy; beyond a point it creates problems.
Problems of rapid growth: depletion of resources (the most serious), unemployment, and pressure on services like schools, hospitals, housing and transport.
Population decline is also a concern: it indicates that resources that supported a former population are now insufficient; it also brings ageing and a shrinking workforce.

ex.q: Compare the main population problems of a fast-growing country and a shrinking one.
st: Fast-growing: strain on resources, jobs and services.
Shrinking: ageing, fewer workers, and a sign that resources/economy no longer support the earlier population.
Both call for planning.
ex.a: Fast growth strains resources; decline brings ageing and shrinking workforce

topics.rl: Indian cities like Bengaluru face traffic, water and housing stress from rapid growth, while states like Kerala are already planning for an ageing population.

rv.summary: Developed countries generally grow slowly and developing countries faster, so growth is negatively correlated with development. Rapid growth depletes resources and strains jobs and services, while decline brings ageing and a shrinking workforce.
focus: Spatial pattern of growth vs development
Problems of rapid growth vs problems of decline
Per-person share when population rises and resources stay fixed
remember: Population growth is negatively correlated with economic development
Most serious problem of rapid growth: depletion of resources
A small increase is desirable in a growing economy
Decline: ageing, shrinking workforce; resources no longer sufficient for the former population
traps: Don't assume richer countries grow faster
Don't mix up the problems: unemployment goes with rapid growth, ageing with decline

topics.ch: Human: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
topics.h: Two hundred years ago, every country had high births and high deaths. Today some have cradles empty and pensions full. The demographic transition explains the journey.
p: Demographic transition theory: population changes from high births and high deaths to low births and low deaths as society moves from rural, agrarian and illiterate to urban, industrial and literate. It helps describe and predict population.

Stage I: high fertility and high mortality, so slow growth; people mostly in agriculture, large families, low life expectancy, mostly illiterate, low technology. About 200 years ago all countries were in this stage.
Stage II: fertility remains high at first and declines with time; mortality falls due to better sanitation and health — the gap between births and deaths causes a large increase in population.
Stage III: both fertility and mortality decline considerably; population is stable or grows slowly; society is urbanised, literate, with high technical know-how and deliberately controls family size.

On the diagram, the birth-rate and death-rate curves start high, the death-rate curve falls first, the birth-rate curve falls later; total population rises steeply in the gap. Countries today are at different stages.

ex.q: A country has a birth rate of 38 and a death rate of 12 per thousand, with death rates falling fast due to new hospitals. Which stage is it in?
st: High birth rate still (38).
Death rate already falling (12).
Large gap → rapid growth.
This matches Stage II.
ex.a: Stage II

topics.rl: India moved from Stage II (high births, falling deaths after 1951) towards Stage III, with total fertility rate now at about 2.0 (NFHS-5) — below replacement level.

rv.summary: Demographic transition theory says population moves from high births and high deaths to low births and low deaths as society becomes urban, industrial and literate. Growth is slow in Stage I, fastest in Stage II (deaths fall first), and slow again in Stage III.
focus: Features of Stages I, II and III
Why the gap in Stage II causes rapid growth
Reading the diagram: death rate falls first
remember: Stage I: high fertility, high mortality, slow growth; agrarian, illiterate, low technology
Stage II: fertility high then declining; mortality falls (sanitation, health) → large increase
Stage III: both low; slow or stable growth; urban, literate, family size controlled
traps: High births alone do not mean fast growth — in Stage I high deaths cancel them
The birth-rate curve does not fall first; the death rate falls first

topics.ch: Human: The World Population: Distribution, Density and Growth
topics.h: In 1798 an English clergyman predicted that people would outgrow food and face famine. Was Thomas Malthus right?
p: Family planning is the spacing or preventing of the birth of children; access to family planning services helps limit population growth and improves women's health.
Government measures include propaganda (awareness campaigns), free availability of contraceptives and tax disincentives for large families.
Thomas Malthus (1798): the number of people would increase faster than the food supply; any further increase would result in a population crash caused by famine, disease and war.
Malthus' natural (physical) checks are famine, disease and war; preventive checks (like late marriage and self-restraint) are better than physical checks.
Exam focus: distribution factors, positive vs negative growth, CBR/CDR numericals and stages of demographic transition.

ex.q: Classify Malthus' checks: delayed marriage, famine, epidemic, self-restraint, war.
st: Natural/physical checks occur through suffering: famine, epidemic (disease), war.
Preventive checks are chosen by people: delayed marriage, self-restraint.
ex.a: Natural checks: famine, epidemic, war; preventive checks: delayed marriage, self-restraint

topics.rl: India launched the world's first national family planning programme in 1952; schemes like Mission Parivar Vikas promote access to contraceptives in high-fertility districts.

rv.summary: Family planning means spacing or preventing births; governments use awareness campaigns, free contraceptives and tax disincentives. Malthus (1798) said population grows faster than food supply, leading to a crash through famine, disease and war unless preventive checks are used.
focus: Malthus' theory and its date
Natural (physical) checks vs preventive checks
Government population-control measures
remember: Malthus, 1798: population grows faster than food supply
Natural (physical) checks: famine, disease, war; preventive checks: late marriage, self-restraint
Measures: propaganda, free contraceptives, tax disincentives for large families
traps: Don't call delayed marriage a natural check — it is preventive
Tax disincentives discourage large families; they are not incentives

topics.h: A city's GDP doubles, but its rivers turn black and its children still skip school. Has it grown or developed?
p: Both growth and development refer to changes over a period of time.
Growth is quantitative and value neutral: it may be positive (increase) or negative (decrease).
Development means a qualitative change and is always value positive; development occurs when there is positive growth plus a positive change in quality.
For a long time, a country's development was measured only by economic growth (GNP, per capita income): a bigger economy was assumed to mean a more developed country.
Paradox: a country can show high economic growth while most of its people still lack good health, education and choices.

ex.q: A town's population rises from 50,000 to 70,000, but traffic, slums and pollution worsen. Is this growth, development or both?
st: Population increased — a quantitative change, so growth (positive).
Quality of life worsened, so there is no positive qualitative change.
Hence growth without development.
ex.a: Growth, but not development

topics.rl: India's GDP grew fast after 1991, yet NFHS surveys showed high child stunting — a reminder that growth alone does not guarantee development.

rv.summary: Growth is a quantitative, value-neutral change that can be positive or negative; development is a qualitative change that is always value positive. Development needs positive growth plus a positive change in quality, so a country can grow without developing.
focus: Distinguishing growth (quantitative, value neutral) from development (qualitative, value positive)
Spotting growth without development in a case
Why economic growth alone was once used to measure development
remember: Growth: quantitative and value neutral; can be positive or negative
Development: qualitative change, always value positive
Development = positive growth + positive change in quality
traps: Development is not value neutral — growth is
Rising income does not automatically mean development

topics.t: The concept of human development: Haq and Sen
topics.h: A Pakistani economist and an Indian economist, friends from college, changed how the world measures progress.
p: The concept of human development was introduced by Dr Mahbub-ul-Haq, a Pakistani economist: development should enlarge people's choices and improve their lives; people are central to all development.

Prof. Amartya Sen saw an increase in freedom (or decrease in unfreedom) as the main objective of development; social and political institutions and processes play an important role in increasing freedom.
The Human Development Report has been published annually by the UNDP since 1990.
The most important aspects: leading a long and healthy life, being able to gain knowledge, and having enough means to live a decent life.
Hence access to resources, health and education are the key areas; lack of these capabilities limits people's choices.

ex.q: Why does lack of education limit a person's choices, according to the human development concept?
st: Human development is about enlarging choices.
Choices need capabilities — health, knowledge and resources.
Without education, a person cannot access many jobs or information, so choices shrink.
ex.a: Without knowledge (a key capability), people's choices narrow

topics.rl: Kerala's investment in schools and health clinics has long given it top human development indicators in India, showing Haq's idea of putting people first.

rv.summary: Dr Mahbub-ul-Haq introduced human development: enlarging people's choices, with people at the centre. Prof. Amartya Sen saw development as increasing freedom, helped by social and political institutions. UNDP has published the Human Development Report every year since 1990.
focus: Who said what: Haq (enlarging choices) and Sen (freedom)
The three most important aspects of human development
UNDP and the 1990 Human Development Report
remember: Mahbub-ul-Haq (Pakistani economist): development enlarges people's choices; people are central
Amartya Sen: increase in freedom (decrease in unfreedom) is the main objective; institutions matter
Human Development Report: published annually by UNDP since 1990
Key aspects: a long and healthy life, gaining knowledge, means for a decent life
traps: Don't credit Amartya Sen with introducing the concept — that was Mahbub-ul-Haq
The HDR is published by UNDP, not the World Bank

topics.t: Pillars of human development: equity and sustainability
topics.h: Imagine a house on four pillars. Remove one, and the roof tilts. Human development stands on four such pillars.
p: The four pillars of human development are equity, sustainability, productivity and empowerment.
Equity: making equal access to opportunities available to everybody, irrespective of gender, race, income and, in the Indian case, caste.
Example: in India, a large number of women and persons from socially and economically backward groups drop out of school — this shows how access to knowledge is limited by unequal opportunity.
Sustainability: continuity in the availability of opportunities; each generation must have the same opportunities. Misuse of environmental, financial and human resources reduces future options.
Example: if a community does not stress sending girls to school, many opportunities are lost to these young women when they grow up.

ex.q: A village over-pumps groundwater for paddy, leaving dry wells for the next generation. Which pillar is violated?
st: The issue is about future availability of a resource.
Future generations will have fewer opportunities.
That breaks sustainability.
ex.a: Sustainability

topics.rl: Schemes like Beti Bachao Beti Padhao and scholarships for SC/ST students try to strengthen equity in education.

rv.summary: Human development rests on four pillars: equity, sustainability, productivity and empowerment. Equity means equal access to opportunities for all irrespective of gender, race, income and caste; sustainability means every generation keeps the same opportunities.
focus: Naming the four pillars
Telling equity from sustainability in a case
Indian examples: school dropouts, not educating girls
remember: Four pillars: equity, sustainability, productivity, empowerment
Equity: equal access to opportunities irrespective of gender, race, income and (in India) caste
Sustainability: continuity in the availability of opportunities for every generation
traps: Don't swap equity (equal access now) with sustainability (opportunities for future generations)
Income, welfare, basic needs and capability are approaches, not pillars

topics.t: Pillars of human development: productivity and empowerment
topics.h: A worker who is healthy and skilled produces more. A woman who can decide for herself shapes her family's future. Two more pillars!
p: Productivity means human labour productivity, or productivity in terms of human work; it must be constantly enriched by building capabilities in people.
Efforts to increase knowledge or provide better health facilities lead to better work efficiency — people are the real wealth of nations.
Empowerment means having the power to make choices; it comes from increasing freedom and capability.
Good governance and people-oriented policies are required to empower people; empowerment of socially and economically disadvantaged groups is of special importance.

ex.q: A state trains rural women in digital skills and helps them form self-help groups that take their own loan decisions. Which pillars are strengthened?
st: Training builds capabilities → productivity.
Taking their own decisions → power to make choices → empowerment.
ex.a: Productivity and empowerment

topics.rl: Kudumbashree in Kerala and SHG-bank linkage programmes have empowered millions of rural women, improving both productivity and decision-making.

rv.summary: Productivity means human labour productivity, enriched by building people's capabilities through knowledge and health. Empowerment means having the power to make choices; it comes from freedom and capability and needs good governance and people-oriented policies.
focus: Defining productivity and empowerment
Identifying the pillar in a case (skill training vs decision-making power)
Role of good governance in empowerment
remember: Productivity: human labour productivity, enriched by building capabilities in people
Better knowledge and health → better work efficiency; people are the real wealth of nations
Empowerment: the power to make choices, from increasing freedom and capability
traps: Productivity is not machine output — it is human work efficiency
Empowerment does not depend only on income

topics.h: Is development about more money, more welfare schemes, basic needs, or building abilities? Four approaches, four answers.
p: Income approach: one of the oldest; human development is linked to income; the level of income reflects the level of freedom an individual enjoys — higher income, higher development.

Welfare approach: looks at human beings as beneficiaries or targets of development activities; argues for higher government expenditure on education, health, social security and amenities; people are passive recipients, not participants.

Basic needs approach: initially proposed by the International Labour Organisation (ILO); six basic needs — health, education, food, water supply, sanitation and housing; the question of human choices is ignored; the emphasis is on providing basic needs to defined sections.
Capability approach: associated with Prof. Amartya Sen; building human capabilities in health, education and access to resources is the key to increasing human development.

ex.q: A scheme gives free rations and housing to poor families but offers no skill training or voice in decisions. Which approach is this closest to?
st: The scheme supplies items from the list of basic needs (food, housing) to a defined group.
People's own choices and abilities are not considered.
Providing basic needs while ignoring choices is the basic needs approach.
ex.a: Basic needs approach

topics.rl: PM Awas Yojana (housing) and Jal Jeevan Mission (tap water) meet basic needs, while Skill India builds capabilities — India uses a mix of approaches.

rv.summary: There are four approaches to human development: income (oldest; higher income, higher development), welfare (people as passive beneficiaries of government spending), basic needs (ILO; six needs, ignores choices) and capability (Amartya Sen; building health, education and access to resources).
focus: Matching each approach to its idea and originator
The six basic needs
How the welfare approach treats people
remember: Income approach: one of the oldest; income reflects freedom
Welfare approach: people as beneficiaries; more government spending on education, health, social security, amenities
Basic needs approach (ILO): health, education, food, water supply, sanitation, housing; ignores choices
Capability approach: Amartya Sen; build capabilities in health, education, access to resources
traps: Don't link Sen with the income approach — his is the capability approach
Electricity is not one of the six basic needs

topics.h: One number between 0 and 1 that sums up a nation's health, learning and living standard. That's the HDI.
p: The Human Development Index (HDI) ranks countries based on their performance in health, education and access to resources; scores range from 0 to 1 — the closer to 1, the higher the human development.
Health indicator: life expectancy at birth — a longer life expectancy means a greater chance of a long and healthy life.
Education indicator: earlier, adult literacy rate and gross enrolment ratio; now measured by mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling.
Access to resources: measured in terms of purchasing power (in US dollars), i.e. GNI per capita (PPP).
Each dimension gets a weightage of 1/3; in NCERT's simple description, the HDI is the sum of the weights assigned to all three dimensions.

ex.q: Using NCERT's equal weightage of 1/3, find the HDI if the health index is 0.90, education index 0.70 and income index 0.80.

topics.rl: In UNDP's Human Development Report, India falls in the medium human development category; improving life expectancy and schooling years helps push its score up.

rv.summary: The HDI ranks countries on health (life expectancy at birth), education (mean and expected years of schooling) and access to resources (purchasing power in US dollars). Each gets a weight of 1/3, and the score runs from 0 to 1 — closer to 1 means higher development.
focus: The three dimensions and their indicators
Calculating HDI with equal 1/3 weights
Comparing countries by HDI score
remember: HDI score ranges from 0 to 1; closer to 1 = higher human development
Health: life expectancy at birth; education: mean and expected years of schooling
Access to resources: purchasing power in US dollars (GNI per capita, PPP)
Each dimension gets a weightage of 1/3
traps: Don't add the three indices without dividing by 3
HDI is not a percentage out of 100

topics.t: Human Poverty Index and Gross National Happiness
topics.h: HDI tells you how far a country has come. Another index asks: how many are still left behind? And Bhutan asks: are people happy?
p: HDI measures attainment (what has been achieved); the Human Poverty Index (HPI) measures shortfall (what is still lacking).
HPI is a non-income measure using: probability of not surviving till age 40, adult illiteracy rate, number of people without access to clean water, and number of small children who are underweight.
Gross National Happiness (GNH): Bhutan officially measures progress by happiness; it stresses spiritual, non-material and qualitative aspects of well-being.
These measures remind us that development is more than income — material progress should not come at the cost of the environment, culture or spiritual life.

ex.q: Two countries have the same HDI. Country A has 30% underweight children; B has 10%. Which index would show the difference, and how?
st: HDI shows the same attainment for both.
HPI includes underweight children, a shortfall measure.
A would show higher human poverty.
ex.a: The HPI would show greater shortfall (poverty) in Country A

topics.rl: Bhutan's Gross National Happiness approach inspired discussions in India on measuring well-being beyond GDP, including environmental and cultural indicators.

rv.summary: HDI measures attainment; the Human Poverty Index measures shortfall using non-income indicators. Bhutan's Gross National Happiness stresses spiritual, non-material and qualitative well-being, reminding us development is more than income.
focus: HDI (attainment) vs HPI (shortfall)
The four HPI indicators
Gross National Happiness and Bhutan
remember: HPI indicators: probability of not surviving till 40, adult illiteracy rate, people without clean water, small children underweight
HPI is a non-income measure
Bhutan officially measures progress by Gross National Happiness
traps: Don't reverse them: HDI = attainment, HPI = shortfall
Life expectancy at birth is an HDI indicator, not an HPI one

topics.h: Sri Lanka ranks above India in human development though its economy is far smaller. Size isn't everything!
p: Size of territory and per capita income are not directly related to human development; small countries often do better than large ones, and relatively poorer nations can rank higher than richer neighbours.
Countries are grouped by HDI score: very high (0.800 and above), high (0.700–0.799), medium (0.550–0.699) and low (below 0.550).
Very high and high HDI countries invest more in the social sector and are generally free of political turmoil; examples include Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Australia.
Medium HDI countries mostly emerged after the colonial period (after World War II); many are trying to become more people-oriented; India is in this group.
Low HDI countries are mostly small countries going through political turmoil and social instability — civil war, famine or high incidence of diseases; many are in sub-Saharan Africa.

ex.q: Classify countries with HDI scores 0.91, 0.74, 0.63 and 0.48.
st: 0.91 ≥ 0.800 → very high.
ex.a: Very high, high, medium, low

topics.rl: India's improvement in life expectancy and schooling has steadily raised its HDI, but it remains in the medium category, behind neighbours like Sri Lanka.

rv.summary: Size and per capita income are not directly related to human development. Countries are grouped as very high (0.800+), high (0.700–0.799), medium (0.550–0.699) and low (below 0.550); India is medium, and low HDI countries often face turmoil, many in sub-Saharan Africa.
focus: Placing an HDI score in the right category
Features of very high, medium and low HDI groups
Why size and income do not decide human development
remember: India is in the medium HDI group
Low HDI: political turmoil, civil war, famine, disease; many in sub-Saharan Africa
traps: Don't round 0.77 up to very high — it is high
Bigger or richer countries do not always have higher HDI

topics.t: Governance, HDI maps and exam practice
topics.h: Why do some poorer countries beat richer ones in HDI? Look at how they spend and how they govern.
p: Good governance and higher spending on the social sector (education, health, water, sanitation) raise human development faster than income growth alone.
A world map of HDI shows very high HDI in North America, Europe, Australia, New Zealand and Japan; low HDI concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa.
Tables of the top and bottom countries help compare: European nations dominate the top, while several African countries fill the bottom ranks.
Exam focus: pillars and approaches (MCQs), growth vs development, the four pillars, key areas of human development, and HDI categories with their characteristics.

ex.q: Two states have equal income per head. State A spends 30% of its budget on health and education; state B spends 12%. Which will likely have higher human development, and why?
st: Income is equal, so the difference comes from spending.
A invests more in the social sector.
Better health and education raise HDI indicators.
ex.a: State A, because of greater social sector investment

topics.rl: Kerala, with moderate per capita income but high spending on health and schooling, has long topped Indian states in human development.

rv.summary: Good governance and higher social-sector spending raise human development faster than income growth alone. Very high HDI is found in North America, Europe, Australia, New Zealand and Japan, while low HDI is concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa.
focus: World pattern of HDI on a map
Why social spending and governance raise HDI
Revising pillars, approaches and the growth–development distinction
remember: Very high HDI: North America, Europe, Australia, New Zealand, Japan
Low HDI concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa
Key areas of human development: health, education, access to resources
traps: Large area or population does not raise HDI
Don't assume every Asian country is medium — Japan is very high

topics.h: A coal miner in Jharia, a fisherwoman in Kerala and a wheat farmer in Punjab share one thing: they earn directly from the earth.
p: Human economic activities are grouped as primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary and quinary.

Primary activities depend directly on the environment and use earth's resources like land, water, vegetation, building materials and minerals: hunting, gathering, pastoral activities, fishing, forestry, agriculture, and mining and quarrying.
People engaged in primary activities are called red-collar workers because of the outdoor nature of their work.
As an economy develops, the share of its workforce in primary activities falls and more people move to secondary and tertiary work.

ex.q: Classify: (a) a quarry worker in Rajasthan, (b) a textile mill worker in Surat, (c) a bank clerk in Kolkata.
st: (a) Quarrying uses earth's resources directly → primary.
(b) Turning cotton into cloth → secondary.
(c) Providing a service → tertiary.
ex.a: (a) primary, (b) secondary, (c) tertiary

topics.rl: Over 40% of India's workforce is still in agriculture (PLFS), while in the USA it is under 2% — a clear sign of different development levels.

rv.summary: Economic activities are primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary and quinary. Primary activities depend directly on the environment — hunting, gathering, pastoralism, fishing, forestry, agriculture, mining — and their workers are called red-collar workers; their share falls as an economy develops.
focus: Identifying primary activities and separating them from secondary and tertiary
Why primary workers are called red-collar workers
How the share of primary workers changes with development
remember: Primary activities use earth's resources directly: land, water, vegetation, building materials, minerals
Primary: hunting, gathering, pastoral activities, fishing, forestry, agriculture, mining and quarrying
Red-collar workers = primary workers, named for their outdoor work
traps: Manufacturing is not primary — it transforms raw materials (secondary)
Developed economies do not have most workers in primary activities

topics.h: Ever chewed gum? Its original base, chicle, was gathered from the sap of the Zapota tree in Central America.
p: The earliest humans depended on their immediate environment for food, shelter and clothing; hunting and gathering are the oldest economic activities.
Early hunters used primitive tools made of stones, twigs or arrows; people near coasts also fished.

Gathering is practised in high latitudes (northern Canada, northern Eurasia, southern Chile) and low latitudes (Amazon basin, tropical Africa, northern fringe of Australia and interior parts of South-east Asia).

Modern gathering is market-oriented: bark for quinine, tannin extract and cork; leaves for beverages, drugs and cosmetics; fibres for thatch and cloth; nuts for food and oils; tree trunks for rubber, balata, gums and resins. Chicle from Zapota tree milk makes chewing gum.
Gathering needs little capital and low technology; yield per person is very low and little or no surplus is produced.

ex.q: Why is gathering unlikely to be important in the global economy?
st: It uses very low technology and little capital.
Yield per person is low and there is hardly any surplus to sell.
Synthetic substitutes of better quality and lower price have replaced many gathered products.
ex.a: Low yield, no surplus and competition from synthetic products

topics.rl: Tribal communities in Jharkhand and Odisha collect tendu leaves, mahua and sal seeds; cooperatives like TRIFED help them sell these forest products.

rv.summary: Hunting and gathering are the oldest economic activities, using primitive tools and the immediate environment. Gathering survives in high and low latitudes, and modern gathering is partly market-oriented, but low yield, no surplus and synthetic substitutes limit it.
focus: High-latitude and low-latitude gathering zones
Plant parts gathered and their products (bark, leaves, fibres, nuts, trunks)
Features of gathering and why it is declining globally
remember: High latitudes: northern Canada, northern Eurasia, southern Chile
Low latitudes: Amazon basin, tropical Africa, northern Australia, interior South-east Asia
Bark → quinine, tannin, cork; chicle from Zapota tree milk → chewing gum
traps: Gathering does not produce a large surplus — yield per person is low
Modern gathering is not purely for self-use; it is partly market-oriented

topics.h: Every summer, Gaddi shepherds in Himachal drive thousands of sheep up to high meadows; every winter they bring them down. This ancient rhythm has a name — transhumance.
p: After hunting, people learned to domesticate animals; pastoralism may be subsistence (nomadic herding) or commercial (livestock rearing).

Nomadic herding or pastoral nomadism is a primitive subsistence activity: herders depend on animals for food, clothing, shelter, tools and transport, moving with their livestock for pasture and water.
Animals vary by region: cattle in tropical Africa; sheep, goats and camels in the Sahara and Asiatic deserts; yak in Tibet; llamas in the Andes; reindeer in the Arctic and sub-Arctic.

Three main regions: (1) the core region from the Atlantic shores of North Africa eastwards across the Arabian peninsula into Mongolia and Central China; (2) the tundra region of Eurasia; (3) South-west Africa and the island of Madagascar.

Transhumance: seasonal migration from plains to mountain pastures in summer and back to the plains in winter — e.g. Gujjars, Bakarwals, Gaddis and Bhotiyas in the Himalayas. Pastoral nomadism is declining due to political boundaries and new settlement plans.

ex.q: A Bakarwal family in Jammu moves its goats to the high pastures of Kashmir in April and returns in October. Explain the movement.
st: Summer: plains get hot and dry; mountain pastures are green → move up.
Winter: mountains get snow-covered → move down.
This seasonal vertical movement is transhumance.
ex.a: Transhumance (seasonal vertical migration)

topics.rl: Raika camel herders of Rajasthan and Gaddi shepherds of Himachal still practise pastoralism, though grazing land is shrinking.

rv.summary: Pastoralism may be subsistence (nomadic herding) or commercial. Nomads depend on animals for almost all needs and move for pasture and water in three main regions; transhumance is seasonal movement up to mountain pastures in summer and down in winter.
focus: Matching herded animals to regions
The three main regions of nomadic herding
Transhumance and Himalayan communities; causes of decline
remember: Cattle — tropical Africa; sheep, goats, camels — Sahara and Asiatic deserts; yak — Tibet; llama — Andes; reindeer — Arctic and sub-Arctic
Regions: North Africa to Mongolia and Central China; tundra of Eurasia; South-west Africa and Madagascar
Transhumance: Gujjars, Bakarwals, Gaddis, Bhotiyas — up in summer, down in winter
traps: Don't swap llama (Andes) and yak (Tibet)
Don't reverse the seasons: herders go up to the mountains in summer, not winter

topics.h: New Zealand has about five sheep for every person! Its fenced ranches export wool and meat worldwide.
p: Commercial livestock rearing is more organised and capital intensive than nomadic herding; it is associated with western cultures and practised on permanent ranches.

Ranches cover large areas divided into parcels fenced to regulate grazing; when one parcel is grazed, animals move to another (rotational grazing). The number of animals is kept within the pasture's carrying capacity.
It is a specialised activity rearing one type of animal — sheep, cattle, goats or horses; meat, wool, hides and skin are processed and packed scientifically and exported to world markets.
Emphasis on breeding, genetic improvement, disease control and health care.
Important countries: New Zealand, Australia, Argentina, Uruguay and the USA.

ex.q: Give three differences between nomadic herding and commercial livestock rearing.
st: Nomadic: subsistence, moving herds; commercial: market-oriented, permanent ranches.
Nomadic: many types of animals kept; commercial: one type of animal (specialised).
Nomadic: little capital or science; commercial: capital intensive with scientific breeding and disease control.
ex.a: Subsistence vs commercial; mixed vs single animal; low vs high capital and science

topics.rl: India's dairy and poultry giants use scientific breeding and veterinary care, borrowing practices from commercial livestock rearing.

rv.summary: Commercial livestock rearing is organised, capital intensive and practised on permanent fenced ranches with rotational grazing. It specialises in one animal, uses scientific breeding and exports processed products; key countries include New Zealand, Australia and Argentina.
focus: Features of commercial livestock rearing
Differences from nomadic herding
Main countries of commercial ranching
remember: Permanent ranches divided into fenced parcels for rotational grazing within carrying capacity
Specialised: one type of animal — sheep, cattle, goats or horses
Countries: New Zealand, Australia, Argentina, Uruguay, USA
traps: Mongolia is a nomadic herding area, not a commercial ranching country
Commercial rearing is not a subsistence activity — it serves world markets

topics.h: In Mizoram's hills, smoke rises from burning forest patches in March. It's not a wildfire — it's jhum cultivation.
p: Agriculture is practised under many combinations of physical and socio-economic conditions, giving different farming systems.
Subsistence agriculture: the farming area consumes all, or nearly all, of the produce grown locally. It has two types: primitive and intensive.
Primitive subsistence agriculture or shifting cultivation is practised by many tribes in the tropics, especially in Africa, South and Central America and South-east Asia.

Vegetation is cleared by fire and ashes add to soil fertility (slash and burn); patches are small and tools primitive (sticks, hoes); after 3 to 5 years the soil loses fertility and the farmer shifts. The jhum cycle shortens as fertility falls and population grows.
Regional names: Jhuming in north-eastern India, Milpa in Central America and Mexico, Ladang in Indonesia and Malaysia.

ex.q: A farmer clears a hill patch by fire, grows rice and maize for 4 years, then moves to a new patch. What are the advantages and problems?
st: Advantage: ash fertilises soil, little capital needed.
Problem: soil loses fertility after 3–5 years.
Problem: as population grows, fallow periods shorten, causing deforestation and soil erosion.
ex.a: Cheap and simple, but leads to short fallow cycles, deforestation and soil erosion

topics.rl: Nagaland and Meghalaya still have large areas under jhum; schemes promote settled terrace farming and agroforestry as alternatives.

rv.summary: In subsistence agriculture farmers consume nearly all their produce. Primitive subsistence or shifting cultivation (slash and burn) is practised by tropical tribes: forest is cleared by fire, small plots are farmed for 3–5 years, then abandoned; the cycle is shortening.
focus: The slash-and-burn process and why plots are abandoned
Regional names of shifting cultivation
Why the jhum cycle is getting shorter
remember: Jhuming — north-eastern India; Milpa — Central America and Mexico; Ladang — Indonesia and Malaysia
Ashes add to soil fertility; soil loses fertility after 3 to 5 years
Practised in tropical Africa, South and Central America, South-east Asia
traps: Don't mix the regional names — Ladang is Indonesia/Malaysia, Milpa is Mexico
Shifting cultivators use primitive tools like sticks and hoes, not machinery
