Grierson's figures and scheduled languages
Spatial distribution of religious groups
remember: Grierson: 179 languages, 544 dialects; 22 scheduled languages
Austric = Nishada (Munda, Mon-Khmer); Dravidian = Dravida; Sino-Tibetan = Kirata; Indo-European = Aryan
Sikhs: Punjab, Haryana, Delhi; Muslims majority in Kashmir valley and Lakshadweep
traps: Don't confuse 179 languages with 544 dialects
Munda languages are Austric, not Dravidian

topics.ch: India: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
topics.t: Working population: main, marginal and non-workers
topics.h: Only about 4 in 10 Indians worked in 2011. Who are the workers, and what do they do?
p: The Census divides population into main workers (work for at least 183 days, about six months, in a year), marginal workers (work for less than 183 days) and non-workers.
Work participation rate (main + marginal workers as a share of population) was about 39.8 per cent in 2011, leaving about 60 per cent as non-workers — a high dependency ratio.
Work participation tends to be higher in economically less developed states, where many manual workers are needed for subsistence activities.

Census occupational categories: cultivators, agricultural labourers, household industrial workers, and other workers (non-household industries, trade, commerce, construction, repair and other services).
About 54.6 per cent of all workers are cultivators and agricultural labourers; about 3.8 per cent are in household industries and about 41.6 per cent are other workers.

ex.q: A villager works on a construction site for 120 days a year and is otherwise unemployed. Is she a main or marginal worker?
st: Main workers work at least 183 days a year.
120 days < 183 days.
So she is a marginal worker.
ex.a: Marginal worker

topics.rl: MGNREGA guarantees 100 days of wage work a year to rural households — such work alone would still classify a person as a marginal worker in Census terms.

rv.summary: The Census classes people as main workers (at least 183 days a year), marginal workers (less than 183 days) and non-workers. Work participation was about 39.8% in 2011; about 54.6% of workers are cultivators and agricultural labourers, 3.8% in household industries and 41.6% other workers.
focus: Main, marginal and non-workers
Work participation rate and dependency
The four occupational categories and their shares
remember: Main worker ≥ 183 days a year; marginal < 183 days
Work participation rate 2011 ≈ 39.8%; ~60% non-workers
Cultivators + agricultural labourers ≈ 54.6%; household industry ≈ 3.8%; other workers ≈ 41.6%
traps: Household industries do not employ the largest share — agriculture does
100 days of work makes a person marginal, not main

topics.ch: India: Population: Distribution, Density, Growth and Composition
topics.t: Occupational composition: gender and regional patterns
topics.h: In Nagaland most workers own and till their land; in Andhra Pradesh many work on others' fields; in Delhi most work in services.
p: Male workers outnumber female workers in all three sectors (primary, secondary, tertiary).
The number of female workers is relatively high in the primary sector, though women's participation in secondary and tertiary sectors has been improving.
Himachal Pradesh and Nagaland have a very large share of cultivators.
Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal and Madhya Pradesh have a higher proportion of agricultural labourers.

Highly urbanised areas like Delhi, Chandigarh and Puducherry have a very large proportion of workers in 'other services'. Exam focus: census, density types, growth phases, regional variation, adolescents, occupational composition and map work.

ex.q: Why does Delhi have a much higher share of 'other workers' than Nagaland?
st: Delhi is highly urbanised with trade, offices, industry and services.
Nagaland is rural and hilly; most workers are cultivators.
So Delhi's workers are mainly in secondary and tertiary jobs.
ex.a: Urbanisation in Delhi creates service and industrial jobs

topics.rl: Self-help groups and the rise of women in IT, banking and healthcare are slowly raising female work participation outside agriculture.

rv.summary: Male workers outnumber female workers in all sectors; women are relatively more in the primary sector, though their share in secondary and tertiary work is improving. Himachal Pradesh and Nagaland have many cultivators and Delhi many 'other workers'.
focus: Gender pattern of workers by sector
States with many cultivators vs many agricultural labourers
Urbanised areas and 'other workers'
remember: Males outnumber females in all three sectors; females relatively high in primary sector
Many cultivators: Himachal Pradesh, Nagaland; many labourers: Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Jharkhand, West Bengal, MP
Many 'other workers': Delhi, Chandigarh, Puducherry
traps: Women's participation in secondary and tertiary sectors is improving, not declining
Don't put Delhi among cultivator states

topics.h: A tiny dhani in the Thar with five huts and Greater Mumbai with 1.8 crore people are both 'settlements'. What makes them so different?
p: A human settlement is a cluster of dwellings of any type or size where human beings live; settlements may be temporary or permanent.
Settlements range from hamlets to metropolitan cities; as size grows, their economic character and social structure change.
Rural settlements are smaller and sparsely located; most people are engaged in primary activities like agriculture, fishing and forestry; they supply food and raw materials.
Urban settlements are generally compact and larger; people are engaged in non-primary (secondary and tertiary) activities.

Rural people are less mobile and have intimate social relations; urban life is complex and fast with formal social relations; cities act as nodes of economic growth, providing goods and services to towns and villages.

ex.q: List three differences between a village in Punjab and the city of Ludhiana.
st: Size: village is small and sparse; Ludhiana is large and compact.
Work: village mainly farming; city mainly industry, trade and services.
Social life: intimate relations in the village; formal relations in the city.
ex.a: Size, main activities and nature of social relations differ

topics.rl: Bengaluru draws software engineers from across India while villages around it supply milk, vegetables and flowers — the rural-urban link.

rv.summary: A settlement is any cluster of dwellings where people live, temporary or permanent. Rural settlements are small and sparse with mainly primary work; urban ones are compact and larger with secondary and tertiary work, formal social relations and links to villages.
focus: Rural vs urban settlements: size, work, social life
How settlements change with size
Rural–urban linkages
remember: Settlement = cluster of dwellings of any type or size where people live
Rural: small, sparse, primary activities; supply food and raw materials
Urban: compact, larger, non-primary activities; formal relations; nodes of economic growth
traps: Cities do depend on villages — the two are linked
Urban social relations are formal, not intimate

topics.t: Rural settlement types: factors and clustered settlements
topics.h: In the Ganga plains, village houses huddle together around a pond and a temple; in the Meghalaya hills, huts are scattered on slopes. Why?
p: Types of rural settlement are determined by the extent of the built-up area and the inter-house distance.
Factors: physical — nature of terrain, altitude, climate and availability of water; cultural and ethnic — social structure, caste and religion; security — defence against thefts and robberies.
Four types: clustered (agglomerated or nucleated), semi-clustered (fragmented), hamleted, and dispersed (isolated).

Clustered settlements: compact, closely built-up houses; the living area is distinct and separated from surrounding farms, barns and pastures; streets may form rectangular, radial or linear patterns. Common in fertile alluvial plains and the north-eastern states.

People may live in compact villages for security, as in the Bundelkhand region of central India and in Nagaland; in Rajasthan, scarcity of water has made compact settlements necessary to make maximum use of available water.

ex.q: Why are villages in western Rajasthan often clustered around a single water source?
st: Water is very scarce in the desert.
Living close together helps share and make maximum use of the available water.
So scarcity of water leads to compact (clustered) settlements.
ex.a: Scarcity of water forces compact settlements

topics.rl: Many Bundelkhand villages grew compact around forts and tanks for protection — a security factor shaping settlement.

rv.summary: Rural settlement types depend on the built-up area and inter-house distance, shaped by physical, cultural-ethnic and security factors. The four types are clustered, semi-clustered, hamleted and dispersed; clustered villages are compact and common in fertile plains.
focus: Factors deciding rural settlement types
Features and regions of clustered settlements
Security and water scarcity as causes of compact villages
remember: Types: clustered (agglomerated/nucleated), semi-clustered (fragmented), hamleted, dispersed (isolated)
Factors: physical (terrain, altitude, climate, water); cultural-ethnic (social structure, caste, religion); security
Compact for security: Bundelkhand, Nagaland; for water: Rajasthan
traps: Clustered villages can show rectangular, radial or linear patterns
Caste and religion are cultural factors, not physical ones

topics.h: In parts of Uttar Pradesh a single village is split into small 'nagla's; in Rajasthan's desert they're 'dhani's. Same village name, separate clusters!
p: Semi-clustered or fragmented settlements may result from a tendency of clustering in a restricted area of dispersed settlement, or from fragmentation of a large compact village where one or more sections live a little away from the main cluster. Such settlements are widespread in the Gujarat plain and some parts of Rajasthan.
In such villages, NCERT notes that the land-owning, dominant community often occupies the central part while other groups settle on the outer flanks — a pattern shaped by social history.

Hamleted settlements: a settlement fragmented into several units physically separated from each other but bearing a common name; locally called panna, para, palli, nagla, dhani etc. Often motivated by social and ethnic factors; found in the middle and lower Ganga plain, Chhattisgarh and lower valleys of the Himalayas.

Dispersed or isolated settlements: isolated huts or hamlets of a few huts in remote jungles or on small hills with farms or pastures on slopes; extreme dispersion is caused by the extremely fragmented terrain and land resource base. Found in many areas of Meghalaya, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Kerala.
Activity: on a picture or map, compact blocks = clustered; a main cluster with a detached part = semi-clustered; several separate units with one name = hamleted; scattered single huts = dispersed.

ex.q: A map shows one large cluster of houses with a smaller group of houses some distance away on the edge. Which type is this?
st: Not fully compact (so not clustered).
Not many separate units with one name (so not hamleted).
One main cluster with a fragment away from it → semi-clustered (fragmented).
ex.a: Semi-clustered (fragmented) settlement

topics.rl: Kerala's houses are spread along roads and among coconut groves rather than clustered — a classic dispersed pattern linked to its terrain and land use.

rv.summary: Semi-clustered villages have a main cluster with a part a little away (Gujarat plain, parts of Rajasthan). Hamleted villages are separate units with one name — panna, para, palli, nagla, dhani — often for social reasons. Dispersed settlements are isolated huts on fragmented terrain.
focus: Identifying semi-clustered, hamleted and dispersed settlements
Regions of each type
Causes: social-ethnic factors vs fragmented terrain
remember: Semi-clustered: Gujarat plain, parts of Rajasthan
Hamleted: units with a common name; middle and lower Ganga plain, Chhattisgarh, lower Himalayan valleys
Dispersed: fragmented terrain; Meghalaya, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Kerala
traps: Hamlets share one village name, not different names
Don't put dispersed settlements in flat plains

topics.t: Urban settlements and the Census definition of urban
topics.h: Is a place with 6,000 people a town? Only if it passes three Census tests!
p: Urban centres are generally compact and larger, with a variety of non-agricultural economic and administrative functions.
Cities are functionally linked to rural areas around them: they exchange goods and services, either directly or through a series of market towns and cities.

Census definition of an urban place: (a) all places with a municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee; or (b) all other places satisfying all three criteria — a minimum population of 5,000, at least 75 per cent of the male main working population in non-agricultural pursuits, and a density of at least 400 persons per sq km.
Places meeting criterion (b) without a municipal body are called census towns.

ex.q: A place has 7,000 people, an area of 20 sq km, and 80% of male main workers in non-farm jobs. It has no municipality. Is it urban by the Census?
st: Population 7,000 ≥ 5,000 ✓.
Density = 7,000 ÷ 20 = 350 per sq km — less than 400 ✗.
Male non-farm workers 80% ≥ 75% ✓.
One criterion fails, so it is not urban.
ex.a: No — its density (350) is below 400 per sq km

topics.rl: Census 2011 recorded about 3,894 census towns — places that met urban criteria without a municipal body, showing 'hidden' urbanisation.

rv.summary: By the Census, a place is urban if it has a municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee, or if it meets all three tests: at least 5,000 people, at least 75% of male main workers in non-farm work, and density of at least 400 per sq km.
focus: The two parts of the Census definition of urban
Applying all three criteria to a place
Census towns
remember: Automatically urban: municipality, corporation, cantonment board, notified town area committee
Otherwise all three: population ≥ 5,000; ≥ 75% male main workers non-agricultural; density ≥ 400 per sq km
Places meeting the three tests without a municipal body = census towns
traps: Two out of three criteria are not enough — all three must be met
The density threshold is 400, not India's average of 382

topics.t: Evolution of towns: prehistoric, ancient and medieval
topics.h: Varanasi is often called one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. India's urban story is over 4,500 years old!
p: Towns flourished in India since prehistoric times — Harappa and Mohenjodaro of the Indus Valley civilisation are examples.
Ancient towns: about 45 towns over 2,000 years old; most developed as religious and cultural centres — e.g. Varanasi, Prayag (Allahabad, now Prayagraj), Pataliputra (Patna) and Madurai.
Medieval towns: about 100 of today's towns have roots in the medieval period; most developed as headquarters of principalities and kingdoms.
Many medieval towns are fort towns built on the ruins of ancient towns — e.g. Delhi, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Lucknow, Agra and Nagpur.

ex.q: Classify: Madurai, Jaipur, Mohenjodaro, Pataliputra, Lucknow.
st: Prehistoric: Mohenjodaro.
Ancient: Madurai, Pataliputra (religious/cultural or capital centres over 2,000 years old).
Medieval: Jaipur, Lucknow (kingdom headquarters, fort towns).
ex.a: Prehistoric: Mohenjodaro; ancient: Madurai, Pataliputra; medieval: Jaipur, Lucknow

topics.rl: Patna, built over ancient Pataliputra, shows how Indian cities keep growing on old foundations.

rv.summary: Indian towns go back to prehistoric Harappa and Mohenjodaro. About 45 ancient towns over 2,000 years old grew as religious and cultural centres (Varanasi, Prayag, Pataliputra, Madurai); about 100 medieval towns grew as kingdom headquarters, many as fort towns (Delhi, Jaipur, Lucknow, Agra).
focus: Prehistoric, ancient and medieval towns with examples
Main function of ancient vs medieval towns
Ancient names of modern cities
remember: Prehistoric: Harappa, Mohenjodaro
Ancient (about 45, over 2,000 years): Varanasi, Prayag, Pataliputra (Patna), Madurai — religious/cultural
Medieval (about 100): headquarters of kingdoms; fort towns — Delhi, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Lucknow, Agra, Nagpur
traps: Jaipur and Lucknow are medieval, not prehistoric
Ancient towns were not industrial centres

topics.h: Chandigarh was designed from scratch by Le Corbusier after 1947. Gurugram grew from fields into glass towers within decades. Modern India builds new towns!
p: Modern towns: the British and other Europeans developed towns, starting with trading ports — Surat, Daman, Goa, Pondicherry (Puducherry).
The British later consolidated their hold around three nodes — Mumbai (Bombay), Chennai (Madras) and Kolkata (Calcutta) — built in western style.
They introduced administrative centres, hill towns as summer resorts, and added civil, administrative and military areas to towns.
After 1850, towns based on modern industries also developed, e.g. Jamshedpur.

After Independence: new administrative headquarters (Chandigarh, Bhubaneswar, Gandhinagar, Dispur), industrial centres (Durgapur, Bhilai, Sindri, Barauni), and satellite towns around metropolitan cities (Ghaziabad, Rohtak, Gurugram around Delhi).

ex.q: Classify these post-independence towns: Bhilai, Gandhinagar, Ghaziabad, Bhubaneswar.
st: Bhilai → industrial centre (steel).
Gandhinagar, Bhubaneswar → administrative headquarters (state capitals).
Ghaziabad → satellite town of Delhi.
ex.a: Bhilai: industrial; Gandhinagar, Bhubaneswar: administrative; Ghaziabad: satellite

topics.rl: Shimla, Darjeeling and Ooty grew as British hill resorts; today they are major tourist towns.

rv.summary: Europeans began modern towns as trading ports (Surat, Daman, Goa, Pondicherry); the British built Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata, administrative centres and hill resorts, and industrial towns like Jamshedpur came after 1850. After 1947 came new capitals, industrial centres and satellite towns.
focus: European and British contributions to towns
Post-independence administrative, industrial and satellite towns
Classifying a modern town by origin
remember: European trading ports: Surat, Daman, Goa, Pondicherry; British nodes: Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata
Post-1947 capitals: Chandigarh, Bhubaneswar, Gandhinagar, Dispur
Industrial: Durgapur, Bhilai, Sindri, Barauni; satellite towns of Delhi: Ghaziabad, Rohtak, Gurugram
traps: Satellite towns grew around metropolitan cities, not villages
Fort towns of Rajput kings are medieval, not British

topics.t: Urbanisation in India: level and trends
topics.h: In 1901, only about 1 in 10 Indians lived in towns. By 2011, it was about 1 in 3.
p: The level of urbanisation is measured as the percentage of urban population to total population.
Urbanisation in India was 31.16 per cent in 2011 — low compared with developed countries.
The urban population increased eleven-fold during the twentieth century, through enlargement of urban centres and emergence of new towns.
The growth rate of urbanisation has slowed down during the last two decades.

ex.q: By how many percentage points did India's level of urbanisation rise from 1901 (10.84%) to 2011 (31.16%)?
st: = 20.32 percentage points.
ex.a: 20.32 percentage points

topics.rl: States like Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Maharashtra are far more urbanised than Bihar or Himachal Pradesh, showing big regional differences.

rv.summary: The level of urbanisation is the percentage of urban population to total population. India's rose from 10.84% in 1901 to 31.16% in 2011 — still low compared with developed countries. Urban population grew eleven-fold in the 20th century, but its growth rate has slowed recently.
focus: Meaning of level of urbanisation
Urbanisation figures for 1901, 2001 and 2011
Causes of urban growth and its recent slowdown
remember: Level of urbanisation = urban population ÷ total population × 100
Urban population grew eleven-fold in the 20th century
traps: The growth rate of urbanisation has slowed, not accelerated
Don't confuse the 2011 urban share (31.16%) with the rural share (68.8%)

topics.t: Size classes, urban agglomerations, mega cities and Smart Cities
topics.h: Greater Mumbai had about 1.84 crore people in 2011 — more than many countries. It is India's largest urban agglomeration.
p: The Census classifies urban centres into six classes by population size; Class I towns have a population of one lakh (1,00,000) or more.
Cities with a population between 1 and 5 million are called metropolitan cities; those with more than 5 million are mega cities.

An urban agglomeration (UA) may consist of: (i) a town and its adjoining urban outgrowths (like railway colonies, university campuses, port areas, cantonments); (ii) two or more contiguous towns with or without outgrowths; or (iii) a city and one or more adjoining towns with their outgrowths forming a contiguous spread.
Most metropolitan and mega cities are urban agglomerations. Greater Mumbai is the largest UA (about 18.4 million in 2011), followed by Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Bengaluru.
Smart Cities Mission: promotes cities that provide core infrastructure, a decent quality of life, a clean and sustainable environment and application of 'smart solutions'.

ex.q: Classify: a city of 3.5 million, a city of 7 million, and a town of 2.5 lakh.
st: 3.5 million is between 1 and 5 million → metropolitan city.
7 million > 5 million → mega city.
2.5 lakh ≥ 1 lakh → Class I town.
ex.a: Metropolitan; mega city; Class I town

topics.rl: Under the Smart Cities Mission, 100 cities such as Pune, Surat and Bhubaneswar developed command centres, smart roads and better public spaces.

rv.summary: The Census groups urban centres into six classes; Class I towns have one lakh or more people. Cities of 1–5 million are metropolitan and above 5 million are mega cities. Urban agglomerations join towns and outgrowths; Greater Mumbai (about 18.4 million) is the largest.
focus: Class I, metropolitan and mega city thresholds
Three forms of an urban agglomeration
Largest UAs and the Smart Cities Mission
remember: Six size classes; Class I ≥ 1,00,000
Metropolitan: 1–5 million; mega city: more than 5 million
UA: town + outgrowths, contiguous towns, or city + adjoining towns; Greater Mumbai largest (~18.4 million)
traps: Don't swap metropolitan (1–5 million) and mega (above 5 million)
Class I starts at one lakh, not at 5,000 (the urban threshold)

topics.h: Shillong runs a state, Jamshedpur makes steel, Itarsi switches trains, Saharanpur trades wood. Every town has a 'main job'.
p: Towns are classified on the basis of their dominant or specialised functions.
Administrative towns and cities: support administrative headquarters of higher order — Chandigarh, New Delhi, Bhopal, Shillong, Guwahati, Imphal, Srinagar, Gandhinagar, Jaipur, Chennai.
Industrial towns: industries are the prime motive force — Mumbai, Salem, Coimbatore, Modinagar, Jamshedpur, Hugli, Bhilai.

Transport cities: ports engaged mainly in export and import — Kandla, Kochi, Kozhikode, Visakhapatnam; or hubs of inland transport — Agra, Dhulia, Mughal Sarai (now Pt. Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Junction), Itarsi, Katni.
Commercial towns: specialise in trade and commerce — Kolkata, Saharanpur, Satna.

ex.q: Classify: Itarsi, Bhopal, Coimbatore, Kandla, Satna.
st: Itarsi — inland transport hub (rail junction).
Bhopal — administrative (state capital).
Coimbatore — industrial.
Kandla — transport (port).
Satna — commercial.
ex.a: Itarsi: transport; Bhopal: administrative; Coimbatore: industrial; Kandla: transport (port); Satna: commercial

topics.rl: Coimbatore's textile and pump industries earned it the nickname 'Manchester of South India' — a classic industrial town.

rv.summary: Towns are classed by their dominant function: administrative (Chandigarh, Bhopal, Shillong), industrial (Mumbai, Salem, Coimbatore, Modinagar, Jamshedpur, Bhilai), transport — ports like Kandla and Kochi or inland hubs like Itarsi and Katni — and commercial (Kolkata, Saharanpur, Satna).
focus: Classifying towns by dominant function
Examples of administrative, industrial, transport and commercial towns
Ports vs inland transport hubs
remember: Administrative: Chandigarh, New Delhi, Bhopal, Shillong, Guwahati, Imphal, Gandhinagar, Jaipur, Chennai
Industrial: Mumbai, Salem, Coimbatore, Modinagar, Jamshedpur, Hugli, Bhilai
Transport: ports Kandla, Kochi, Kozhikode, Visakhapatnam; inland Agra, Dhulia, Mughal Sarai, Itarsi, Katni; commercial: Kolkata, Saharanpur, Satna
traps: Agra is an inland transport hub, not a port
Not every transport city is a port

topics.h: Digboi pumped oil before most of India had cars; Mhow trains soldiers; Pilani trains engineers; Pushkar hosts a camel fair. Specialised towns everywhere!
p: Mining towns: developed in mineral-rich areas — Raniganj, Jharia, Digboi, Ankaleshwar, Singrauli.
Garrison cantonment towns: Ambala, Jalandhar, Mhow, Babina, Udhampur. Educational towns: Roorkee, Varanasi, Aligarh, Pilani, Allahabad (Prayagraj).
Religious and cultural towns: Varanasi, Mathura, Amritsar, Madurai, Puri, Ajmer, Pushkar, Tirupati, Kurukshetra, Haridwar, Ujjain.
Tourist towns: Nainital, Mussoorie, Shimla, Pachmarhi, Jodhpur, Jaisalmer, Udagamandalam (Ooty), Mount Abu.

Cities are dynamic; their functions change over time, and even specialised cities become multi-functional as they grow into metropolises (e.g. Varanasi is both religious and educational). Exam focus: settlement types, town functions, urban agglomeration and evolution of towns.

ex.q: Why does Varanasi appear in two functional categories?
st: It is a major religious and cultural centre on the Ganga.
It also has Banaras Hindu University, a major educational centre.
Large cities often become multi-functional.
ex.a: It is both religious-cultural and educational — cities are multi-functional

topics.rl: IIT Roorkee, BITS Pilani and Aligarh Muslim University make their towns famous educational centres.

rv.summary: Specialised towns include mining (Raniganj, Jharia, Digboi, Ankaleshwar, Singrauli), garrison (Ambala, Mhow, Babina, Udhampur), educational (Roorkee, Pilani), religious (Ujjain, Puri) and tourist towns (Shimla, Ooty). Cities are dynamic and become multi-functional.
focus: Examples of mining, garrison, educational, religious and tourist towns
Why cities become multi-functional
remember: Mining: Raniganj, Jharia, Digboi, Ankaleshwar, Singrauli
Garrison: Ambala, Jalandhar, Mhow, Babina, Udhampur; educational: Roorkee, Varanasi, Aligarh, Pilani, Prayagraj
Tourist: Nainital, Mussoorie, Shimla, Pachmarhi, Jodhpur, Jaisalmer, Udagamandalam (Ooty), Mount Abu
traps: Raniganj and Jharia are mining towns, not garrison towns
A city can have more than one function (e.g. Varanasi)

topics.t: Land use categories I: forests to barren land
topics.h: Every patch of India's land is recorded by the patwari in revenue records under one of nine categories. Which box does your school fall in?
p: Land is a basic resource; land-use records are maintained by the land revenue department.

Land-use categories add up to the reporting area, which differs somewhat from the geographical area; the Survey of India measures the geographical area of administrative units, while some areas are unsurveyed (some remote and disputed areas).

Revenue records classify land into nine categories: forests; land put to non-agricultural uses; barren and wastelands; permanent pastures and grazing lands; miscellaneous tree crops and groves; culturable wasteland; current fallow; fallow other than current fallow; and net area sown.
Forests: the area under actual forest cover is different from the area classified as forest — the latter is the area the Government has identified and demarcated for forest growth.

Land put to non-agricultural uses: rural and urban settlements, infrastructure (roads, canals), industries, shops etc. Barren and wastelands: land that cannot be brought under cultivation with available technology — barren hilly terrain, desert lands, ravines.

ex.q: A block has 1,000 sq km of reporting area, of which 210 sq km are demarcated as forest, 90 sq km are under roads and settlements, and 60 sq km are ravines. What percentage is under non-agricultural uses?
st: Non-agricultural uses = 90 sq km.

topics.rl: Expanding cities like Hyderabad and Pune convert farmland into 'land put to non-agricultural uses' every year.

rv.summary: Land-use records are kept by the land revenue department in nine categories; their total is the reporting area, which differs from the geographical area measured by the Survey of India. Forest means demarcated area, and barren lands cannot be cultivated with present technology.
focus: The nine land-use categories
Reporting area vs geographical area
Forest, non-agricultural uses and barren land
remember: Records: land revenue department; geographical area: Survey of India
Nine categories, from forests to net area sown
Barren and wastelands: barren hills, deserts, ravines — not cultivable with available technology
traps: Area classified as forest is not the same as actual forest cover
Barren land is not the same as culturable wasteland

topics.t: Land use categories II: pastures, fallows and net sown area
topics.h: A field left empty for one season, for three years, or for six years falls in three different land-use categories. Timing is everything!
p: Permanent pastures and grazing lands: mostly owned by the village panchayat or the government; only a small part is privately owned; land owned by the panchayat comes under 'common property resources'.
Miscellaneous tree crops and groves (not included in net sown area): land under orchards and fruit trees, mostly privately owned.
Culturable wasteland: any land left fallow (uncultivated) for more than five years; it can be brought under cultivation after improving it through reclamation practices.

Current fallow: land left without cultivation for one or less than one agricultural year; fallowing is a cultural practice to give land rest and recoup fertility. Fallow other than current fallow: cultivable land left uncultivated for more than a year but less than five years.
Net area sown: the physical extent of land on which crops are sown and harvested.

ex.q: Classify: (a) a field rested for one season; (b) a field uncultivated for 3 years; (c) a field uncultivated for 7 years but reclaimable.
st: (a) ≤ 1 agricultural year → current fallow.
(b) More than 1 but less than 5 years → fallow other than current fallow.
(c) More than 5 years → culturable wasteland.
ex.a: (a) current fallow, (b) fallow other than current fallow, (c) culturable wasteland

topics.rl: Mango orchards in Malihabad (Lucknow) are 'miscellaneous tree crops and groves', not part of net sown area.

rv.summary: Pastures are mostly panchayat or government land; orchards are tree crops and groves; current fallow is uncultivated for one year or less, other fallow for 1–5 years, and culturable wasteland for more than 5 years but reclaimable. Net area sown is the land actually cropped.
focus: Telling the three fallow categories apart by time
Pastures, groves and net area sown
Why farmers leave land fallow
remember: Current fallow: ≤ 1 agricultural year
Fallow other than current: more than 1 but less than 5 years
Culturable wasteland: fallow for more than 5 years; reclaimable
traps: Culturable wasteland can be cultivated after reclamation
Orchards are not included in net area sown

topics.h: As India's economy shifted from farms to factories and offices, its land quietly changed too. How?
p: Land use in a region is influenced by the nature of economic activities, which change over time. Changes depend on: the size of the economy, the composition of the economy, and the pressure of population.
Size of the economy: as the economy grows (more goods and services), pressure on land increases and marginal lands come under use.
Composition of the economy: over time, secondary and tertiary sectors grow faster than agriculture, so land shifts from agricultural to non-agricultural uses.
Although agriculture's share in GDP declines, pressure on agricultural land does not fall, because a large share of the population still depends on farming for its livelihood.

ex.q: Why does agricultural land stay under pressure even though agriculture's share of GDP is falling?
st: Agriculture's GDP share falls as industry and services grow.
But a large share of people still depend on farming for livelihood.
Population keeps growing, so demand for food and land stays high.
ex.a: Because dependence on agriculture and population pressure remain high

topics.rl: New expressways, airports (like Noida's Jewar airport) and industrial corridors are taking up farmland — a sign of changing economic composition.

rv.summary: Land use changes with the size of the economy, its composition and population pressure. As the economy grows, marginal lands come into use, and as industry and services grow, land shifts to non-agricultural uses; yet farmland stays under pressure because many still depend on farming.
focus: The three factors of land-use change
Shift from agricultural to non-agricultural uses
Why pressure on farmland stays high
remember: Factors: size of economy, composition of economy, pressure of population
Growing economy → more pressure on land; marginal lands used
Secondary and tertiary sectors grow faster → land moves to non-agricultural uses
traps: A falling GDP share of agriculture does not reduce pressure on farmland
Economic size does affect land use

topics.h: Between 1950–51 and 2014–15, India's land under roads, towns and factories grew fastest of all. Which categories shrank?
p: Four categories increased: forest, land under non-agricultural uses, current fallow and net area sown.
Four categories declined: barren and wasteland, culturable wasteland, area under pastures and tree crops, and fallow lands other than current fallow.

Reasons: the rate of increase is highest for non-agricultural uses due to the changing structure of the economy (industry, services), infrastructure and expansion of settlements; forest area rose mainly due to more demarcated area, not an actual increase in forest cover; current fallow fluctuates with rainfall and cropping cycles; net area sown increased recently due to use of culturable wasteland for agriculture.
Barren and wastelands declined as pressure on land brought them into use; pastures declined due to pressure from agricultural land and illegal encroachment by expanding cultivation.
In a bar graph of shares, compare the height of each category's bar in 1950–51 and 2014–15 to see increase or decline.

ex.q: Classify these as having increased or declined (1950–51 to 2014–15): forest, culturable wasteland, non-agricultural uses, permanent pastures.
st: Increased: forest (demarcation), non-agricultural uses (urbanisation, industry).
Declined: culturable wasteland (brought under farming), permanent pastures (encroachment).
ex.a: Increased: forest, non-agricultural uses; declined: culturable wasteland, pastures

topics.rl: Village grazing commons in many states have been encroached for cultivation, hurting landless herders who depended on them.

rv.summary: From 1950–51 to 2014–15, forest, non-agricultural uses, current fallow and net area sown increased, while barren land, culturable wasteland, pastures and tree crops, and other fallow declined. Non-agricultural uses grew fastest; forest rose mainly through more demarcation.
focus: Which categories increased and which declined
Reasons behind each trend
Reading a land-use bar graph
remember: Increased: forest, non-agricultural uses, current fallow, net area sown
Declined: barren and wasteland, culturable wasteland, pastures and tree crops, fallow other than current
Forest rise = more demarcated area; pastures fell by encroachment
traps: Land under non-agricultural uses has increased, not declined
The forest increase does not mean actual tree cover grew that much

topics.h: A landless family in Rajasthan grazes goats on the village oran and collects firewood from the common forest. Without these commons, they couldn't survive.
p: By ownership, land is private land (owned by an individual or group) or common property resources (CPRs), owned by the state for the use of the community.
CPRs provide fodder for livestock and fuel for households, along with minor forest products like fruits, nuts, fibre and medicinal plants.

In rural areas, CPRs are especially important for the livelihood of landless and marginal farmers and other weaker sections, who depend on income from their livestock; they are also important for women, who mostly collect fodder and fuel.

Examples: community forests, pasture lands, village water bodies and other public spaces where a group larger than a household shares rights of use and responsibility of management; every member has a right of access and use within defined rules, and the community must protect them.

ex.q: Why does loss of village pasture hurt a landless family more than a large landowner?
st: The landless family has no own land for fodder.
It depends on the common pasture for grazing livestock — its main income.
The landowner can grow his own fodder.
ex.a: The landless depend fully on CPRs for fodder and income

topics.rl: Sacred groves (orans) in Rajasthan and van panchayats in Uttarakhand are community-managed commons that protect forests and water.

rv.summary: Common property resources are owned by the state for community use — community forests, pastures, village ponds. They provide fodder, fuel and minor forest products, and matter most to landless and marginal farmers and to women, who collect fodder and fuel.
focus: Meaning and examples of CPRs
What CPRs provide
Who depends most on CPRs and why
remember: CPRs: owned by the state for the community's use; every member has a right of access within rules
Provide fodder, fuel, fruits, nuts, fibre, medicinal plants
Vital for landless, marginal farmers and weaker sections; women collect fodder and fuel
traps: CPRs are not private land
Loss of CPRs hurts the landless most, not big landowners

topics.t: Agricultural land use and cropping intensity
topics.h: India can't create new land — so how can it grow more food? By growing more crops on the same field each year.
p: Land is more crucial for people who depend on agriculture than for those in other sectors: agriculture is purely land-based, and the quality of land directly affects productivity.
In rural areas, land ownership has social value and acts as security for credit, natural hazards and life contingencies; landlessness is closely linked with poverty.
Total stock of agricultural land = net sown area + all fallow lands + culturable wasteland.
The scope for bringing more land under cultivation is very limited, as most cultivable land is already in use; so India must raise output from existing land.
This means increasing cropping intensity and productivity. Cropping intensity (%) = (gross cropped area ÷ net sown area) × 100.

ex.q: A district has a net sown area of 2,00,000 ha and a gross cropped area of 3,00,000 ha. Find its cropping intensity.
st: Cropping intensity = GCA ÷ NSA × 100.

topics.rl: Punjab's cropping intensity is close to 190% thanks to irrigation, while many rainfed districts barely exceed 110%.

rv.summary: Agriculture is purely land-based, so land quality decides productivity, and land ownership gives security. Total agricultural land = net sown area + all fallows + culturable wasteland. With little new land, India must raise cropping intensity = (GCA ÷ NSA) × 100.
focus: Formula for total stock of agricultural land
Cropping intensity calculations
Why India must intensify rather than expand
remember: Total stock of agricultural land = NSA + all fallow lands + culturable wasteland
Cropping intensity (%) = (gross cropped area ÷ net sown area) × 100
Scope for bringing more land under cultivation is very limited
traps: Cropping intensity can exceed 100% when land is cropped more than once
Don't divide NSA by GCA — it is GCA ÷ NSA

topics.t: Cropping seasons: kharif, rabi and zaid
topics.h: Paddy transplanting begins with the June monsoon; wheat sowing waits for October's cool; watermelons ripen in May's heat. India farms in three seasons.
p: India has three distinct cropping seasons in the northern and interior parts: kharif, rabi and zaid.

Kharif largely coincides with the south-west monsoon and supports tropical crops: rice, cotton, jute, jowar, bajra and tur (in the north: rice, cotton, bajra, maize, jowar, tur; in the south: rice, maize, ragi, jowar, groundnut).

Rabi begins with the onset of winter in October–November and ends in March–April; low temperatures favour temperate and subtropical crops: wheat, gram, mustard (north: wheat, gram, rapeseed and mustard, barley; south: rice, maize, ragi, groundnut, jowar).
Zaid is a short-duration summer season after the rabi harvest: watermelons, cucumbers, vegetables and fodder crops on irrigated lands (south: rice, vegetables, fodder).
This distinction does not exist in southern parts: temperatures are high enough to grow tropical crops in any period if soil moisture is available.

ex.q: Assign the season: (a) wheat in Punjab; (b) jute in West Bengal; (c) watermelon in Uttar Pradesh in May.
st: (a) Sown Oct–Nov, harvested Mar–Apr → rabi.
(b) Grown with the south-west monsoon → kharif.
(c) Short summer crop after rabi, irrigated → zaid.
ex.a: (a) rabi, (b) kharif, (c) zaid

topics.rl: The government announces Minimum Support Prices separately for kharif and rabi crops each year — farmers plan around these two seasons.

rv.summary: North and interior India have three cropping seasons: kharif with the south-west monsoon (rice, cotton, jute, jowar, bajra, tur), rabi from October–November to March–April (wheat, gram, mustard, barley), and short summer zaid on irrigated land. South India has no such distinction.
focus: Timing and crops of kharif, rabi and zaid
Why rabi crops are temperate
Why southern India lacks distinct seasons
remember: Kharif: with south-west monsoon; rice, cotton, jute, jowar, bajra, tur
Rabi: Oct–Nov to Mar–Apr; wheat, gram, rapeseed and mustard, barley
Zaid: short summer season on irrigated land; watermelons, cucumbers, vegetables, fodder
traps: Wheat is rabi, not kharif
Zaid crops need irrigation; they are not mostly unirrigated

topics.t: Types of farming: irrigated and rainfed
topics.h: Ragi in Karnataka's dry uplands and rice in Kerala's waterlogged fields — both are rainfed. One is dryland farming, the other wetland!
p: By main source of moisture, farming is irrigated or rainfed (barani).

Irrigated farming: protective irrigation protects crops from soil moisture deficiency, acting as a supplement to rainfall; productive irrigation provides sufficient soil moisture to achieve high productivity — its water input per unit area is higher.

Rainfed farming is of two types: dryland farming, largely in regions with annual rainfall below 75 cm, growing hardy, drought-resistant crops like ragi, bajra, moong, gram and guar (fodder), with soil moisture conservation and rainwater harvesting.

Wetland farming: rainfall exceeds the soil moisture requirement of plants in the rainy season; such regions may face floods and soil erosion; they grow water-intensive crops such as rice, jute and sugarcane and practise aquaculture in fresh water bodies.
Map reading: compare a rainfall map with an irrigation map — low-rainfall areas with little irrigation practise dryland farming; high-rainfall areas practise wetland farming.

ex.q: A district gets 60 cm annual rainfall and has little irrigation. What type of farming and crops would you expect?
st: 60 cm < 75 cm → dryland area.
Rainfed, little irrigation → dryland farming.
Crops: hardy, drought-resistant — bajra, ragi, moong, gram, guar.
ex.a: Dryland farming with bajra, ragi, moong, gram, guar

topics.rl: Telangana's Mission Kakatiya revived village tanks to support protective irrigation for rainfed crops.

rv.summary: Farming is irrigated or rainfed (barani). Protective irrigation supplements rain to save crops; productive irrigation uses more water for high yields. Rainfed farming is dryland (below 75 cm rain; ragi, bajra, moong, gram, guar) or wetland (excess rain; rice, jute, sugarcane).
focus: Protective vs productive irrigation
Dryland vs wetland farming and their crops
Moisture conservation in drylands
remember: Rainfed = barani farming
Dryland: annual rainfall below 75 cm; hardy crops — ragi, bajra, moong, gram, guar
Wetland: rain exceeds plant needs; rice, jute, sugarcane; floods and erosion risk
traps: Don't swap protective (supplement rain) and productive (high water input) irrigation
Dryland farmers do need moisture conservation and rainwater harvesting

topics.h: In West Bengal, farmers grow rice three times a year and give each crop a name: aus, aman and boro.
p: Foodgrains — cereals and pulses — dominate India's cropping pattern. Cereals are classified as fine grains (rice, wheat) and coarse grains (jowar, bajra, maize, ragi etc.).

Rice is the staple food for most Indians; NCERT (2016 data) ranks India second after China; recent estimates (2024–25) put India marginally ahead. It is grown from humid tropics to the hills; in West Bengal three crops — aus, aman and boro — are grown, while in the Himalayas and north-west it is a kharif crop.

Leading rice producers: West Bengal, Punjab and Uttar Pradesh; yields are high in Punjab, Tamil Nadu, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, West Bengal and Kerala. Rice is rainfed in many humid areas; in Punjab and Haryana it is grown under irrigation.

Wheat is the second most important cereal; being a temperate crop, it is grown in the rabi season, mostly under irrigation. About 85% of its area is in the north and central regions — Indo-Gangetic plain, Malwa plateau and Himalayas up to 2,700 m.
Leading wheat producers: Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh; yields are very high in Punjab and Haryana.

ex.q: Why is wheat a rabi crop in India while rice is mostly a kharif crop?
st: Wheat is a temperate crop needing cool weather → grown in winter (rabi).
Rice is a tropical crop needing heat and water → grown with the monsoon (kharif).
Season matches each crop's climatic needs.
ex.a: Wheat needs cool winters; rice needs monsoon heat and water

topics.rl: The Public Distribution System and PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana rely on rice and wheat procured from states like Punjab, Haryana and Madhya Pradesh.

rv.summary: Foodgrains dominate Indian cropping. Rice, the staple, grows from humid tropics to hills (three crops — aus, aman, boro — in West Bengal); NCERT ranks India second after China. Wheat is a temperate rabi crop, 85% of its area in the north and centre, with high yields in Punjab and Haryana.
focus: Fine vs coarse cereals
Rice: seasons, leading states, India's rank
Wheat: season, area and leading states
remember: Fine grains: rice, wheat; coarse grains: jowar, bajra, maize, ragi
Rice: aus, aman, boro in West Bengal; leaders West Bengal, Punjab, UP
Wheat: rabi; ~85% area in north and central India; leaders UP, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, MP
traps: Rice is not only a kharif crop everywhere
Wheat is a temperate crop, not tropical

topics.t: Coarse cereals: jowar, bajra and maize
topics.h: The UN declared 2023 the International Year of Millets at India's suggestion. Jowar and bajra are back in fashion!
p: Coarse cereals together cover a sizeable part of the cropped area; jowar (sorghum) is the main food crop in semi-arid areas of central and southern India. Maharashtra alone produces more than half of India's jowar; other leading states are Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh and Telangana.
Jowar is sown in both kharif and rabi seasons in the south, but is a kharif crop in the north, where it is mostly grown as fodder.

Bajra (pearl millet) is sown in hot and dry conditions in north-western and western India; a hardy crop that resists frequent dry spells and drought; grown alone and in mixed cropping. Leading states (NCERT): Maharashtra, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Haryana.

Maize is a food as well as fodder crop grown in semi-arid conditions and over inferior soils; it is grown all over India except the eastern and north-eastern regions. Leading states: Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh.

Map work: mark leading states of rice (West Bengal, UP, Punjab), wheat (UP, Punjab, Haryana), cotton (Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana), jute (West Bengal), sugarcane (UP), tea (Assam) and coffee (Karnataka).

ex.q: A farmer in western Rajasthan with sandy soil and erratic, scanty rain wants a cereal. Which would you suggest and why?
st: Conditions: hot, dry, drought-prone.
Bajra is a hardy crop resisting dry spells and drought.
So bajra is the best choice.
ex.a: Bajra — it is hardy and drought-resistant

topics.rl: Millet-based mid-day meals in Karnataka and Odisha's Millet Mission have revived ragi, jowar and bajra for nutrition.

rv.summary: Jowar is the main food crop of semi-arid central and southern India; Maharashtra grows more than half of it. Bajra is a hardy, drought-resistant crop of hot, dry north-western and western India. Maize, a food and fodder crop on inferior soils, grows everywhere except the east and north-east.
focus: Regions and leading states of jowar, bajra and maize
Seasons of jowar in north and south
Matching states to the crops they lead
remember: Jowar: Maharashtra > half of India's output; kharif fodder crop in the north
Bajra: hot, dry north-west and west; hardy and drought-resistant
Maize: food and fodder; all India except east and north-east; Karnataka leads coffee (map work)
traps: Bajra does not need wet conditions
In the north, jowar is mostly a kharif fodder crop, not a rabi food crop

topics.h: Dal-chawal on your plate and mustard oil in the kitchen — pulses and oilseeds fuel India's kitchens and fix nitrogen in its soils.
p: Pulses are a rich source of protein in vegetarian diets; being legumes, they increase soil fertility through nitrogen fixation. They are grown mainly on drylands of the Deccan and central plateaus and north-western India; yields are low and fluctuate as they are rainfed.

Gram: a subtropical, mostly rainfed rabi crop of central, western and north-western India; one or two light showers or irrigations suffice; displaced by wheat in Haryana, Punjab and northern Rajasthan after the Green Revolution. Leading states: Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan.

Tur (arhar, red gram or pigeon pea): the second important pulse; grown on marginal lands under rainfed conditions in the dry areas of central and southern India; Maharashtra contributes about one-third of production; yields are very low.

Oilseeds are grown for edible oils, mainly in drylands of the Malwa plateau, Marathwada, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Telangana, Rayalaseema (Andhra Pradesh) and the Karnataka plateau. Groundnut: a rainfed kharif crop of drylands (also rabi in the south); leading states include Gujarat, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka; yields are higher in Tamil Nadu where it is partly irrigated.

Rapeseed and mustard (rai, sarson, toria, taramira): subtropical rabi crops of north-western and central India; frost-sensitive with fluctuating yields; Rajasthan contributes about one-third of production. Soyabean is grown mainly in Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra; sunflower in Karnataka and adjoining Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra.

ex.q: Why do pulses improve soil fertility, and why are their yields often low?
st: Pulses are legumes; root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen into the soil.
But they are mostly rainfed crops of drylands.
So yields are low and fluctuate with rainfall.
ex.a: They fix nitrogen; yields are low because they are rainfed dryland crops

topics.rl: India is the world's largest producer and consumer of pulses, yet still imports some — so missions to raise pulse yields are a policy priority.

rv.summary: Pulses are protein-rich legumes that fix nitrogen; they are mostly rainfed dryland crops with low yields. Gram is a rabi pulse, tur (arhar) the second pulse with Maharashtra giving a third. Oilseeds include groundnut, rapeseed and mustard, soyabean and sunflower.
focus: Why pulses fix nitrogen and have low yields
Gram, tur and their leading states
Main oilseeds and their regions
remember: Pulses fix nitrogen; mostly rainfed drylands; low, fluctuating yields
Gram: rainfed rabi; displaced by wheat in Punjab, Haryana, northern Rajasthan; tur = arhar = red gram = pigeon pea, Maharashtra ≈ 1/3
Rapeseed and mustard: frost-sensitive rabi crops; Rajasthan ≈ 1/3; soyabean: MP and Maharashtra
traps: Rapeseed and mustard are rabi crops, not kharif
Tur is not Bengal gram

topics.t: Fibre and other crops: cotton, jute, sugarcane, tea and coffee
topics.h: Assam tea, Coorg coffee, Gujarat cotton and Bengal jute — each crop has found its perfect home.
p: Cotton: a tropical kharif crop of semi-arid areas; India grows short staple (Indian) and long staple (American) cotton called 'narma' in the north-west; needs clear sky during flowering. Three areas: north-west (Punjab, Haryana, northern Rajasthan), west (Gujarat, Maharashtra) and south (plateaus of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu). Leading producers: Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana; India is among the world's top cotton producers.

Jute: used for coarse cloth, bags, sacks and decorative items; a cash crop of West Bengal and adjoining eastern parts; India lost large jute-growing areas to East Pakistan (Bangladesh) at partition. West Bengal produces about three-fourths of India's jute; Bihar and Assam are other jute areas.

Sugarcane: a tropical crop, rainfed in sub-humid and humid climates but largely irrigated in India; Uttar Pradesh produces about two-fifths; Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh are other leaders. India is the second largest producer after Brazil.

Tea: a plantation beverage crop introduced by the British in the 1840s in the Brahmaputra valley of Assam; later in Darjeeling, Jalpaiguri and Cooch Behar (West Bengal) and on lower slopes of the Nilgiri and Cardamom hills; grown on well-drained soils in humid and sub-humid tropics and subtropics. Assam produces more than half of India's tea; India is second after China.

Coffee: a tropical plantation crop with three varieties — arabica, robusta and liberica; India mostly grows superior arabica, in demand internationally; grown in the highlands of the Western Ghats in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu; Karnataka produces more than two-thirds of India's coffee.

ex.q: Match each state with the crop of which it produces the largest share: Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Assam, Karnataka.
st: Uttar Pradesh → sugarcane (about two-fifths).
West Bengal → jute (about three-fourths).
Assam → tea (more than half).
Karnataka → coffee (more than two-thirds).
ex.a: UP–sugarcane, WB–jute, Assam–tea, Karnataka–coffee

topics.rl: Kolkata's jute mills, Gujarat's cotton textile hubs and Maharashtra's sugar cooperatives all depend on these crops.

rv.summary: Cotton is a tropical kharif crop of semi-arid areas (Gujarat, Maharashtra, Telangana lead). West Bengal grows about three-fourths of jute. Tea, introduced in Assam in the 1840s, comes over half from Assam, and Karnataka grows over two-thirds of coffee, mostly arabica.
focus: Climate, season and leading states of cotton
Leading states of jute, sugarcane, tea and coffee
Why India lost jute areas at partition
remember: Cotton: tropical kharif; needs clear sky at flowering; 'narma' = long staple American cotton
Jute: West Bengal ≈ 3/4; sugarcane: UP ≈ 2/5; India second after Brazil
Tea: Assam (1840s), > half of output; coffee: arabica, Karnataka > 2/3
traps: Cotton is a kharif crop, not a rabi crop of cold regions
India mostly grows arabica, not robusta

topics.t: Agricultural development and the Green Revolution
topics.h: In the mid-1960s India imported foodgrains after two droughts. Within a decade, it became self-reliant. The Green Revolution changed everything.
p: Agriculture remains a very important sector: more than half of India's workforce (54.6% in Census 2011) depends on it for livelihood.

After Independence, the strategy was to increase foodgrain production by: switching from cash crops to food crops; intensification of cropping over already cultivated land; and bringing cultivable and fallow land under the plough.

In the 1960s, the Intensive Agricultural District Programme (IADP) and Intensive Agricultural Area Programme (IAAP) were launched; after two droughts in the mid-1960s caused a food crisis, high yielding varieties (HYVs) of wheat (from Mexico) and rice (from the Philippines) were introduced with chemical fertilisers in irrigated areas of Punjab, Haryana, western UP, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu — the Green Revolution. Assured irrigation was a basic prerequisite.

The Green Revolution made India self-reliant in foodgrains but was initially confined to irrigated areas, causing regional disparities until it spread to central and eastern India. In the 1980s the Planning Commission focused on rainfed areas; agro-climatic planning began in 1988, with diversification into dairy, poultry, horticulture, livestock and aquaculture. Liberalisation and the WTO in the 1990s exposed agriculture to international competition.

Output and yields of rice and wheat rose impressively; sugarcane, oilseeds and cotton also grew. As per NCERT data, India ranks first in pulses, jute, cattle and milk, and second in rice, wheat, groundnut, sugarcane and vegetables. Gross irrigated area and use of fertilisers and HYV seeds expanded greatly.

ex.q: Arrange these in time order: agro-climatic planning; HYV seeds from Mexico and the Philippines; liberalisation and WTO pressure; shift from cash crops to food crops.
st: Just after 1947: shift from cash crops to food crops.
Mid-1960s: HYV seeds and Green Revolution.
1988: agro-climatic planning.
1990s: liberalisation and WTO.
ex.a: Food crops shift → HYV/Green Revolution → agro-climatic planning (1988) → liberalisation/WTO (1990s)

topics.rl: Norman Borlaug's dwarf wheat and M. S. Swaminathan's work in India made Punjab the 'granary of India'.

rv.summary: After mid-1960s droughts, HYV wheat (Mexico) and rice (Philippines) with fertilisers and assured irrigation brought the Green Revolution and self-reliance, but initially regional disparities.
focus: Post-independence strategy for food production
The Green Revolution: sources of seeds, areas, prerequisites
Later phases: rainfed focus, agro-climatic planning (1988), liberalisation
remember: HYV wheat from Mexico, rice from the Philippines; initially Punjab, Haryana, western UP, AP, Tamil Nadu
Assured irrigation was the basic prerequisite
Agro-climatic planning: 1988; India first in pulses, jute, cattle, milk
traps: Don't swap the sources: wheat — Mexico; rice — Philippines
The Green Revolution made India self-reliant, not more import-dependent

topics.h: A large part of India's cropland still waits for the monsoon each year. One bad monsoon can push lakhs of farmers into debt.
p: Dependence on erratic monsoon: NCERT notes that irrigation covers only about one-third of the cultivated area (recent official data put it nearer half); the rest depends on rainfall, which is erratic — droughts and floods are common.

Low productivity: yields of most crops are low compared to international levels; high pressure on land and low labour productivity. Constraints of financial resources and indebtedness: inputs like HYVs, fertilisers and machinery are expensive; crop failures and low returns push farmers into debt and distress.

Lack of land reforms: unequal distribution of land and exploitation by landlords; land reforms were not effectively implemented. Small farm size and fragmentation: more than 60 per cent of ownership holdings are smaller than one hectare, and holdings are fragmented — uneconomic for modern farming.

Lack of commercialisation: many farmers grow crops for self-consumption; small farms cannot afford commercial crops. Vast underemployment: seasonal unemployment ranging from about 4 to 8 months in a year.

Degradation of cultivable land: faulty irrigation causes salinisation, alkalinisation and waterlogging; excessive chemicals reduce fertility; soil erosion by water and wind. Exam focus: fallow vs culturable wasteland, CPRs, dryland vs wetland, Green Revolution, problems and map marking.

ex.q: A farmer with 0.6 ha split into three plots in different places relies on rain and works only 6 months a year. List three problems shown.
st: 0.6 ha in three plots → small and fragmented holding.
Relies on rain → dependence on erratic monsoon.
Works only 6 months → seasonal underemployment.
ex.a: Small fragmented holding, monsoon dependence, underemployment

topics.rl: PM-KISAN income support, crop insurance (PMFBY) and Soil Health Cards are government responses to these problems.

rv.summary: Indian agriculture faces erratic monsoons (NCERT: only about one-third irrigated), low productivity, costly inputs and debt, weak land reforms, small fragmented holdings (over 60% below 1 ha), seasonal underemployment and land degradation.
focus: The main problems of Indian agriculture
Causes of land degradation
Revising fallow vs culturable wasteland
remember: Irrigation ≈ one-third of cultivated area (NCERT)
More than 60% of ownership holdings are smaller than one hectare
Seasonal unemployment: about 4 to 8 months a year
Faulty irrigation → salinisation, alkalinisation, waterlogging
traps: Small fragmented holdings are uneconomic, not more efficient
Current fallow is ≤ 1 year; culturable wasteland is > 5 years — don't reverse them

topics.t: Water resources of India: the big numbers
topics.h: India has about one-sixth of the world's people but only about 4% of its water. Every drop matters!
p: Water is a cyclic, renewable resource, but its quantity is limited; demand is rising while quality is declining.

India accounts for about 2.45 per cent of the world's surface area and 4 per cent of its water resources, but about one-sixth of its population (16 per cent in NCERT's figure; 17.5 per cent in Census 2011).
Total water available from precipitation in a year is about 4,000 cubic km; availability from surface water and replenishable groundwater is 1,869 cubic km.
Only about 60 per cent of this can be put to beneficial use, so the total utilisable water resource is only 1,122 cubic km.

ex.q: Show that about 60% of 1,869 cubic km gives the utilisable water figure.
st: = 1,121.4 cubic km ≈ 1,122 cubic km.
ex.a: About 1,122 cubic km

topics.rl: Chennai's 'Day Zero' scare in 2019, when reservoirs ran dry, showed how limited India's usable water really is.

rv.summary: Water is cyclic and renewable but limited. India has about 2.45% of world area, 4% of its water and about one-sixth of its people. Precipitation gives about 4,000 cubic km a year, 1,869 cubic km is available from surface and groundwater, and only 1,122 cubic km is utilisable.
focus: India's shares of world area, water and population
The key water figures: 4,000, 1,869, 1,122 cubic km
Why water is scarce though renewable
remember: Precipitation ≈ 4,000 cubic km a year
Surface + replenishable groundwater = 1,869 cubic km; about 60% usable
Utilisable water = 1,122 cubic km
traps: Renewable does not mean unlimited
Not all available water can be used — only about 60%

topics.h: The Ganga, Brahmaputra and Barak drain only about a third of India's area but carry about 60% of its surface water.
p: Surface water has four main sources: rivers, lakes, ponds and tanks.
India has about 10,360 rivers and tributaries longer than 1.6 km each; the mean annual flow in all river basins is estimated at 1,869 cubic km.
Due to topographical, hydrological and other constraints, only about 690 cubic km of surface water can be utilised.

Water flow in a river depends on the size of its catchment (river basin) and the rainfall within it. The Ganga, Brahmaputra and Barak have extremely large catchments with high rainfall; though covering only about one-third of the country's area, they have about 60 per cent of its surface water resources.
Much of the annual flow of south Indian rivers like the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri has been harnessed, but this is yet to be done in the Ganga and Brahmaputra basins.

ex.q: Why do the Ganga, Brahmaputra and Barak have so much more water than peninsular rivers?
st: Flow depends on catchment size and rainfall in the catchment.
These rivers have huge catchments with high rainfall (and Himalayan snowmelt).
So they carry about 60% of India's surface water.
ex.a: Large catchments with heavy rainfall

topics.rl: Cauvery water-sharing disputes between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu arise because the river's flow is already heavily used.

rv.summary: Surface water comes from rivers, lakes, ponds and tanks. India has about 10,360 rivers and tributaries over 1.6 km, with mean annual flow of 1,869 cubic km, but only about 690 cubic km is usable. The Ganga, Brahmaputra and Barak hold about 60% of surface water.
focus: Sources and figures of surface water
What decides river flow
Harnessed southern rivers vs northern basins
remember: Rivers and tributaries > 1.6 km: about 10,360; mean annual flow 1,869 cubic km
Usable surface water: about 690 cubic km
Ganga, Brahmaputra, Barak: about one-third of area, about 60% of surface water
traps: The Ganga and Brahmaputra basins are not yet fully harnessed — the southern rivers are
Usable surface water is 690 cubic km, not the total 1,869

topics.h: In parts of Punjab, the water table has dropped so low that farmers must bore hundreds of feet. Groundwater is running out!
p: India's total replenishable groundwater resources are about 432 cubic km.
The Ganga and Brahmaputra basins have about 46 per cent of the total replenishable groundwater.
Groundwater utilisation is relatively high in river basins of the north-west and parts of south India — very high in Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu.
States like Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Tripura and Maharashtra use groundwater at a moderate rate, while Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Kerala use only a small proportion of their potential.
If the present trend continues, demand will exceed supply; over-exploitation lowers the water table and can harm development and cause social disruption — so sustainable use is essential.

ex.q: What share of the 432 cubic km of replenishable groundwater lies in the Ganga and Brahmaputra basins (about 46%)? Work out the volume.
st: = 198.72 cubic km.
ex.a: About 198.72 cubic km

topics.rl: The Atal Bhujal Yojana works with villages in water-stressed states like Haryana, Rajasthan and Gujarat to manage groundwater sustainably.

rv.summary: India's replenishable groundwater is about 432 cubic km, about 46% of it in the Ganga and Brahmaputra basins. Use is very high in Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu, moderate in states like Gujarat and Bihar, and low in Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Kerala; over-use lowers the water table.

High, moderate and low groundwater-use states
Effects of over-exploitation
remember: Replenishable groundwater ≈ 432 cubic km; Ganga + Brahmaputra ≈ 46%
Very high use: Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu
Moderate: Gujarat, UP, Bihar, Tripura, Maharashtra; low: Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Kerala
