Don't put Odisha or Kerala among high-use states

topics.t: Lagoons, backwaters and India's agrarian base
topics.h: Kerala's backwaters, Odisha's Chilika and Bengal's coastal lakes hold huge amounts of water — but it is salty!
p: India has a vast and, in some states, highly indented coastline, which has led to the formation of many lagoons and lakes.
Kerala, Odisha and West Bengal have vast surface water resources in such lagoons and lakes.
The water in these water bodies is generally brackish, but it is used for fishing and for irrigating certain varieties of paddy crops and coconut.
India has traditionally been an agrarian economy; about two-thirds of its population has depended on agriculture, so water demand is dominated by farming.

ex.q: Why can't lagoon water be used for drinking, though it is used for fishing and some paddy?
st: Lagoon water is mixed with sea water — brackish.
Brackish water is unfit for drinking without treatment.
But some fish and salt-tolerant paddy and coconut can use it.
ex.a: It is brackish; only salt-tolerant uses are possible

topics.rl: Chilika, Asia's largest brackish-water lagoon, supports thousands of fishing families and migratory birds.

rv.summary: India's indented coastline has many lagoons and lakes, especially in Kerala, Odisha and West Bengal. Their water is generally brackish, used for fishing and for some paddy and coconut. Because about two-thirds of people have depended on farming, agriculture dominates water demand.
focus: Where lagoons are found and why
Uses of brackish lagoon water
Link between agrarian economy and water demand
remember: Lagoons and lakes: Kerala, Odisha, West Bengal; formed by indented coastline
Lagoon water is brackish; used for fishing and irrigating some paddy and coconut
About two-thirds of population traditionally depended on agriculture
traps: Lagoon water is not fresh and potable
Brackish water still has uses — it is not useless

topics.h: Out of every 100 litres of surface water India uses, about 89 go to farms. Industry gets just 2!
p: Agriculture accounts for most water use: 89 per cent of surface water and 92 per cent of groundwater utilisation.
Industry uses only 2 per cent of surface water and 5 per cent of groundwater.
The domestic sector uses 9 per cent of surface water — higher than its share of groundwater (3 per cent).
In future, demand from the industrial and domestic sectors is expected to increase with industrialisation and urbanisation.
A pie chart of sectoral use shows agriculture's huge slice in both surface and groundwater.

ex.q: Using the sectoral shares, find the domestic share of groundwater use.
st: Groundwater: agriculture 92% + industry 5% = 97%.
Domestic = 100 − 97 = 3%.

topics.rl: Drip and sprinkler irrigation under 'Per Drop More Crop' (PMKSY) aim to cut agriculture's huge share of water use.

rv.summary: Agriculture uses 89% of surface water and 92% of groundwater. Industry uses only 2% of surface water and 5% of groundwater, and the domestic sector 9% of surface and 3% of groundwater. Industrial and domestic demand will rise with industrialisation and urbanisation.
focus: Sectoral shares of surface water and groundwater use
Working out a missing share from the others
Future changes in demand
remember: Surface water: agriculture 89%, industry 2%, domestic 9%
Groundwater: agriculture 92%, industry 5%, domestic 3%
Industrial and domestic demand expected to rise
traps: Industry does not use more water than agriculture
Don't swap surface (89%) and groundwater (92%) farm shares

topics.t: Demand for irrigation and its problems
topics.h: Punjab irrigates over 85% of its net sown area — and now worries about arsenic, fluoride and a vanishing water table.
p: Irrigation is needed because rainfall is unevenly distributed in space and time: large tracts (north-western India, Deccan plateau) are rainfall-deficient and drought-prone; winter and summer are dry in most parts; even in high-rainfall states like West Bengal and Bihar, breaks or failure of monsoon cause dry spells.
Some crops like rice, sugarcane and jute need a lot of water; multiple cropping is possible only with irrigation; HYV crops need regulated moisture.

Irrigation raises productivity: in Punjab, Haryana and western UP, more than 85 per cent of net sown area is irrigated, and wheat and rice there are grown mainly with irrigation, largely from wells and tube wells.

Problems of excessive irrigation: over-drawing of groundwater lowers the water table; fluoride concentration has increased in Rajasthan and Maharashtra and arsenic in West Bengal and Bihar; intensive irrigation also raises soil salinity.

ex.q: Give three reasons why a farmer in Haryana relies on tube wells.
st: Haryana gets limited rainfall concentrated in a few months.
Wheat (rabi) is grown in the dry winter.
HYV crops and multiple cropping need assured, regulated water.
ex.a: Scanty seasonal rain, dry-season crops and HYV/multiple cropping needs

topics.rl: Punjab's 'Paani Bachao, Paisa Kamao' scheme pays farmers to save electricity and groundwater used for irrigation.

rv.summary: India needs irrigation because rainfall is uneven in space and time, some crops need much water, and multiple cropping and HYVs need assured moisture. Over-irrigation lowers the water table and raises salinity, fluoride and arsenic.
focus: Reasons for irrigation demand
Irrigation and productivity in north-west India
Problems of excessive irrigation
remember: Punjab, Haryana, western UP: more than 85% of net sown area irrigated
Water-hungry crops: rice, sugarcane, jute; HYVs need regulated moisture
Fluoride: Rajasthan, Maharashtra; arsenic: West Bengal, Bihar
traps: Don't swap the fluoride and arsenic states
Excessive irrigation does not always improve soil — it can raise salinity

topics.t: Emerging water problems: availability and pollution
topics.h: The same Yamuna that is clear near its source becomes one of India's most polluted rivers after Delhi. What goes wrong?
p: Per capita availability of water is declining due to the increase in population.
Available water resources are also getting polluted by industrial, agricultural and domestic effluents, which limits usable water further.
Water quality refers to the purity of water, i.e. water without unwanted foreign substances; pollution happens when toxic substances enter lakes, streams, rivers, oceans and other water bodies.

Polluted water harms aquatic life and human health. CPCB data show organic and bacterial contamination as the main pollution source in rivers; the Yamuna is most polluted between Delhi and Etawah, and the Ganga is highly polluted at Kanpur and Varanasi; other polluted rivers include the Sabarmati at Ahmedabad, Gomti at Lucknow and Musi at Hyderabad.

ex.q: If a city's water supply stays at 300 crore litres a day while its population rises from 1.5 crore to 2 crore, what happens to per capita supply?
st: Before: 300 ÷ 1.5 = 200 litres per person per day.
After: 300 ÷ 2 = 150 litres per person per day.
Per capita availability falls by 50 litres.
ex.a: Falls from 200 to 150 litres per person per day

topics.rl: The Namami Gange programme sets up sewage treatment plants in Kanpur, Varanasi and other cities to clean the Ganga.

rv.summary: Per capita water availability is falling as population rises, and industrial, agricultural and domestic effluents pollute water further. CPCB data show organic and bacterial contamination as the main river pollutant; the Yamuna is worst between Delhi and Etawah and the Ganga at Kanpur and Varanasi.
focus: Causes of falling per capita water availability
Sources of water pollution and its effects
Most polluted river stretches
remember: Per capita availability falls with population growth
Pollution sources: industrial, agricultural and domestic effluents; main: organic and bacterial contamination
Yamuna: Delhi–Etawah; Ganga: Kanpur, Varanasi; also Sabarmati, Gomti, Musi
traps: Water quality is about purity, not quantity
Polluted water does harm aquatic life

topics.t: Water conservation: pollution control and recycling
topics.h: A Bengaluru apartment treats its own sewage and uses it to flush toilets and water gardens — saving lakhs of litres of fresh water.
p: Declining availability and rising demand make conservation and effective management of water essential.

Strategies: water-saving technologies and methods, prevention of pollution, watershed development, rainwater harvesting, water recycling and reuse, conjunctive use of surface and groundwater, and long-term planning.

Prevention of pollution: the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), with State Pollution Control Boards, monitors water quality. Laws like the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 have not been implemented effectively; public awareness is needed.

Recycle and reuse: lower-quality reclaimed waste water can be used by industries for cooling and fire-fighting; in cities, water from bathing and washing utensils (and vehicle washing) can be used for gardening — reducing demand for fresh water.

ex.q: Suggest two ways a factory and two ways a household can recycle water.
st: Factory: use treated waste water for cooling; use it for fire-fighting.
Household: use bathing/utensil water for gardening; reuse vehicle-washing water for plants.
ex.a: Factory — cooling, fire-fighting; household — gardening with used water

topics.rl: Many Indian cities now mandate sewage treatment plants in large housing societies and reuse treated water for non-drinking purposes.

rv.summary: Water must be conserved through pollution control, watershed development, rainwater harvesting and recycling. CPCB monitors quality; the Water Act (1974) and Environment Act (1986) need better enforcement. Reused water can serve cooling and gardening.
focus: Strategies for water conservation
Pollution control bodies and laws
Recycling and reuse in industry and homes
remember: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974; Environment (Protection) Act 1986
CPCB with State Pollution Control Boards monitors water quality
Reclaimed water: industrial cooling and fire-fighting; household grey water: gardening
traps: Don't swap the years of the Water Act (1974) and Environment Act (1986)
Laws alone have not solved water pollution

topics.h: Ralegan Siddhi, a drought-hit village in Maharashtra, turned green by building check dams and planting trees — through people's own efforts.
p: Watershed management means efficient management and conservation of surface and groundwater resources: preventing runoff, and storing and recharging groundwater through percolation tanks, recharge wells etc.
In a broad sense it includes conservation, regeneration and judicious use of all natural (land, water, plants, animals) and human resources within a watershed; community participation is essential.

Haryali: a Central Government–sponsored watershed project enabling rural people to conserve water for drinking, irrigation, fisheries and afforestation; executed by Gram Panchayats with people's participation.

Neeru-Meeru ('Water and You') in Andhra Pradesh and Arvary Pani Sansad in Alwar (Rajasthan) built water-harvesting structures like percolation tanks, dug-out ponds (johads) and check dams through people's participation.
Ralegan Siddhi (Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra) is a celebrated example of village-led watershed development that ended water scarcity.

ex.q: Match the programme to its state: Neeru-Meeru, Arvary Pani Sansad.
st: Neeru-Meeru means 'Water and You' — Andhra Pradesh.
Arvary Pani Sansad — Alwar district, Rajasthan.
ex.a: Neeru-Meeru — Andhra Pradesh; Arvary Pani Sansad — Rajasthan

topics.rl: Tarun Bharat Sangh's johads revived the Arvari river in Alwar — a model of people-led watershed management.

rv.summary: Watershed management conserves surface and groundwater by stopping runoff and recharging aquifers with percolation tanks and recharge wells; it needs community participation, as in Haryali, Neeru-Meeru and Arvary Pani Sansad.
focus: Meaning and wider scope of watershed management
Haryali and other people's programmes
Structures used to recharge groundwater
remember: Watershed management: efficient management and conservation of surface and groundwater
Haryali: central scheme run by Gram Panchayats; water for drinking, irrigation, fisheries, afforestation
Neeru-Meeru: Andhra Pradesh; Arvary Pani Sansad: Alwar, Rajasthan; Ralegan Siddhi: Ahmednagar, Maharashtra

Don't place Neeru-Meeru in Rajasthan — it is Andhra Pradesh

topics.h: Tamil Nadu made rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for buildings — and Chennai's groundwater levels improved in response!
p: Rainwater harvesting is a method of capturing and storing rainwater for various uses; it is also used to recharge groundwater aquifers.
It is a low-cost and eco-friendly technique for preserving every drop of water by guiding rainwater to bore wells, pits and wells.
Traditional methods: lakes, ponds and irrigation tanks in rural areas; in Rajasthan, rainwater is stored in kunds or tankas (covered underground tanks) near houses or villages.

Benefits: increases water availability, checks the declining groundwater table, improves groundwater quality by diluting contaminants like fluoride and nitrates, prevents soil erosion and flooding, and arrests salt-water intrusion in coastal areas if used to recharge aquifers.
Tamil Nadu has made rooftop rainwater harvesting structures compulsory in all houses — no building can be constructed without them.

ex.q: A rooftop of 100 sq m receives 800 mm (0.8 m) of rain a year. Ideally, how many litres can be harvested? (1 cubic m = 1,000 litres)
st: Volume = area × rainfall = 100 × 0.8 = 80 cubic m.
ex.a: 80,000 litres

topics.rl: The Jal Shakti Abhiyan's 'Catch the Rain' campaign urges every household to harvest rain 'where it falls, when it falls'.

rv.summary: Rainwater harvesting captures and stores rain and recharges aquifers; it is low-cost and eco-friendly. Traditional forms include tanks and Rajasthan's kunds or tankas. It checks falling water tables and dilutes contaminants; Tamil Nadu made rooftop harvesting compulsory.
focus: Meaning and methods of rainwater harvesting
Benefits of rainwater harvesting
Calculating harvestable rain from roof area
remember: Captures and stores rainwater; recharges aquifers via wells, pits, bore wells
Kunds or tankas: covered underground tanks in Rajasthan
Tamil Nadu: rooftop harvesting compulsory in all houses
traps: Rainwater harvesting is not costly or harmful

topics.t: National Water Policy and Jal Kranti Abhiyan
topics.h: When water is scarce, who gets it first — farms, factories or families? India's National Water Policy answers: drinking water comes first.
p: The National Water Policy (2002) stipulates water allocation priorities: drinking water gets the top priority, followed by irrigation, hydropower and other uses such as industry and navigation.

Other NWP features: irrigation and multipurpose projects should include a drinking-water component; groundwater exploitation should be regulated; water quality should be improved; water should be conserved by efficient use; farmers and stakeholders should participate in management.

Jal Kranti Abhiyan (2015–16): aims to ensure water security through per capita availability of water; water-scarce villages in each district are selected as 'Jal Grams' for integrated water security plans; model command areas are developed; it promotes traditional and modern conservation with people's participation.
Exam focus: water figures (4,000; 1,869; 1,122; 432 cubic km), sectoral use, causes of declining water resources, emerging problems, watershed management and rainwater harvesting.

ex.q: Arrange these uses by the priority given in the National Water Policy: irrigation, drinking water, hydropower.
st: Top priority: drinking water.
Next: irrigation.
Then: hydropower (followed by other uses).
ex.a: Drinking water → irrigation → hydropower

topics.rl: The Jal Jeevan Mission aims to give a functional tap connection to every rural household — putting drinking water first, as the NWP intends.

rv.summary: The National Water Policy (2002) gives drinking water top priority, then irrigation, hydropower and other uses; it calls for regulated groundwater use, better quality and stakeholder participation. Jal Kranti Abhiyan (2015–16) seeks water security, choosing water-scarce villages as Jal Grams.

Jal Kranti Abhiyan and Jal Grams

topics.h: The iron in your bicycle, the copper in your phone charger and the mica in your iron box all came out of India's ancient rocks.
p: India is fortunate to have fairly rich and varied mineral resources due to its varied geological structure; most valuable minerals are products of pre-Palaeozoic age, associated with the metamorphic and igneous rocks of Peninsular India.
A mineral is a natural substance of organic or inorganic origin with definite chemical and physical properties.

Characteristics: minerals are unevenly distributed over space; there is an inverse relationship between quality and quantity — good quality minerals are less in quantity than low quality ones; all minerals are exhaustible, take long to develop geologically and cannot be replenished immediately.
Minerals are the base of industrial development — iron for steel, bauxite for aluminium, coal and oil for energy.

ex.q: Why must minerals be used carefully even though India has many of them?
st: Minerals are exhaustible.
They take millions of years to form and cannot be replenished immediately.
High-quality deposits are especially limited (inverse quality–quantity relation).
ex.a: They are exhaustible and slow to form, and good quality deposits are few

topics.rl: National Mineral Policy and auctions of mining blocks aim to use India's limited high-grade ores efficiently.

rv.summary: A mineral is a natural organic or inorganic substance with definite chemical and physical properties. India's varied geology gives rich minerals, mostly in old Peninsular rocks. Minerals are unevenly spread, show an inverse quality–quantity relation, and are exhaustible.

topics.h: Iron and copper are both metals — but one is 'ferrous' and the other isn't. And coal is a mineral too!
p: Minerals are of two main types: metallic and non-metallic.
Metallic minerals are sources of metals: ferrous minerals contain iron (iron ore, manganese, chromite); non-ferrous minerals do not contain iron (copper, bauxite, lead, zinc, gold).
Non-metallic minerals are either organic in origin — fossil fuels like coal and petroleum — or inorganic — mica, limestone, graphite.
Flowchart: Minerals → Metallic (Ferrous | Non-ferrous) and Non-metallic (Organic | Inorganic).

ex.q: Classify: bauxite, chromite, coal, mica, manganese.
st: Bauxite → metallic, non-ferrous.
Chromite, manganese → metallic, ferrous.
Coal → non-metallic, organic (fossil fuel).
Mica → non-metallic, inorganic.
ex.a: Ferrous: chromite, manganese; non-ferrous: bauxite; organic: coal; inorganic: mica

topics.rl: Steel plants need ferrous ores; aluminium smelters need bauxite; power plants burn organic coal — each mineral class feeds a different industry.

rv.summary: Minerals are metallic or non-metallic. Metallic minerals are ferrous (with iron: iron ore, manganese, chromite) or non-ferrous (copper, bauxite, lead, zinc, gold). Non-metallic minerals are organic (coal, petroleum) or inorganic (mica, limestone, graphite).

topics.t: Distribution of minerals and the North-eastern Plateau belt
topics.h: Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh sit on top of India's richest treasure chest of iron, coal and manganese.
p: Most metallic minerals in India occur in the old crystalline rocks of the Peninsular plateau.
Over 97 per cent of coal reserves occur in the valleys of the Damodar, Sone, Mahanadi and Godavari.
Petroleum reserves are in the sedimentary basins of Assam, Gujarat and Mumbai High (offshore in the Arabian Sea); new reserves have been found in the Krishna-Godavari and Kaveri basins.
Minerals are concentrated in three broad belts, plus scattered occurrences: the North-eastern Plateau region, the South-western Plateau region and the North-western region.
North-eastern Plateau region: covers Chotanagpur (Jharkhand), the Odisha plateau, West Bengal and parts of Chhattisgarh; has a variety of minerals — iron ore, coal, manganese, bauxite and mica.

ex.q: Why is the North-eastern Plateau region ideal for iron and steel plants?
st: It has iron ore, coal and manganese close together.
These are the main raw materials for steel.
Short transport distances reduce cost.
ex.a: Iron ore, coal and manganese occur together there

topics.rl: Steel plants at Jamshedpur, Bokaro, Rourkela and Bhilai all lie in or near this mineral-rich plateau.

rv.summary: Most metallic minerals lie in the old crystalline rocks of the Peninsula; over 97% of coal is in the Damodar, Sone, Mahanadi and Godavari valleys; petroleum is in sedimentary basins of Assam, Gujarat and Mumbai High. The North-eastern Plateau belt has iron ore, coal, manganese, bauxite and mica.
focus: Where metallic minerals, coal and petroleum occur
The three mineral belts
Minerals of the North-eastern Plateau region
remember: Coal: over 97% in Damodar, Sone, Mahanadi, Godavari valleys
Petroleum: sedimentary basins of Assam, Gujarat, Mumbai High; new finds in Krishna-Godavari and Kaveri

topics.t: South-western, North-western and Himalayan mineral belts
topics.h: Rajasthan's marble built the Taj Mahal; Karnataka's Kolar gave India its gold; Kerala's beaches hide thorium-rich monazite.
p: South-western Plateau region: Karnataka, Goa and contiguous Tamil Nadu uplands and Kerala; rich in ferrous metals and bauxite; high-grade iron ore, manganese and limestone; Neyveli lignite (Tamil Nadu); monazite sands in Kerala; Kolar gold mines (Karnataka). It is less diversified than the North-eastern belt.

North-western region: along the Aravalis in Rajasthan and part of Gujarat; non-ferrous minerals like copper and zinc; building stones — sandstone, granite, marble; gypsum and Fuller's earth; dolomite and limestone for cement; Gujarat has petroleum; salt from Gujarat and Rajasthan.
Himalayan belt: copper, lead, zinc, cobalt and tungsten occur in the east and west; Assam valley has mineral oil deposits; oil is also found offshore near Mumbai (Mumbai High).
Map reading: shade the three belts — NE plateau (Jharkhand–Odisha–Chhattisgarh), SW plateau (Karnataka–Goa–Kerala) and NW (Rajasthan–Gujarat).

ex.q: Assign to belts: Kolar gold, Rajasthan marble, Neyveli lignite, Gujarat salt.
st: Kolar gold → South-western Plateau.
Rajasthan marble → North-western region.
Neyveli lignite → South-western Plateau (Tamil Nadu).
Gujarat salt → North-western region.
ex.a: SW: Kolar, Neyveli; NW: marble, salt

topics.rl: Makrana marble from Rajasthan's Aravali belt was used in the Taj Mahal and is still prized today.

rv.summary: The South-western Plateau (Karnataka, Goa, Tamil Nadu uplands, Kerala) has high-grade iron ore, Neyveli lignite, Kerala monazite and Kolar gold. The North-western Aravali region has copper, zinc, building stones and salt.

topics.h: Bailadila means 'ox's hump': its hills in Chhattisgarh are shaped like one, and they hold some of the world's finest iron ore.
p: India has fairly abundant iron ore — the largest reserve in Asia; the two main types are haematite and magnetite, in great demand internationally because of superior quality.

Iron ore mines are close to coal fields in the north-eastern plateau region, which adds to their advantage. About 95% of reserves are in Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Goa, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.

Odisha: Sundergarh, Mayurbhanj and Jhar — mines at Gurumahisani, Sulaipet, Badampahar (Mayurbhanj), Kiruburu (Kendujhar) and Bonai (Sundergarh). Jharkhand: Noamundi and Gua in Poorbi and Paschimi Singhbhum.

Chhattisgarh: Dalli and Rajhara in Durg; Bailadila in Dantewada. Karnataka: Sandur-Hospet (Ballari), Baba Budan hills and Kudremukh (Chikkamagaluru). Maharashtra (Chandrapur, Bhandara, Ratnagiri), Telangana (Karimnagar, Warangal), Goa and Tamil Nadu (Salem, Nilgiris) also have deposits.
Map work: mark Mayurbhanj (Odisha), Durg and Bailadila (Chhattisgarh), Ballari and Kudremukh (Karnataka).

ex.q: Match mines to states: Noamundi, Kudremukh, Dalli-Rajhara, Badampahar.
st: Noamundi → Jharkhand (Singhbhum).
Kudremukh → Karnataka (Chikkamagaluru).
Dalli-Rajhara → Chhattisgarh (Durg).
Badampahar → Odisha (Mayurbhanj).
ex.a: Noamundi–Jharkhand; Kudremukh–Karnataka; Dalli-Rajhara–Chhattisgarh; Badampahar–Odisha

topics.rl: Bhilai Steel Plant gets its iron ore from Dalli-Rajhara, while Bailadila ore is exported through Visakhapatnam port.

rv.summary: India has Asia's largest iron ore reserve, mainly high-grade haematite and magnetite in demand abroad. About 95% of reserves are in Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Goa, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, and north-eastern mines lie near coal fields.
focus: Types and quality of Indian iron ore
Mines and their states/districts
Advantage of iron ore near coal fields
remember: Main types: haematite and magnetite
Odisha: Gurumahisani, Sulaipet, Badampahar (Mayurbhanj), Kiruburu, Bonai; Jharkhand: Noamundi, Gua
Chhattisgarh: Dalli-Rajhara (Durg), Bailadila (Dantewada); Karnataka: Sandur-Hospet (Ballari), Kudremukh (Chikkamagaluru)
traps: Bailadila is in Chhattisgarh, not Karnataka
Bauxite and laterite are not types of iron ore

topics.h: No steel without manganese, no aluminium without bauxite. Odisha leads India in both!
p: Manganese is an important raw material for smelting iron ore and for making ferro alloys; its deposits occur in almost all geological formations but mainly in the Dharwar system.

Odisha is the leading manganese producer (Bonai, Kendujhar, Sundergarh, Gangpur, Koraput, Kalahandi, Bolangir); Karnataka (Dharwar, Ballari, Belagavi, North Canara, Chikkamagaluru, Shivamogga, Chitradurga, Tumakuru); Maharashtra (Nagpur, Bhandara, Ratnagiri — far from steel plants); Madhya Pradesh (Balaghat–Chhindwara–Nimar–Mandla–Jhabua belt); Telangana, Goa and Jharkhand are minor producers.
India is poorly endowed with non-ferrous metallic minerals except bauxite.
Bauxite is the ore used to make aluminium; it is found mainly in tertiary deposits associated with laterite rocks on the plateaus or hill ranges of Peninsular India and in coastal tracts.

Odisha is the largest bauxite producer (Kalahandi and Sambalpur leading; Bolangir, Koraput); the patlands of Lohardaga (Jharkhand); Gujarat (Bhavnagar, Jamnagar); Chhattisgarh (Amarkantak plateau); Madhya Pradesh (Katni–Jabalpur, Balaghat); Maharashtra (Kolaba, Thane, Ratnagiri, Satara, Pune, Kolhapur).

ex.q: Why do aluminium smelters in Odisha have an advantage?
st: Odisha is the largest bauxite producer (Kalahandi, Koraput etc.).
Raw material is nearby, cutting transport costs.
Power from nearby coal-based plants is also available.
ex.a: Bauxite is available nearby (plus power)

topics.rl: NALCO's bauxite mines at Panchpatmali (Koraput, Odisha) feed one of Asia's largest integrated aluminium complexes.

rv.summary: Manganese, used in smelting iron and making ferro alloys, occurs mainly in Dharwar rocks; Odisha leads production. India is poor in non-ferrous minerals except bauxite, the aluminium ore found in laterite-linked tertiary deposits; Odisha is the largest producer.
focus: Uses, rocks and states of manganese
Bauxite: use, rock association and states
India's poor endowment of non-ferrous minerals
remember: Manganese: smelting iron ore, ferro alloys; Dharwar system; Odisha leads
Bauxite: aluminium ore; tertiary deposits with laterite; Odisha largest (Kalahandi, Sambalpur, Koraput)
India is poorly endowed with non-ferrous minerals except bauxite
traps: Bauxite is the ore of aluminium, not iron or copper
India is not rich in all non-ferrous minerals

topics.t: Copper, mica and other non-metallic minerals
topics.h: The copper in your house wiring may come from Khetri in Rajasthan, and the mica in old electrical insulation from the Gaya–Hazaribagh belt.
p: Copper is indispensable in the electrical industry for wires, electric motors, transformers and generators; it is alloyable, malleable and ductile, and is mixed with gold to give strength to jewellery.

Copper deposits mainly occur in Singhbhum district (Jharkhand), Balaghat district (Madhya Pradesh) and Jhunjhunu (Khetri) and Alwar districts (Rajasthan); minor producers: Agnigundala (Guntur, Andhra Pradesh), Chitradurga and Hassan (Karnataka), South Arcot (Tamil Nadu).
Mica is used mainly in electrical and electronic industries; it can be split into very thin sheets that are tough and flexible.

Mica areas: in Jharkhand, high-quality mica comes from a belt about 150 km long and 32 km wide from Gaya to Hazaribagh; Nellore (Andhra Pradesh) produces the best quality mica; in Rajasthan, a belt of about 320 km from Jaipur to Bhilwara and around Udaipur (with Ajmer and Beawar); also Karnataka (Mysuru, Hassan), Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and West Bengal.

Other non-metallic minerals include limestone, dolomite and phosphate (used in cement, steel flux and fertilisers). Map work: copper — Hazaribagh, Singhbhum, Khetri; bauxite — Katni, Bilaspur, Koraput; mica — Ajmer, Beawar, Nellore, Gaya, Hazaribagh.

ex.q: Why is copper so important to the electrical industry?
st: It is an excellent conductor of electricity.
It is ductile (drawn into wires) and malleable.
So it is used in wires, motors, transformers and generators.
ex.a: Its conductivity, ductility and malleability make it ideal for wires and machines

topics.rl: Hindustan Copper's Khetri complex in Jhunjhunu and Malanjkhand mine in Balaghat are India's major copper sources.

rv.summary: Copper, being alloyable, malleable and ductile, is vital for wires, motors, transformers and generators; deposits are in Singhbhum, Balaghat and Khetri. Mica, split into thin tough sheets, serves the electrical industry; the Gaya–Hazaribagh belt, Nellore and Rajasthan are key areas.
focus: Uses, properties and areas of copper
Uses and areas of mica
Other non-metallic minerals like limestone
remember: Copper: Singhbhum (Jharkhand), Balaghat (MP), Khetri–Jhunjhunu and Alwar (Rajasthan)
Mica: Gaya–Hazaribagh belt (~150 km); Nellore — best quality; Jaipur–Bhilwara belt in Rajasthan
Limestone, dolomite, phosphate: cement, steel flux, fertilisers
traps: Limestone is non-metallic, not a ferrous mineral
Don't confuse Nellore (mica) with Agnigundala, Guntur (copper)

topics.t: Coal: uses, types and Damodar valley fields
topics.h: Most of India's electricity is still generated by burning coal — much of it dug from Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh.
p: Mineral fuels are essential for generating power, needed by agriculture, industry, transport and other sectors.
Coal is mainly used in thermal power generation and in smelting of iron ore.

Coal in India occurs in rock sequences of two main geological ages: Gondwana (a little over 200 million years old), which holds most of the reserves, and Tertiary (about 55 million years old). About 80 per cent of Indian coal is bituminous and of non-coking grade.
The most important Gondwana coalfields are in the Damodar valley, in the Jharkhand–Bengal coal belt: Raniganj, Jharia, Bokaro, Giridih and Karanpura.
Jharia is the largest coalfield, followed by Raniganj.

ex.q: Gondwana coal is a little over 200 million years old and Tertiary coal about 55 million years old. Roughly how many million years older is Gondwana coal?
st: So Gondwana coal is at least about 145 million years older.
ex.a: At least about 145 million years

topics.rl: Coal India Ltd, headquartered in Kolkata, runs mines across the Damodar valley; Jharia's underground fires are a long-standing problem.

rv.summary: Coal is used mainly for thermal power and smelting iron ore. Most reserves are Gondwana coal (a little over 200 million years old), the rest Tertiary (about 55 million years). The Damodar valley's Jharkhand–Bengal belt has Raniganj, Jharia, Bokaro, Giridih and Karanpura; Jharia is the largest.
focus: Uses of coal
Gondwana vs Tertiary coal
Damodar valley coalfields
remember: Coal: thermal power generation and smelting of iron ore
Gondwana coal: >200 million years, most reserves; Tertiary: ~55 million years
Damodar valley fields: Raniganj, Jharia, Bokaro, Giridih, Karanpura; Jharia largest, then Raniganj
traps: Raniganj is second, not the largest
Neyveli is a lignite field in Tamil Nadu, not a Damodar coalfield

topics.t: Other coalfields, tertiary coal and lignite
topics.h: Coal under Cherrapunji, the rainiest place on Earth? Yes — the north-east has young Tertiary coal.
p: Besides the Damodar, other river valleys with Gondwana coal are the Godavari, Mahanadi, Sone and Wardha.

Important mining centres: Singrauli (Madhya Pradesh; part in Uttar Pradesh), Korba (Chhattisgarh), Talcher and Rampur (Odisha), Chanda–Wardha, Kamptee and Bander (Maharashtra), Singareni (Telangana) and Pandur (Andhra Pradesh).

Tertiary coals occur in Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya and Nagaland: Darangiri, Cherrapunji, Mewlong and Langrin (Meghalaya); Makum, Jaipur and Nazira (upper Assam); Namchik–Namphuk (Arunachal Pradesh); and Kalakot (Jammu and Kashmir).
Brown coal or lignite occurs in the coastal areas of Tamil Nadu (Neyveli), Puducherry, Gujarat and Jammu and Kashmir.
Map work: mark Jharia, Bokaro, Raniganj and Neyveli.

ex.q: Classify: Korba, Makum, Neyveli, Singareni.
st: Korba (Chhattisgarh), Singareni (Telangana) → Gondwana coal.
Makum (Assam) → Tertiary coal.
Neyveli (Tamil Nadu) → lignite.
ex.a: Gondwana: Korba, Singareni; Tertiary: Makum; lignite: Neyveli

topics.rl: NLC India's lignite mines at Neyveli fuel thermal power plants supplying electricity to Tamil Nadu and neighbouring states.

rv.summary: Other Gondwana coal lies in the Godavari, Mahanadi, Sone and Wardha valleys — Singrauli, Korba, Talcher, Rampur, Chanda–Wardha, Singareni, Pandur. Tertiary coal occurs in Assam, Arunachal, Meghalaya and Nagaland, and lignite (brown coal) at Neyveli, Puducherry, Gujarat and J&K.
focus: Gondwana coalfields outside the Damodar valley
Tertiary coalfields of the north-east
Lignite deposits
remember: Korba — Chhattisgarh; Talcher, Rampur — Odisha; Singareni — Telangana; Singrauli — MP (part UP)
Tertiary: Darangiri, Cherrapunji, Mewlong, Langrin (Meghalaya); Makum, Jaipur, Nazira (Assam)
Lignite = brown coal: Neyveli (Tamil Nadu), Puducherry, Gujarat, J&K
traps: Lignite is not mainly in the Damodar valley
Singareni is in Telangana, not Andhra Pradesh

topics.h: Mumbai High, 160 km out in the Arabian Sea, was discovered in 1973 and changed India's oil story.
p: Crude petroleum consists of hydrocarbons in liquid and gaseous states, varying in chemical composition, colour and specific gravity; it occurs in sedimentary rocks of the Tertiary period.

It is essential for internal combustion engines in automobiles, railways and aircraft; its by-products feed petrochemical industries — fertilisers, synthetic rubber, synthetic fibre, medicines, vaseline, lubricants, wax, soap and cosmetics. Its value and many uses earn it the name 'liquid gold'.
Oil exploration became systematic after the Oil and Natural Gas Commission (ONGC) was set up in 1956; until then Digboi in Assam (where oil was struck in 1889) was the only oil-producing region.

Oil fields: Assam — Digboi, Naharkatiya, Moran; Gujarat — Ankaleshwar, Kalol, Mehsana, Nawagam, Kosamba, Lunej; Mumbai High (offshore, discovered 1973, production from 1976); Krishna–Godavari and Kaveri basins. Refineries are field-based (e.g. Digboi) or market-based (e.g. Barauni); map work: Mathura, Jamnagar, Barauni refineries.

Natural gas: the Gas Authority of India Limited (GAIL) was set up in 1984 to transport and market natural gas; it is found with oil in all fields, with exclusive reserves along the east coast (Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh), Tripura, Rajasthan and offshore wells of Gujarat and Maharashtra.

ex.q: Classify these refineries as field-based or market-based: Digboi (Assam oil field), Barauni (Bihar, far from oil fields).
st: Digboi is located on an oil field → field-based.
Barauni is located near consumers, away from oil fields → market-based.
ex.a: Digboi — field-based; Barauni — market-based

topics.rl: Reliance's Jamnagar complex in Gujarat is the world's largest refining hub; its products are exported worldwide.

rv.summary: Crude petroleum, found in Tertiary sedimentary rocks, fuels transport and feeds petrochemicals — hence 'liquid gold'. ONGC (1956) made exploration systematic; Digboi was the only field before. Fields are in Assam, Gujarat, Mumbai High (1973) and the east coast; GAIL (1984) handles natural gas.
focus: Occurrence and uses of petroleum
Key dates: Digboi 1889, ONGC 1956, Mumbai High 1973, GAIL 1984
Oil fields; field-based vs market-based refineries
remember: Assam: Digboi, Naharkatiya, Moran; Gujarat: Ankaleshwar, Kalol, Mehsana, Nawagam, Kosamba, Lunej
Mumbai High discovered 1973, production from 1976
Field-based refinery: Digboi; market-based: Barauni
traps: Digboi is field-based, not market-based
Don't mix up ONGC (1956), Mumbai High (1973) and GAIL (1984)

topics.h: Kerala's black beach sands hold some of the world's richest thorium deposits — fuel for India's future nuclear plans.
p: Uranium and thorium are the important minerals used to generate nuclear energy.

Uranium deposits occur in Dharwar rocks: along the Singhbhum copper belt (Jaduguda, Jharkhand); Udaipur, Alwar and Jhunjhunu (Rajasthan); Durg (Chhattisgarh); Bhandara (Maharashtra); and Kullu (Himachal Pradesh).

Thorium is obtained mainly from monazite and ilmenite in beach sands along the coasts of Kerala and Tamil Nadu; the world's richest monazite deposits occur in Palakkad and Kollam districts of Kerala, near Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh) and in the Mahanadi delta (Odisha).
The Atomic Energy Commission was set up in 1948; real progress came after the Atomic Energy Institute at Trombay was set up in 1954, renamed the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in 1967.
Nuclear power projects: Tarapur (Maharashtra), Rawatbhata near Kota (Rajasthan), Kalpakkam (Tamil Nadu), Narora (Uttar Pradesh), Kaiga (Karnataka) and Kakrapar (Gujarat).

ex.q: Arrange in order: BARC renamed, Atomic Energy Commission, Trombay institute.
st: 1948 — Atomic Energy Commission.
1954 — Atomic Energy Institute at Trombay.
1967 — renamed Bhabha Atomic Research Centre.
ex.a: AEC (1948) → Trombay institute (1954) → BARC (1967)

topics.rl: Kudankulam (Tamil Nadu) is now India's largest nuclear power station, built with Russian collaboration.

rv.summary: Uranium (in Dharwar rocks: Jaduguda, Rajasthan, Durg, Bhandara, Kullu) and thorium (from monazite and ilmenite beach sands of Kerala and Tamil Nadu) fuel nuclear energy. The AEC came in 1948, Trombay in 1954 (renamed BARC in 1967).
focus: Uranium and thorium sources
Key dates of India's atomic programme
Locations of nuclear power plants
remember: Uranium: Dharwar rocks; Jaduguda (Jharkhand), Udaipur, Alwar, Jhunjhunu, Durg, Bhandara, Kullu
Thorium: monazite and ilmenite; richest monazite in Palakkad and Kollam (Kerala)
AEC 1948; Trombay 1954; BARC 1967; Rawatbhata near Kota; Kalpakkam in Tamil Nadu; Kakrapar in Gujarat
traps: Kalpakkam is in Tamil Nadu, not Gujarat
Don't give BARC's naming year (1967) as Trombay's founding (1954)

topics.h: Rajasthan's Bhadla solar park, one of the world's largest, sits where the sun shines almost every day of the year.
p: Fossil fuels are exhaustible and cause pollution; non-conventional sources — solar, wind, hydro-geothermal and biomass — are renewable, more equitably distributed and environment-friendly.

Solar energy is tapped by photovoltaic cells and solar thermal technology; solar thermal is cost-competitive, environment-friendly and easy to construct; used in heaters, crop dryers and cookers. Western India (Gujarat, Rajasthan) has great potential.

Wind energy is absolutely pollution-free and inexhaustible; turbines convert the kinetic energy of wind into electricity; permanent winds, monsoon winds, local winds and land and sea breezes can be used. Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka have favourable conditions.

Tidal and wave energy: ocean currents are a store-house of infinite energy; large tidal waves occur along the west coast (e.g. Gulf of Kachchh and Gulf of Khambhat), so India has great potential, not yet utilised. Geothermal energy: heat from the earth's interior, tapped via hot springs and geysers; a plant has been commissioned at Manikaran (Himachal Pradesh); Puga valley (Ladakh) also has potential.

Bio-energy: energy from biological products — agricultural residues, municipal, industrial and other wastes; it can give electricity, heat or cooking gas, improve the rural economy, reduce pollution and pressure on fuel wood. Example: the waste-to-energy project at Okhla, Delhi.

ex.q: Suggest the best non-conventional source for: (a) Jaisalmer; (b) Gulf of Khambhat; (c) Manikaran; (d) a village with lots of cattle dung.
st: (a) Sunny desert → solar.
(b) High tides → tidal energy.
(c) Hot springs → geothermal.
(d) Cattle dung and farm waste → bio-energy (biogas).
ex.a: (a) solar, (b) tidal, (c) geothermal, (d) bio-energy

topics.rl: India's target of 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 is driven mostly by solar parks in Rajasthan and Gujarat and wind farms in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat.

rv.summary: Non-conventional sources — solar, wind, tidal and wave, geothermal and bio-energy — are renewable, more evenly spread and clean. Western India suits solar and wind, the Gulfs of Kachchh and Khambhat suit tidal energy, Manikaran has a geothermal plant, and Okhla turns waste into energy.
focus: Advantages of non-conventional energy
Best location for each source
Bio-energy and waste-to-energy
remember: Solar: photovoltaic and solar thermal; Gujarat, Rajasthan
Wind: kinetic energy → electricity; Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka
Tidal: Gulf of Kachchh, Gulf of Khambhat (not yet used); geothermal: Manikaran (HP); bio-energy: Okhla (Delhi)
traps: India has not yet utilised its tidal potential
Non-conventional sources are not exhaustible or polluting

topics.t: Conservation of mineral and energy resources
topics.h: An old aluminium can melted and remade uses about 95% less energy than making new aluminium from bauxite. Recycling is mining above ground!
p: Sustainable development requires integrating economic development with environmental concerns, conserving minerals and energy for future generations.
Alternative energy sources like solar, wind, wave and geothermal energy are inexhaustible and should be developed to replace exhaustible sources.

For metallic minerals, using scrap metals enables recycling — especially important for copper, lead and zinc, of which India's reserves are meagre. Using substitutes for scarce metals can also reduce consumption.
Export of strategic and scarce minerals must be reduced so that existing reserves last longer; improved mining techniques can reduce wastage.

Exam focus: classification of minerals; distribution of iron ore, manganese, bauxite, coal and petroleum; nuclear minerals; non-conventional energy; conservation measures; and map marking of mines and refineries.

ex.q: Suggest three ways to conserve copper in India.
st: Recycle scrap copper from old wires and machines.
Use substitutes (like aluminium wiring or optical fibre) where possible.
Reduce exports and wastage in mining and processing.
ex.a: Recycling scrap, using substitutes, reducing exports and waste

topics.rl: India's Steel Scrap Recycling Policy (2019) and e-waste rules encourage recovery of metals instead of fresh mining.

rv.summary: Sustainable development means balancing economic growth with environmental care and saving minerals and energy for the future. Ways include renewable energy, recycling scrap, substitutes and cutting exports of scarce minerals.
focus: Measures to conserve minerals and energy
Why recycling matters for copper, lead and zinc
Revising mines and minerals for map work
remember: Recycle scrap — especially copper, lead and zinc (meagre reserves)
Use substitutes for scarce metals; reduce export of strategic and scarce minerals
Develop inexhaustible sources: solar, wind, wave, geothermal
traps: Increasing exports of scarce minerals does not conserve them
Better mining techniques reduce, not increase, wastage

topics.ch: India: Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context
topics.t: Planning: meaning, sectoral and regional planning
topics.h: From 1951 to 2017, India ran its economy through Five Year Plans. Why plan at all — and plan for whom: sectors or regions?
p: Planning is the process of thinking, formulating a scheme or programme and implementing a set of actions to achieve some goal.
In India, planning was done through Five Year Plans prepared by the Planning Commission, set up in 1950; the First Five Year Plan began in 1951.

Sectoral planning: formulating and implementing schemes for development of various sectors of the economy — agriculture, irrigation, manufacturing, power, construction, transport, communication, social infrastructure and services.
Regional planning: development is not uniform over space; some regions are more developed than others, so regional planning aims to reduce regional imbalances in development.

ex.q: A state draws up a plan to build roads, schools and irrigation specifically for its backward southern districts. Is this sectoral or regional planning?
st: The plan targets a particular region (backward districts).
Its aim is to reduce imbalance with other regions.
So it is regional planning.
ex.a: Regional planning

topics.rl: The Aspirational Districts Programme (2018) focuses on 112 lagging districts — a modern example of regional planning.

rv.summary: Planning means thinking, formulating a scheme and implementing actions to reach a goal. India planned through Five Year Plans of the Planning Commission (1950; First Plan 1951). Sectoral planning develops sectors; regional planning reduces regional imbalances.
focus: Definition of planning
Sectoral vs regional planning with examples
Why India needs regional planning
remember: Planning Commission set up in 1950; First Five Year Plan began in 1951
Sectoral planning: agriculture, irrigation, manufacturing, power, construction, transport, communication, services
Regional planning: reduce regional imbalances in development
traps: Sectoral planning does not aim at reducing regional differences — regional planning does
The Planning Commission came in 1950, not 1951

topics.ch: India: Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context
topics.t: NITI Aayog and target area planning
topics.h: On 1 January 2015, the 65-year-old Planning Commission was replaced by a 'think tank' — NITI Aayog.
p: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015. It acts as a think tank giving strategic and technical advice to the Central and State Governments, follows a bottom-up, decentralised approach and promotes cooperative federalism.
To arrest growing regional and social disparities, the Planning Commission introduced target area and target group approaches.
Target area programmes: Command Area Development Programme, Drought Prone Area Programme, Desert Development Programme and Hill Area Development Programme.
Target group programmes: Small Farmers Development Agency (SFDA) and Marginal Farmers Development Agency (MFDA).
In the Eighth Five Year Plan, special area programmes were designed to develop infrastructure in hill areas, north-eastern states, tribal areas and backward areas.

ex.q: Classify: Drought Prone Area Programme, Small Farmers Development Agency, Hill Area Development Programme, Marginal Farmers Development Agency.
st: Programmes for a type of area → target area: DPAP, HADP.
Programmes for a group of people → target group: SFDA, MFDA.
ex.a: Target area: DPAP, HADP; target group: SFDA, MFDA

topics.rl: NITI Aayog ranks states on the SDG India Index and health and education indicators — encouraging competitive and cooperative federalism.

rv.summary: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015 as a think tank promoting cooperative federalism. To reduce disparities, target area programmes (command area, drought-prone, desert, hill) and target group programmes (SFDA, MFDA) were started.
focus: NITI Aayog: date, full form, role
Target area vs target group programmes
Special area programmes of the Eighth Plan
remember: NITI Aayog = National Institution for Transforming India; from 1 January 2015
Target area: Command Area Development, DPAP, Desert Development, Hill Area Development
Target group: Small Farmers Development Agency, Marginal Farmers Development Agency
traps: SFDA and MFDA are target group, not target area, programmes
NITI Aayog promotes cooperative federalism, not centralism

topics.ch: India: Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context
topics.h: Apple orchards in Uttarakhand, tea in Darjeeling, Nilgiri dairy cooperatives — hill development must suit the hills.
p: The Hill Area Development Programme was initiated during the Fifth Five Year Plan, covering 15 districts: all the hilly districts of Uttar Pradesh (now Uttarakhand), Mikir Hill and North Cachar hills of Assam, Darjeeling district of West Bengal and Nilgiri district of Tamil Nadu.

The National Committee on the Development of Backward Areas (1981) recommended that all hill areas with a height above 600 m and not covered under the tribal sub-plan be treated as backward hill areas.
Detailed plans were drawn to harness indigenous resources through horticulture, plantation agriculture, animal husbandry, poultry, forestry, and small-scale and village industries.
The plans were to take into account the topography, ecological, social and economic conditions of each area.

ex.q: Why would large heavy industries not be a suitable focus for hill area development?
st: Hill topography is rugged and the ecology fragile.
Plans must suit local topography, ecology and resources.
So horticulture, plantations, animal husbandry, forestry and small industries are better.
ex.a: They don't suit hill topography and fragile ecology; local-resource activities do

topics.rl: Himachal's apple economy and Uttarakhand's organic farming and homestays reflect the HADP idea of using local resources.

rv.summary: The Hill Area Development Programme began in the Fifth Plan, covering 15 districts — hilly Uttarakhand, Mikir Hill and North Cachar (Assam), Darjeeling and Nilgiri. Hill areas above 600 m outside the tribal sub-plan were treated as backward; plans used local resources like horticulture and forestry.
focus: Plan period and districts of HADP
The 600 m criterion for backward hill areas
Activities suited to hill development
remember: HADP: Fifth Five Year Plan; 15 districts
Districts: hilly UP (now Uttarakhand), Mikir Hill and North Cachar (Assam), Darjeeling (WB), Nilgiri (TN)
1981 Committee: hill areas above 600 m not under tribal sub-plan = backward hill areas
traps: HADP began in the Fifth Plan; DPAP in the Fourth
Darjeeling was included in HADP

topics.ch: India: Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context
topics.t: Drought Prone Area Programme: aims and approach
topics.h: In a drought year, a farmer in Marathwada loses his crop and his income. DPAP tried to give him work — and long-term water security.
p: The Drought Prone Area Programme (DPAP) was initiated during the Fourth Five Year Plan with the objectives of providing employment to people in drought-prone areas and creating productive assets.
Initially it emphasised the construction of labour-intensive civil works.

Later it emphasised irrigation projects, land development programmes, afforestation, grassland development and creation of basic rural infrastructure such as electricity, roads, markets, credit and services.
The National Committee on Development of Backward Areas found that the programme was largely confined to agriculture and allied sectors, with a major focus on restoration of ecological balance.

ex.q: Why did DPAP shift from labour-intensive civil works to irrigation, afforestation and grassland development?
st: Civil works gave short-term jobs but not lasting drought-proofing.
Irrigation, afforestation and pastures build productive assets and restore ecology.
These reduce the impact of future droughts.
ex.a: To create lasting productive assets and restore ecological balance

topics.rl: MGNREGA works like farm ponds, check dams and tree planting continue the DPAP idea of employment plus drought-proofing assets.

rv.summary: The Drought Prone Area Programme began in the Fourth Plan to provide jobs and create productive assets in drought-prone areas. It first stressed labour-intensive civil works, then irrigation, land development, afforestation, grassland development and rural infrastructure.
focus: Plan period and objectives of DPAP
Shift from civil works to asset building
Committee's observation on DPAP
remember: DPAP: Fourth Five Year Plan; employment + productive assets
Initially: labour-intensive civil works
Later: irrigation, land development, afforestation, grassland, rural infrastructure (electricity, roads, markets, credit)
traps: DPAP targeted drought-prone rural areas, not urban unemployment
DPAP began in the Fourth Plan, not the Fifth

topics.ch: India: Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context
topics.t: Drought-prone areas of India and watershed approach
topics.h: Rajasthan, Marathwada, Rayalaseema, Telangana — these names often appear in drought headlines. Why these regions?
p: Growing population pressure forces people to use marginal lands for agriculture, causing ecological degradation; so alternative employment opportunities are needed in drought-prone areas.
The strategy for these areas is an integrated watershed development approach at the micro level: restoring ecological balance among water, soil, plants, and human and animal populations.

In 1967 the Planning Commission identified 67 districts (entirely or partly) as drought-prone; in 1972 the Irrigation Commission introduced the criterion of 30 per cent irrigated area to demarcate drought-prone areas.

Drought-prone areas mostly cover the semi-arid and arid tracts of Rajasthan, Gujarat, western Madhya Pradesh, Marathwada (Maharashtra), the Rayalaseema and Telangana plateaus, the Karnataka plateau and the highlands and interior parts of Tamil Nadu.
Drought-prone areas of Punjab, Haryana and northern Rajasthan are largely protected because of the spread of irrigation.

ex.q: A district has 18% of its net sown area irrigated and gets low, erratic rainfall. Is it drought-prone by the Irrigation Commission's criterion?
st: The 1972 criterion uses 30% irrigated area.
With low, erratic rainfall, it would be classed as drought-prone.
ex.a: Yes — its irrigated area is below the 30% criterion

topics.rl: Maharashtra's Jalyukt Shivar Abhiyan built check dams and farm ponds in Marathwada villages using a watershed approach.

rv.summary: Population pressure pushes farming onto marginal land in drought-prone areas, so they need alternative jobs and integrated micro-level watershed development. In 1967, 67 districts were identified as drought-prone; in 1972 the Irrigation Commission used a 30% irrigated-area criterion.
focus: Identification of drought-prone areas (1967, 1972)
Drought-prone regions of India
Watershed strategy and why Punjab–Haryana are protected
remember: 1967: 67 districts identified as drought-prone
1972 Irrigation Commission: 30% irrigated area criterion
Drought-prone: Rajasthan, Gujarat, western MP, Marathwada, Rayalaseema, Telangana, Karnataka plateau, interior TN
traps: Marathwada is drought-prone, not assured of irrigation
Don't confuse 67 drought-prone districts with HADP's 15 districts

topics.ch: India: Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context
topics.h: High in the Himachal Himalayas, the Gaddi shepherds of Bharmaur move their flocks with the seasons, speaking their own Gaddiali dialect.
p: The Bharmaur tribal area comprises the Bharmaur and Holi tehsils of Chamba district, Himachal Pradesh; it has been a notified tribal area since 21 November 1975.
It is inhabited by the Gaddis, a tribal community who have maintained a distinct identity in the Himalayan region; they practised transhumance and converse in the Gaddiali dialect.

The region has harsh climatic conditions, a low resource base and a fragile environment. The Ravi and its tributaries, the Budhil and Tundahen, drain it and carve deep gorges; it lies between the Dhaula Dhar range (south) and Pir Panjal (north) and has four physiographic divisions — Holi, Khani, Kugti and Tundah.
Winters are freezing with snowfall (mean January temperature about 4°C); summers are mild (July about 26°C). Gaddis traditionally migrate to lower areas in winter.

The economy was based on agriculture and allied activities like sheep and goat rearing; the region was economically and socially backward and isolated. On a map, Bharmaur lies in Chamba district in the north-west of Himachal Pradesh.

ex.q: What is the difference between the mean July and January temperatures in Bharmaur?
st: July ≈ 26°C; January ≈ 4°C.
Difference = 26 − 4 = 22°C.

topics.rl: Gaddi shepherds still move flocks between Chamba's high pastures and Kangra's lower valleys — a living tradition of transhumance.

rv.summary: Bharmaur (Bharmaur and Holi tehsils, Chamba, Himachal Pradesh) has been a notified tribal area since 21 November 1975. Its Gaddis practised transhumance and speak Gaddiali. Drained by the Ravi, Budhil and Tundahen between Dhaula Dhar and Pir Panjal, it has harsh winters.

The Gaddis: identity, dialect and transhumance
Physical setting and climate

traps: Bharmaur's economy was agro-pastoral, not industrial
Bharmaur is in Chamba, not Kullu or Kangra

topics.ch: India: Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context
topics.t: Bharmaur: Integrated Tribal Development Project and outcomes
topics.h: In 1971, fewer than 2 in 100 women in Bharmaur could read. By 2011, about 65 did. What changed?
p: Development of Bharmaur began in the 1970s when the Gaddis were included among Scheduled Tribes. The tribal sub-plan was introduced in 1974 under the Fifth Five Year Plan, and Bharmaur was designated as one of five Integrated Tribal Development Projects (ITDP) in Himachal Pradesh.

Aim: improve the quality of life of the Gaddis and narrow the gap in development between Bharmaur and other areas of Himachal Pradesh; highest priority to transport and communications, agriculture and allied activities, and social and community services.

Outcomes: infrastructure — schools, health care facilities, potable water, roads, communications and electricity. Villages along the Ravi in Holi and Khani areas benefited most; remote villages in Tundah and Kugti are still outside the ambit of development.

Social benefits: big rise in literacy, improved sex ratio and decline in child marriage; female literacy rose from 1.88 per cent in 1971 to 65 per cent in 2011, and the gender gap in literacy declined.

Economic change: shift from subsistence agro-pastoral economy (foodgrains, livestock) to more pulses and cash crops (though with traditional tools); only about one-tenth of households now practise transhumance, and many Gaddis migrate to Kangra and nearby areas in winter for wage labour.

ex.q: By how many percentage points did female literacy in Bharmaur rise from 1971 to 2011?
st: Increase = 65 − 1.88 = 63.12 percentage points.
ex.a: 63.12 percentage points

topics.rl: Roads and schools under ITDP connected Holi and Khani villages to Chamba town, opening jobs and colleges to young Gaddis.

rv.summary: Bharmaur's development began in the 1970s; the tribal sub-plan came in 1974 (Fifth Plan) and Bharmaur became one of five ITDPs in Himachal Pradesh. Female literacy rose from 1.88% (1971) to 65% (2011), and only about a tenth of households still practise transhumance.
focus: Tribal sub-plan and ITDP priorities
Infrastructure and social outcomes
Economic change and decline of transhumance
remember: Tribal sub-plan: 1974, Fifth Five Year Plan; Bharmaur one of five ITDPs in HP
Priorities: transport and communications, agriculture and allied, social and community services
Female literacy 1.88% (1971) → 65% (2011); transhumance now ≈ one-tenth of households
traps: Remote Tundah and Kugti villages benefited least; Holi and Khani along the Ravi benefited most
ITDP did not prioritise heavy industry

topics.ch: India: Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context
topics.h: In 1987, a commission led by Norway's Prime Minister gave the world a definition of development that every exam still asks for.
p: The concept of development has changed: earlier it meant economic growth (GNP, per capita income); later it came to include social welfare and qualitative change in people's lives.
In the late 1960s, growing environmental awareness in the western world was reflected in books like 'The Population Bomb' by Ehrlich (1968) and 'The Limits to Growth' by Meadows and others (1972).

The United Nations set up the World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED), headed by Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland; its report 'Our Common Future' (1987), also called the Brundtland Report, popularised sustainable development.
Sustainable development: development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
It integrates ecological, social and economic aspects of development; the UN's 17 Sustainable Development Goals (adopted in 2015) carry this idea forward.

ex.q: A town wants to grow by cutting down its watershed forest for housing. Using the Brundtland definition, explain why this may not be sustainable.
st: It meets present housing needs.
But it destroys the forest that protects water and soil for the future.
This compromises future generations' ability to meet their needs.
ex.a: It meets present needs at the cost of future generations

topics.rl: India's National Action Plan on Climate Change and SDG India Index by NITI Aayog track progress towards sustainable development.

rv.summary: Development once meant only economic growth; later it included social welfare and the environment. After books like 'The Population Bomb' (Ehrlich, 1968) and 'The Limits to Growth' (Meadows, 1972), the Brundtland Report 'Our Common Future' (1987) defined sustainable development.
focus: The Brundtland definition of sustainable development
WCED, Brundtland and 'Our Common Future'
Earlier books on environmental limits
remember: Sustainable development: meets present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs
WCED headed by Gro Harlem Brundtland; 'Our Common Future' (1987)
The Population Bomb — Ehrlich (1968); The Limits to Growth — Meadows and others (1972)
traps: Brundtland did not write The Limits to Growth
Sustainable development is not stopping all growth

topics.ch: India: Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context
topics.t: Indira Gandhi Canal: origin, stages and command area
topics.h: A canal running hundreds of kilometres through the Thar desert, parallel to the Pakistan border — the Indira Gandhi Canal turned sand into fields.
p: The Indira Gandhi Canal (earlier the Rajasthan Canal) is one of the largest canal systems in India; conceived by Kanwar Sain in 1948, it was launched on 31 March 1958.
It originates at the Harike barrage in Punjab and runs parallel to the Pakistan border at an average distance of 40 km in the Thar desert (Marusthali) of Rajasthan.
The total planned length of the system is 9,060 km, serving a culturable command area of 19.63 lakh hectares; about 70 per cent was to be irrigated by flow and the rest by lift irrigation.

Stage I: command area in Ganganagar, Hanumangarh and northern Bikaner districts; gently undulating topography; culturable command area 5.53 lakh ha; irrigation from the early 1960s. Stage II: Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Barmer, Jodhpur, Nagaur and Churu districts; desert with shifting sand dunes and summer temperatures up to 50°C; command area 14.10 lakh ha; irrigation from the mid-1980s.
In lift canals, water is lifted up to make it flow against the slope of the land. Map reading: trace the canal from Harike (Punjab) south-west through Ganganagar to Jaisalmer and Barmer.

ex.q: Check that the two stages add up to the total culturable command area.
st: Stage I = 5.53 lakh ha; Stage II = 14.10 lakh ha.
This equals the total command area.
ex.a: 19.63 lakh hectares

topics.rl: Ganganagar, once desert, is now called the 'food basket of Rajasthan' thanks to Stage I of the canal.

rv.summary: The Indira Gandhi Canal, conceived by Kanwar Sain (1948) and launched on 31 March 1958, starts at Harike barrage and runs about 40 km from the Pakistan border. It is 9,060 km long with 19.63 lakh ha command area: Stage I 5.53 lakh ha, Stage II 14.10 lakh ha.

Stage I vs Stage II districts and areas
Flow vs lift irrigation

Don't put Jaisalmer and Barmer in Stage I

topics.ch: India: Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context
topics.t: Indira Gandhi Canal: positive and negative impacts
topics.h: Where camels once grazed on bajra stubble, farmers now grow wheat and cotton — but some fields have turned white with salt.
p: Positive impacts: availability of soil moisture increased; afforestation and pasture development programmes greened the land; soil erosion, wind erosion and siltation of canals reduced; canal water also met drinking water needs.
Agricultural changes: cultivated area and intensity of cropping increased tremendously.
Traditional crops — gram, bajra and guar — have been replaced by wheat, cotton, groundnut and rice.
Negative impacts: intensive irrigation and excessive use of water have led to the twin environmental problems of waterlogging and soil salinity, raising doubts about long-term sustainability.

ex.q: Why does excessive canal irrigation in a desert cause soil salinity?
st: Too much water raises the water table (waterlogging).
In high heat, water evaporates from the surface.
Dissolved salts are left behind on the soil — salinity.
ex.a: Waterlogging plus high evaporation leaves salts on the surface

topics.rl: Parts of the canal command area now need drainage and gypsum treatment to reclaim salt-affected soils.

rv.summary: The canal raised soil moisture, greened the land through afforestation and pastures, cut erosion and supplied drinking water. Cropped area and intensity rose, and gram, bajra and guar gave way to wheat, cotton, groundnut and rice. But overuse of water brought waterlogging and soil salinity.
focus: Positive ecological and agricultural impacts
Change in cropping pattern
Waterlogging and salinity as negative impacts
remember: Positive: more soil moisture, afforestation, pastures, less soil and wind erosion, drinking water
Old crops gram, bajra, guar → wheat, cotton, groundnut, rice
Negative: waterlogging and soil salinity from intensive irrigation
traps: The canal increased, not reduced, soil moisture
Don't swap the old crops (gram, bajra, guar) with the new ones

topics.ch: India: Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context
topics.t: Sustainable development in the canal area: water and land measures
topics.h: Warabandi: a rotating timetable that gives every farmer on a canal outlet a fair turn of water. Simple idea, big impact!
p: The first and foremost requirement is strict implementation of the water management policy: protective irrigation in Stage I, and extensive irrigation of crops and pasture development in Stage II.
The cropping pattern should not include water-intensive crops; people should be encouraged to grow plantation crops such as citrus fruits instead.

Command Area Development (CAD) programmes — lining of watercourses, land development and levelling, and the warabandi system (equal distribution of canal water in the command area of an outlet) — should be implemented to reduce conveyance loss of water.
Areas affected by waterlogging and soil salinity should be reclaimed.

ex.q: Why is lining of watercourses an important CAD measure?
st: Unlined channels lose water by seepage into sandy soil.
Seepage raises the water table and causes waterlogging.
Lining reduces conveyance loss and waterlogging.
ex.a: It cuts seepage losses and reduces waterlogging

topics.rl: Kinnow and other citrus orchards around Ganganagar show how less water-intensive plantation crops can thrive with canal water.

rv.summary: Sustainable use of the canal needs strict water management: protective irrigation in Stage I and extensive irrigation with pastures in Stage II, no water-intensive crops (grow citrus instead), CAD measures like lining, levelling and warabandi, and reclamation of waterlogged and saline land.
focus: Water management in Stage I and Stage II
Suitable cropping pattern
CAD measures including warabandi
remember: Stage I: protective irrigation; Stage II: extensive irrigation of crops and pasture development
Avoid water-intensive crops; encourage plantation crops like citrus
CAD: lining watercourses, land levelling, warabandi (equal distribution of water at an outlet)
traps: Lining watercourses reduces, not increases, seepage
Don't swap the irrigation types of the two stages

topics.ch: India: Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context
topics.t: Sustainable development in the canal area: ecology, people and economy
topics.h: Rows of trees planted as shelterbelts now break the desert winds that once buried canals in sand.
p: Eco-development through afforestation, shelterbelt plantation and pasture development is necessary, particularly in the fragile environment of Stage II.
Social sustainability requires that land allottees with poor economic backgrounds be given adequate financial and institutional support to cultivate their land.

Agriculture and allied activities must develop along with other sectors of the economy (like agro-processing and marketing), diversifying the economic base and linking villages, agro-service centres and market centres.

Exam focus: DPAP, ITDP and IGC case studies; sectoral vs regional planning; target area planning; HADP; Bharmaur outcomes; the concept of sustainable development; and measures for sustainability in the canal command area.

ex.q: Why are shelterbelts especially important in Stage II of the canal area?
st: Stage II has shifting sand dunes and strong winds.
Shelterbelts (rows of trees) break wind speed.
They reduce wind erosion and protect canals and fields from sand.
ex.a: They break desert winds and reduce erosion and sand deposition

topics.rl: Food parks and mandis in Ganganagar and Hanumangarh help farmers process and sell kinnow, cotton and wheat — diversifying the canal economy.

rv.summary: Sustainability in the canal area also needs eco-development (afforestation, shelterbelts, pastures), especially in fragile Stage II; financial and institutional support for poor land allottees; and growth of agro-processing and marketing alongside farming to diversify the economy.
focus: Eco-development in Stage II
Social sustainability for poor allottees
Diversifying the economic base
remember: Afforestation, shelterbelts and pastures, especially in Stage II
Poor land allottees need financial and institutional support
Develop agro-processing and marketing with agriculture; link villages, agro-service and market centres
traps: Sustainability does not depend only on agriculture
Shelterbelts reduce wind erosion; they do not dry up canals

topics.t: Transport and communication: lifelines of the economy
topics.h: Every packet of Amul butter in Guwahati, every Aadhaar SMS in a village — all depend on India's transport and communication networks.
p: Transport and communication are the lifelines of an economy: they move goods, services, people and ideas from places of production to places of consumption.
Their means evolved from ancient routes — the Grand Trunk road and the Silk Route — to modern road, rail, air and digital networks.
Modes of transport: land (roads and railways), water (inland waterways and oceanic routes), air and pipelines.
Communication may be personal (letters, phone, internet) or mass communication (radio, television, newspapers, films).

ex.q: Classify: (a) a WhatsApp message to a friend; (b) a Doordarshan news bulletin; (c) a goods train; (d) an oil pipeline.
st: (a) Personal communication.
(b) Mass communication.
(c) Land transport (rail).
(d) Pipeline transport.
ex.a: (a) personal comm., (b) mass comm., (c) rail transport, (d) pipeline

topics.rl: PM Gati Shakti integrates rail, road, waterway, airport and pipeline planning into one digital master plan.

rv.summary: Transport and communication are lifelines of the economy, moving goods, people and ideas from production to consumption. Modes of transport are land (roads, rail), water, air and pipelines; communication is personal (letters, phone, internet) or mass (radio, TV, newspapers, films).

Modes of transport
Personal vs mass communication
remember: Modes: land (roads, railways), water (inland, oceanic), air, pipelines
Personal communication: letters, phone, internet; mass: radio, TV, newspapers, films
Ancient routes: Grand Trunk road, Silk Route

Pipelines carry liquids and gases, not passengers

topics.h: Sher Shah Suri's Shahi road ran from Sonargaon in Bengal to Peshawar. Today its stretch from Amritsar to Kolkata is still busy!
p: Pathways and unmetalled roads have been used since ancient times; modern roads developed with economic and technological growth.

Sher Shah Suri built the Shahi (Royal) road from Sonargaon (now in Bangladesh) to Peshawar (now in Pakistan); the British renamed it the Grand Trunk (GT) road, connecting Calcutta (Kolkata) and Peshawar. Today it extends from Amritsar to Kolkata.
India has one of the largest road networks in the world, over 60 lakh km long; about 85 per cent of passenger and 70 per cent of freight traffic are carried by road every year.
Road development plans: the Nagpur Plan (1943) and the twenty-year road plan (1961).

ex.q: If roads carry 70% of freight, and total freight is 500 million tonnes in a year, how much moves by road?
st: = 350 million tonnes.
ex.a: 350 million tonnes

topics.rl: The Bharatmala Pariyojana is building economic corridors and expressways to cut freight time across India.

rv.summary: Sher Shah Suri built the Shahi road from Sonargaon to Peshawar; the British renamed it the Grand Trunk road, which now runs from Amritsar to Kolkata. India's road network exceeds 60 lakh km and carries about 85% of passengers and 70% of freight; road plans came in 1943 (Nagpur) and 1961.

topics.t: Classification of roads and National Highways
topics.h: National Highways are only about 2% of India's road length — yet they carry about 40% of road traffic!
p: For construction and maintenance, roads are classified as National Highways, State Highways, District Roads, Rural Roads and other roads (Border Roads and International Highways).

National Highways (NH) are constructed and maintained by the Central Government; they are used for inter-state transport and movement of defence personnel and material in strategic areas; they connect state capitals, major cities, ports and railway junctions.
NHs constitute only about 2 per cent of total road length but carry about 40 per cent of road traffic.
The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), operationalised in 1995, is an autonomous body under the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways that develops, maintains and operates NHs.
Major NHAI projects: the Golden Quadrilateral (Delhi–Mumbai–Chennai–Kolkata), the North–South Corridor (Srinagar to Kanyakumari) and the East–West Corridor (Silchar in Assam to Porbandar in Gujarat).

ex.q: Name the end points of the North–South and East–West corridors and where they cross India's four metros route.
st: North–South: Srinagar (J&K) to Kanyakumari (Tamil Nadu).
East–West: Silchar (Assam) to Porbandar (Gujarat).
Both intersect the Golden Quadrilateral linking Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata.
ex.a: NS: Srinagar–Kanyakumari; EW: Silchar–Porbandar

topics.rl: FASTag electronic tolling on NHAI highways has cut waiting time at toll plazas across India.

topics.t: State highways, district and rural roads, border roads and road density
topics.h: The Manali–Leh road climbs over passes above 5,000 m and stays open only a few months a year. Who builds roads like that?
p: State Highways are constructed and maintained by state governments; they join state capitals with district headquarters and other important towns.
District roads connect district headquarters with other important nodes in the district; they are maintained by the Zila Parishad.

Rural roads are vital for providing links in rural areas; about 80 per cent of total road length is rural roads. The Pradhan Mantri Grameen Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) aims to link every village to a major town by an all-season motorable road.

Other roads: Border roads — the Border Roads Organisation (BRO), established in May 1960, builds strategically important roads along northern and north-eastern borders, e.g. Chandigarh–Manali–Leh road (average altitude about 4,270 m). International highways promote harmonious relationships with neighbouring countries.
Road distribution is uneven: road density is highest in Kerala and lowest in Jammu and Kashmir (and Ladakh) — affected by terrain and level of economic development.

ex.q: Why is road density low in Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh but high in Kerala?
st: J&K and Ladakh: mountainous, rugged terrain, snow, sparse population → costly to build roads.
Kerala: plains and coastal lowlands, dense population, high development.
So density differs with terrain and economy.
ex.a: Rugged terrain and sparse population vs plains, dense population and development

topics.rl: BRO's Atal Tunnel and roads in Arunachal Pradesh connect remote border villages and support defence.

rv.summary: State Highways (state governments) join capitals with district HQs; district roads are kept by Zila Parishads; rural roads are about 80% of road length, with PMGSY linking villages. BRO (1960) builds strategic border roads like Chandigarh–Manali–Leh. Road density is highest in Kerala, lowest in J&K.
