topics.t: Indian Railways: history, network and gauges
topics.h: On 16 April 1853, India's first train puffed 34 km from Bombay to Thane. Today Indian Railways carries crores of passengers every day.
p: Indian Railways is a major mode for long-distance freight and passenger traffic; the first train ran from Mumbai to Thane in 1853, covering 34 km.
It is one of the largest government undertakings in India, with a network of about 68,000 route km, divided into zones for administration.
Gauges: broad gauge (1.676 m), metre gauge (1 m) and narrow gauges (0.762 m and 0.610 m). Under Project Unigauge, metre and narrow gauge lines are being converted to broad gauge.
Metro rail: Kolkata got India's first metro in 1984; Delhi and many other cities followed. Steam engines have been replaced by diesel and electric locomotives.

ex.q: Arrange the gauges by width and give the difference between broad and metre gauge.
st: Broad (1.676 m) > metre (1 m) > narrow (0.762 m and 0.610 m).
Broad − metre = 1.676 − 1 = 0.676 m.
ex.a: Broad > metre > narrow; difference 0.676 m

topics.rl: Vande Bharat trains and full electrification of broad-gauge routes show how far Indian Railways has come since 1853.

rv.summary: India's first train ran 34 km from Mumbai to Thane in 1853. Indian Railways, a huge government undertaking of about 68,000 route km, uses broad (1.676 m), metre (1 m) and narrow gauges (0.762 m, 0.610 m); Project Unigauge converts lines to broad gauge. Kolkata got the first metro in 1984.

topics.t: Konkan Railway and railways for tourism and freight
topics.h: The Konkan Railway crosses 146 rivers and runs through 73 tunnels along the Western Ghats. Engineers call it a marvel!
p: The Konkan Railway, completed in 1998, is a 760 km route connecting Roha in Maharashtra to Mangaluru in Karnataka.
It is an engineering marvel: it crosses 146 rivers and streams, nearly 2,000 bridges and 73 tunnels; its longest tunnel, nearly 6.5 km long, was described by NCERT as Asia's largest.
Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka are partners in this undertaking.
Railways also promote tourism — the Palace on Wheels, and heritage mountain railways like the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway and Nilgiri Mountain Railway (UNESCO World Heritage).
Dedicated Freight Corridors (Eastern and Western) are being built so that goods trains can run faster on separate tracks, freeing passenger lines.

ex.q: Before the Konkan Railway, why was it hard to build a railway along the west coast?
st: The Western Ghats come close to the sea with steep slopes.
Many west-flowing rivers and creeks cut across the coast.
So many bridges and tunnels were needed — 2,000 bridges and 73 tunnels.
ex.a: Steep ghats and many rivers made it very difficult

topics.rl: The Konkan Railway's Ro-Ro service carries loaded trucks on trains, cutting fuel use and road congestion on the west coast.

rv.summary: The Konkan Railway (1998), 760 km from Roha (Maharashtra) to Mangaluru (Karnataka), is an engineering marvel crossing 146 rivers, about 2,000 bridges and 73 tunnels; Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka are partners. Heritage railways aid tourism, and Dedicated Freight Corridors speed goods trains.

Don't mix up its numbers: 146 rivers, 2,000 bridges, 73 tunnels

topics.h: A barge on the Ganga can carry as much cargo as dozens of trucks — using far less fuel.
p: Water transport is the cheapest means for carrying heavy and bulky goods; it is fuel-efficient and eco-friendly.

Inland waterways include rivers, canals, backwaters and creeks; India has about 14,500 km of navigable waterways. The Inland Waterways Authority of India was set up in 1986 to develop, maintain and regulate national waterways.
National Waterway 1 (NW1): the Ganga between Allahabad (Prayagraj) and Haldia — 1,620 km.
National Waterway 2 (NW2): the Brahmaputra between Sadiya and Dhubri — 891 km.

ex.q: How much longer is NW1 than NW2?
st: Difference = 1,620 − 891 = 729 km.
ex.a: 729 km

topics.rl: Under the Jal Marg Vikas Project, multimodal terminals at Varanasi, Sahibganj and Haldia are boosting cargo movement on NW1.

rv.summary: Water transport is the cheapest way to move bulky goods. India has about 14,500 km of navigable waterways; the Inland Waterways Authority (1986) manages them. NW1 is the Ganga from Allahabad to Haldia (1,620 km); NW2 the Brahmaputra from Sadiya to Dhubri (891 km).

NW2: Brahmaputra, Sadiya – Dhubri, 891 km
traps: Don't swap NW1 (1,620 km) and NW2 (891 km)
Water transport is not more polluting than road transport

topics.t: NW3, other national waterways and oceanic routes
topics.h: About 95% of India's foreign trade by volume travels by sea. India's 7,517 km coastline is its gateway to the world.
p: National Waterway 3 (NW3): the West Coast Canal from Kottapuram to Kollam, along with the Udyogamandal and Champakkara canals — 205 km (Kerala).

NW4: Kakinada–Puducherry stretch of canals with stretches of the Godavari and Krishna rivers; NW5: stretches of the Brahmani, the East Coast Canal and the Mahanadi delta (Odisha–West Bengal). Under the National Waterways Act, 2016, 111 waterways have been declared national waterways.
Oceanic routes: India has a coastline of about 7,517 km including islands; 12 major and about 200 minor ports provide infrastructure.
About 95 per cent of India's foreign trade by volume and 70 per cent by value moves through oceanic routes; they are also used for coastal transport within the country.

ex.q: If India's foreign trade volume is 1,000 million tonnes, how much moves by sea (about 95%)?
st: = 950 million tonnes.
ex.a: 950 million tonnes

topics.rl: Kerala's NW3 carries tourists on houseboats and cargo like coir and timber along the backwaters.

rv.summary: NW3 is Kerala's West Coast Canal from Kottapuram to Kollam (205 km); NW4 and NW5 serve the east coast, and the 2016 Act declared 111 national waterways. India's 7,517 km coastline has 12 major and about 200 minor ports, carrying about 95% of foreign trade by volume and 70% by value.

traps: Don't swap the volume (95%) and value (70%) shares
India has 12 major ports, not one

topics.h: India's air story began in 1911 with an airmail flight of just 10 km — from Allahabad across the river to Naini!
p: Air transport is the fastest, most comfortable and prestigious mode; it can cover very difficult terrain like high mountains, dreary deserts, dense forests and long oceanic stretches.

Air transport in India began in 1911, when airmail operated over 10 km between Allahabad and Naini. The Airports Authority of India provides safe and efficient air traffic and aeronautical communication services.

Air India provides international and domestic services; air transport was nationalised in 1953; Indian Airlines later merged with Air India, and Air India was privatised in 2022 (acquired by the Tata group).

Pawan Hans Helicopters Ltd provides helicopter services to ONGC's offshore operations and to inaccessible areas and difficult terrains like the north-eastern states and the interiors of J&K, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand; it also serves tourism.

UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik) is a regional connectivity scheme to make flying affordable and connect smaller towns. Map work: mark major international airports (Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Hyderabad) and domestic airports.

ex.q: Why is air transport especially important for the north-eastern states?
st: The region is hilly, forested and has many rivers — road and rail are slow and limited.
Air transport overcomes difficult terrain quickly.
Helicopter services (Pawan Hans) reach remote areas.
ex.a: It overcomes difficult terrain and connects remote areas quickly

topics.rl: Under UDAN, small airports like Darbhanga, Jharsuguda and Kalaburagi got regular flights at capped fares.

rv.summary: Air transport is the fastest and can cross difficult terrain. It began in India in 1911 with a 10-km airmail flight from Allahabad to Naini, was nationalised in 1953, and Air India was privatised in 2022. Pawan Hans serves ONGC offshore and remote hills; UDAN makes regional flying affordable.

Role of AAI, Pawan Hans and UDAN
Advantages of air transport

traps: AAI does not manufacture aircraft
Don't confuse the first airmail (10 km) with the first train (34 km)

topics.h: Asia's first cross-country oil pipeline ran 1,157 km from Naharkatiya in Assam to Barauni in Bihar.
p: Pipelines are the most convenient and efficient mode for transporting liquids and gases over long distances; even solids can be transported after converting them into slurry.

Oil India Limited (OIL), under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, is engaged in exploration, production and transportation of crude oil and natural gas; it built Asia's first cross-country pipeline (1,157 km) from Naharkatiya oilfield (Assam) to Barauni refinery (Bihar), later extended to Kanpur.
In western India, important pipelines include Ankaleshwar–Koyali, Mumbai High–Koyali and the Salaya–Koyali–Mathura pipeline from Gujarat to Mathura (with a branch towards Panipat and Jalandhar).

The Gas Authority of India Limited (GAIL), set up in 1984, built the Hazira–Vijaipur–Jagdishpur (HVJ) gas pipeline, linking Mumbai High and Bassein gas fields with fertiliser, power and industrial complexes in western and northern India.
Pipelines reduce the load on roads and railways, give continuous supply with low running cost and little transit loss; Indian Oil operates an extensive pipeline network.

ex.q: Why was a pipeline from Naharkatiya to Barauni preferred over rail tankers?
st: Oil had to travel over 1,100 km from Assam to Bihar.
Pipelines give continuous, low-cost flow with little loss.
They free railways for other traffic.
ex.a: Continuous, cheap, low-loss transport over a long distance

topics.rl: City gas networks fed by GAIL's pipelines now supply piped natural gas (PNG) to kitchens and CNG to vehicles in many Indian cities.

rv.summary: Pipelines efficiently carry liquids and gases (and solids as slurry) over long distances. Oil India built Asia's first cross-country pipeline, 1,157 km from Naharkatiya (Assam) to Barauni (Bihar). GAIL (1984) built the Hazira–Vijaipur–Jagdishpur gas pipeline; Salaya–Koyali–Mathura serves the west.

topics.t: Communication networks: personal and mass communication
topics.h: India Post has over 1.5 lakh post offices — the largest postal network in the world — while India also has one of the world's largest mobile phone networks.
p: Communication has evolved from drum beats, messengers and pigeons to modern telecommunications; it can be personal or mass communication.

Personal communication: the postal service (the largest postal network in the world), telegraph, telephone, mobile phones and the internet. The internet (e-mail, e-commerce, e-governance) is used mostly in urban areas, and the Digital India initiative aims to spread it widely.
Telecommunication: India's mobile phone network is among the largest in the world; Subscriber Trunk Dialling (STD) and optical fibre cables enabled fast long-distance calls and data.

Mass communication: radio broadcasting began in 1923 (Radio Club of Bombay); the government named it All India Radio in 1936 and Akashvani in 1957. Television broadcasting began in 1959; Doordarshan is the national broadcaster with one of the largest terrestrial networks.

Press: newspapers are published in many languages, with Hindi newspapers being the largest in number. Films: India is the largest producer of feature films in the world; the Central Board of Film Certification certifies films.

ex.q: Classify: India Post letter, Akashvani news, a Hindi daily newspaper, a video call.
st: Personal: India Post letter, video call.
Mass: Akashvani (radio) news, Hindi daily newspaper.
ex.a: Personal: letter, video call; mass: radio news, newspaper

topics.rl: Community radio stations and DD Free Dish carry information on farming, health and education to remote villages.

rv.summary: Personal communication includes post (India has the world's largest postal network), phones and the internet; mass communication includes radio (from 1923; AIR 1936; Akashvani 1957), TV (from 1959; Doordarshan), newspapers (Hindi largest in number) and films (India the largest producer).

Press and films

topics.h: Every weather forecast you see on TV uses images from India's own INSAT satellites — and crop and forest maps come from IRS satellites.
p: Satellites are a mode of communication in themselves and also regulate other means of communication; satellite images are used for weather forecasting, monitoring natural calamities, surveillance of border areas and more.
India's satellite system can be grouped into the Indian National Satellite System (INSAT) and the Indian Remote Sensing Satellite System (IRS).
INSAT, established in 1983, is a multi-purpose satellite system for telecommunications, meteorological observation and broadcasting.

The IRS system became operational with the launch of IRS-1A in March 1988; it gives data for resource monitoring and management. The National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) at Hyderabad acquires and processes data; ISRO runs India's space programme.
Exam focus: road classification and NH, BRO, Konkan Railway, national waterways, pipelines, satellite communication, mass communication, and road vs rail transport.

ex.q: Which satellite system would you use for (a) a cyclone warning broadcast on TV, (b) mapping forest cover change?
st: (a) Weather observation and broadcasting → INSAT.
(b) Resource monitoring → IRS (remote sensing).
ex.a: (a) INSAT, (b) IRS

topics.rl: ISRO's Bhuvan portal uses IRS data to map land use, water bodies and disasters for planners across India.

rv.summary: Satellites communicate and regulate other communication, aiding weather forecasting, disaster monitoring and border surveillance. INSAT (1983) serves telecom, meteorology and broadcasting; IRS (from IRS-1A, 1988) gives remote-sensing data for resources, processed at NRSC, Hyderabad.

Don't swap INSAT (1983) and IRS (1988)

topics.h: India sells medicines to Africa, rice to the Gulf and software to the USA, and buys crude oil, gold and electronics. No country is self-sufficient.
p: International trade is the exchange of goods and services among countries; no country is self-sufficient, so trade is necessary.
India's share in world trade is small (NCERT puts it at about 1 per cent), but India is an integral part of the world economy and its trade has grown rapidly.
Exports are goods and services sold abroad; imports are those bought from abroad.
Balance of trade = exports − imports; it is favourable (positive) if exports exceed imports and unfavourable (negative) if imports exceed exports.

ex.q: India exports goods worth ₹30 lakh crore and imports ₹45 lakh crore in a year. Find the balance of trade.
st: Balance = exports − imports = 30 − 45.
= −15 lakh crore.
Imports exceed exports → unfavourable (trade deficit).
ex.a: −₹15 lakh crore (trade deficit)

topics.rl: The Foreign Trade Policy and schemes like 'Districts as Export Hubs' aim to boost India's exports.

rv.summary: No country is self-sufficient, so countries trade. India's share of world trade is small (about 1% per NCERT) but growing. Exports are sold abroad and imports bought from abroad; balance of trade = exports − imports, favourable if exports exceed imports.

Exports vs imports
Calculating and reading the balance of trade

Buying crude oil from abroad is an import, not an export

topics.t: Changing pattern of India's trade and the trade deficit
topics.h: In 1950–51 India's total trade was a little over ₹1,200 crore. Today it runs into lakhs of crores. What drove this boom?
p: The volume of India's international trade has increased manifold since 1950–51 (from about ₹1,214 crore then to many lakh crore today).
Reasons for growth: momentum in the manufacturing sector, liberal policies of the government (especially after liberalisation in 1991), and diversification of markets.
Imports have consistently exceeded exports, so India has a trade deficit (negative balance of trade) that has been increasing.
Reasons for the rising deficit include the price rise of crude petroleum in the international market, and large imports of gold, electronics and machinery.
Graphs of India's exports, imports and trade balance over the years show both lines rising, with imports above exports and the deficit widening.

ex.q: In a year, India's exports are ₹25 lakh crore and imports ₹40 lakh crore. Next year exports are ₹30 lakh crore and imports ₹48 lakh crore. Did the deficit widen?
st: Year 1 deficit = 25 − 40 = −15.
Year 2 deficit = 30 − 48 = −18.
Deficit widened by 3 lakh crore.
ex.a: Yes — from −15 to −18 lakh crore

topics.rl: Rising oil prices in 2022 sharply widened India's trade deficit, as India imports most of its crude oil.

rv.summary: India's trade has grown manifold since 1950–51 thanks to manufacturing, liberal policies after 1991 and diversified markets. But imports have always exceeded exports, so India runs a widening trade deficit, driven by costly crude oil and imports of gold, electronics and machinery.

topics.h: India once exported mostly tea, jute and spices. Today the top items are refined petroleum, engineering goods, medicines and gems.
p: The share of agriculture and allied products (coffee, spices, tea, pulses) in exports has declined, mainly due to stiff international competition.
The share of petroleum and crude products has increased, owing to rising petroleum prices and India's growing refining capacity (India imports crude, refines it and exports products).
Manufactured goods form the bulk of exports (about two-thirds to three-fourths); engineering goods have shown significant growth, and gems and jewellery form a large share.
Exports of floricultural products, fresh fruits, marine products and sugar have increased.
Indian manufacturing exports face strong competition from China and other East Asian countries. A table of commodity shares shows agriculture falling and manufactures and petroleum rising.

ex.q: Why has the share of tea and coffee in India's exports declined?
st: Other countries (Sri Lanka, Kenya, Vietnam, Brazil) compete strongly.
Manufactured and petroleum exports have grown much faster.
So agriculture's share has fallen.
ex.a: International competition and faster growth of other exports

topics.rl: Surat's diamonds, Jamnagar's refined fuels and Hyderabad's pharma exports show the new export basket.

rv.summary: Agriculture's share in India's exports has fallen due to stiff competition, while petroleum products (from imported, refined crude) and manufactures have risen; manufactured goods, especially engineering goods and gems and jewellery, form the bulk.

topics.h: In the 1960s, India imported wheat under the PL-480 scheme to avoid famine. After the Green Revolution, it stopped importing grain — and started importing oil and fertilisers.
p: In the 1950s and 1960s, India faced serious food shortages; foodgrains, capital goods, machinery and equipment were the main imports.
After the Green Revolution in the 1970s, foodgrain imports were discontinued; they were replaced by imports of fertilisers and petroleum.
Machinery and equipment, special steel, edible oil and chemicals largely make up the import basket.
Imports of petroleum and petroleum products have increased greatly — used both as fuel and as industrial raw material — reflecting rising industrialisation and a better standard of living.
Other major imports: pearls and precious stones, gold and silver, metallic ores and metal scrap, non-ferrous metals and electronic goods. A table of import shares shows petroleum at the top.

ex.q: Why did India stop importing foodgrains in the 1970s but start importing more fertilisers?
st: The Green Revolution raised foodgrain output, ending shortages.
But HYV seeds needed large amounts of chemical fertilisers.
So foodgrain imports were replaced by fertiliser (and petroleum) imports.
ex.a: The Green Revolution ended food imports but raised demand for fertilisers

topics.rl: Gold imports peak around Dhanteras and the wedding season, showing how culture also shapes India's import bill.

rv.summary: In the 1950s–60s India imported foodgrains, capital goods and machinery. After the Green Revolution, food imports stopped and fertilisers and petroleum took their place. Today petroleum tops the import basket, followed by machinery, edible oil, gold and stones.

topics.h: The USA buys the most Indian goods, while China sells India the most. Where else does India trade?
p: India has trade relations with most countries and major trading blocs of the world.
Region-wise, India trades with Asia and ASEAN, Europe, America (North and Latin), Africa, and the CIS and Baltic countries.
India aims to double its share in international trade and promotes exports through policy measures.
Major trading partners include the USA, China, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Hong Kong, Switzerland, Germany, Singapore, Belgium and the UK.
Changing pattern: the share of Asia and Oceania in India's trade has been increasing, while the share of Europe has been decreasing. A regional table shows Asia as India's largest trading region.

ex.q: Using the trend, which region's share in India's trade is growing and which is declining?
st: Asia and Oceania: growing share (China, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, ASEAN).
Europe: declining share.
ex.a: Asia and Oceania growing; Europe declining

topics.rl: India's trade agreements with the UAE (CEPA) and Australia (ECTA) show the growing importance of Asia and Oceania.

rv.summary: India trades with most countries and major blocs — Asia and ASEAN, Europe, the Americas, Africa, CIS and Baltic countries. Major partners include the USA, China, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Hong Kong, Switzerland, Germany, Singapore, Belgium and the UK. Asia's share is rising and Europe's falling.

topics.t: Sea ports as gateways of trade
topics.h: When Karachi went to Pakistan in 1947, India lost its main western port overnight. So it built a brand-new one — Kandla.
p: India is surrounded by sea on three sides; ports are gateways of international trade, and about 95 per cent of India's trade by volume moves by sea.
India has a coastline of about 7,517 km with 12 major ports and about 200 minor or intermediate ports.
Major ports are under the control of the Central Government; minor ports are controlled by state governments.
Ports such as Kolkata, Mumbai and Chennai were developed by the British as suction points for India's resources and as entry points for their manufactured goods.
After partition, India lost Karachi port to Pakistan and Chittagong to East Pakistan; to compensate, Kandla was developed on the west coast and Diamond Harbour near Kolkata on the east.

ex.q: Why was Kandla port developed after 1947?
st: Karachi, the main port for north-western India, went to Pakistan.
Mumbai alone could not handle all western traffic.
So Kandla was built on the Gulf of Kachchh to ease the pressure.
ex.a: To replace Karachi and ease pressure on Mumbai

topics.rl: The Sagarmala programme is modernising ports and building new ones like Vadhavan in Maharashtra.

rv.summary: Ports are gateways of India's trade, as about 95% of trade by volume moves by sea. India's 7,517 km coastline has 12 major ports (Central Government) and about 200 minor ports (state governments). After partition, Kandla replaced Karachi and Diamond Harbour was developed near Kolkata.

topics.t: West coast ports I: Kandla, Mumbai and JNPT
topics.h: Nhava Sheva (JNPT), across the harbour from Mumbai, handles the largest share of India's container traffic.
p: Deendayal (Kandla) port, at the head of the Gulf of Kachchh, was developed as a major port to ease pressure on Mumbai after the loss of Karachi; it is a specially designed tidal port. It serves a highly productive granary and industrial belt across J&K, Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Gujarat; it handles petroleum, fertilisers and other bulk cargo, with an offshore terminal at Vadinar for petroleum.

Mumbai port has a spacious natural harbour and is described by NCERT as the biggest port of the country (today Deendayal-Kandla and Paradip handle more cargo); it lies close to the general routes from the Middle East, Mediterranean countries, North Africa, North America and Europe; it has the country's largest oil terminal.
Mumbai's main hinterland includes Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan.
Jawaharlal Nehru Port (JNPT) at Nhava Sheva was developed as a satellite port to relieve pressure on Mumbai port; it is the largest container port in India.

ex.q: Why is Mumbai port so important for India's trade with Europe and North America?
st: It is a natural harbour with deep, sheltered water.
It lies close to sea routes via the Suez Canal to Europe, the Mediterranean and North America.
It has a large, productive hinterland.
ex.a: Natural harbour, nearness to major sea routes and a large hinterland

topics.rl: Most of India's container exports — from garments to auto parts — leave through JNPT at Nhava Sheva.

rv.summary: Deendayal (Kandla), a tidal port at the head of the Gulf of Kachchh, was built after partition to ease pressure on Mumbai. Mumbai, a spacious natural harbour near routes to Europe and North America, is called India's biggest port by NCERT; JNPT (Nhava Sheva) is the largest container port.

topics.t: West coast ports II: Marmagao, New Mangalore and Kochi
topics.h: Kochi, the 'Queen of the Arabian Sea', sits beside one of the world's busiest shipping lanes between Suez and Colombo.
p: Marmagao port, at the entrance of the Zuari estuary, is a natural harbour in Goa; it gained significance after remodelling in 1961 to handle iron ore exports to Japan; the Konkan Railway has considerably extended its hinterland (Karnataka, Goa, southern Maharashtra).

New Mangalore port, in Karnataka, caters to the export of iron ore and iron concentrates (from Kudremukh); it also handles fertilisers, petroleum products, edible oils, coffee, tea, wood pulp, yarn, granite and molasses; Karnataka is its major hinterland.
Kochi port, at the head of the Vembanad Kayal, is popularly known as the 'Queen of the Arabian Sea'; it is a natural harbour.
Kochi has an advantageous location close to the Suez–Colombo route; it caters to Kerala, southern Karnataka and south-western Tamil Nadu.

ex.q: Which west-coast port would export iron ore from Kudremukh, and which from Goa's mines?
st: Kudremukh (Karnataka) ore → New Mangalore port.
Goa's iron ore → Marmagao port.
ex.a: Kudremukh → New Mangalore; Goa → Marmagao

topics.rl: Kochi's International Container Transhipment Terminal at Vallarpadam aims to capture cargo that used to go via Colombo.

rv.summary: Marmagao, a natural harbour at the Zuari estuary in Goa, was remodelled in 1961 for iron ore exports to Japan, and the Konkan Railway widened its hinterland. New Mangalore (Karnataka) exports Kudremukh iron ore. Kochi, the 'Queen of the Arabian Sea', is a natural harbour near the Suez–Colombo route.

topics.t: East coast ports I: Kolkata, Haldia and Paradip
topics.h: Kolkata port is not on the sea at all — it lies 128 km up the Hugli river, and ships fight silt to reach it.
p: Kolkata port is located on the Hugli river, 128 km inland from the Bay of Bengal; developed by the British, it had the early advantage of being at the capital of British India.

It faces silt accumulation in the Hugli and needs constant dredging; it has lost significance as exports were diverted to Visakhapatnam, Paradip and its satellite port Haldia. Its hinterland covers UP, Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Sikkim and the north-eastern states, and it serves landlocked Nepal and Bhutan.

Haldia port, 105 km downstream from Kolkata, was built to reduce congestion at Kolkata; it handles bulk cargo — iron ore, coal, petroleum and its products, fertilisers, jute and jute products, cotton and cotton yarn.

Paradip port, in the Mahanadi delta about 100 km from Cuttack, has the deepest harbour, especially suited for very large vessels; it mainly handles large-scale iron ore exports; its hinterland includes Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand.

ex.q: Why was Haldia port developed downstream of Kolkata?
st: Kolkata is 128 km inland on the Hugli and suffers from silting and congestion.
Haldia, 105 km downstream, is nearer the sea and easier for larger ships to reach.
So it was built to reduce congestion at Kolkata and handle bulk cargo.
ex.a: To reduce congestion at Kolkata and handle bulk cargo nearer the sea

topics.rl: Kolkata port (now Syama Prasad Mookerjee Port) handles transit cargo for Nepal and Bhutan.

rv.summary: Kolkata is a riverine port 128 km up the Hugli; silting is its main problem. Haldia, 105 km downstream, eases Kolkata's congestion with bulk cargo. Paradip in the Mahanadi delta has the deepest harbour and exports iron ore.
focus: Kolkata port: location, problems, hinterland
Haldia's purpose and cargo
Paradip: deepest harbour and iron ore exports
remember: Kolkata: Hugli river, 128 km inland; silting; serves Nepal and Bhutan
Haldia: 105 km downstream of Kolkata; bulk cargo
Paradip: Mahanadi delta, ~100 km from Cuttack; deepest harbour; iron ore exports
traps: Paradip exports iron ore, not tea and coffee
Kolkata's problem is silting, not deep water

topics.t: East coast ports II: Visakhapatnam, Chennai, Ennore and Tuticorin
topics.h: Visakhapatnam's inner harbour is landlocked — ships enter through a channel cut through solid rock!
p: Visakhapatnam port (Andhra Pradesh) is a landlocked harbour connected to the sea by a channel cut through solid rock and sand; an outer harbour handles iron ore, petroleum and general cargo; Andhra Pradesh is its main hinterland.

Chennai port is one of the oldest ports on the east coast; it is an artificial harbour built in 1859; it is not very suitable for large ships because of shallow waters near the coast; Tamil Nadu and Puducherry are its hinterland.
Ennore (now Kamarajar) port was developed 25 km north of Chennai to relieve pressure on Chennai port.

V.O. Chidambaranar (Tuticorin) port, in Tamil Nadu, was also developed to relieve pressure on Chennai; it has a natural harbour and rich hinterland and handles coal, salt, foodgrains, edible oils, sugar, chemicals and petroleum products; it serves trade with Sri Lanka, the Maldives and coastal India.
Map work: mark major ports — Kandla, Mumbai, JNPT, Marmagao, New Mangalore, Kochi (west); Tuticorin, Chennai, Ennore, Visakhapatnam, Paradip, Haldia, Kolkata (east).

ex.q: Arrange these east coast ports from south to north: Paradip, Tuticorin, Visakhapatnam, Chennai, Kolkata.
st: Southernmost: Tuticorin (Tamil Nadu).
Then Chennai, then Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh).
Then Paradip (Odisha) and finally Kolkata (West Bengal).
ex.a: Tuticorin → Chennai → Visakhapatnam → Paradip → Kolkata

topics.rl: Chennai's car factories export vehicles through Ennore (Kamarajar) and Chennai ports to markets worldwide.

rv.summary: Visakhapatnam is a landlocked harbour linked to the sea by a channel cut through rock and sand. Chennai is an old artificial harbour (1859) with shallow coastal waters. Ennore (25 km north of Chennai) and Tuticorin were built to relieve Chennai; Tuticorin trades with Sri Lanka and the Maldives.
focus: Visakhapatnam's landlocked harbour
Chennai's artificial harbour and its limits
Ennore and Tuticorin as relief ports
remember: Visakhapatnam: landlocked harbour; channel cut through solid rock and sand
Chennai: artificial harbour, 1859; shallow waters limit large ships
Ennore (Kamarajar): 25 km north of Chennai; Tuticorin: natural harbour, trade with Sri Lanka and Maldives
traps: Visakhapatnam is not an open natural harbour like Mumbai
Chennai's harbour dates from 1859, not 1961

topics.h: Fresh Alphonso mangoes reach London within a day by air, while iron ore takes weeks by ship. Why does each use a different gateway?
p: Air transport plays an important role in international trade: it takes the least time to carry high-value or perishable goods over long distances.
It is very costly and unsuitable for heavy and bulky commodities, so its share in international trade is low compared with oceanic routes.
Major international airports include Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Delhi, Goa, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Mumbai, Thiruvananthapuram, Amritsar, Guwahati, Kochi and Srinagar, among others.
Map work: mark major international airports of India.
Exam focus: ports and their features, trading partners, changes in export and import composition, causes of the trade deficit, ports as gateways, and the role of air transport.

ex.q: Which gateway — sea port or airport — suits each: (a) 2 lakh tonnes of iron ore; (b) 5 tonnes of cut flowers; (c) a consignment of diamonds?
st: (a) Heavy, bulky, low value per tonne → sea port.
(b) Perishable → airport.
(c) High value, light → airport.
ex.a: (a) sea port, (b) airport, (c) airport

topics.rl: Air cargo hubs at Delhi and Mumbai airports handle pharmaceuticals, electronics and fresh produce for export.

rv.summary: Air transport carries high-value or perishable goods over long distances in the least time, but it is costly and unsuited to bulky goods, so its share in trade is small compared with sea routes. India has many international airports, including Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata, Bengaluru and Guwahati.
focus: Role and limits of air transport in trade
Choosing sea port vs airport for a cargo
Major international airports
remember: Air: fastest; for high-value and perishable goods
Air is costly and unsuitable for heavy, bulky goods; sea carries ~95% by volume
International airports include Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Guwahati, Kochi
traps: Air is not the cheapest mode for bulky goods
Iron ore and coal go by sea, not air

topics.ch: India: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
topics.h: Smoke from a chimney, a pesticide in a stream, a blaring horn and plastic in a field — four different kinds of pollution.
p: Environmental pollution results from the release of substances and energy from waste products of human activities, which harm the natural environment.
Pollution is classified by the medium through which pollutants are transported and diffused: air pollution, water pollution, land pollution and noise pollution.
Pollutants can be classified by origin (natural or human) and by how they travel; they move through air, water and soil, often from one medium to another.
Human activities, not natural processes, are the main cause of concern.

ex.q: Classify: fertiliser runoff into a lake, vehicle exhaust, a garbage dump, a loudspeaker at night.
st: Fertiliser runoff → water pollution.
Vehicle exhaust → air pollution.
Garbage dump → land pollution.
Loudspeaker → noise pollution.
ex.a: Water, air, land, noise

topics.rl: The Central Pollution Control Board monitors air, water and noise quality in Indian cities.

rv.summary: Environmental pollution comes from substances and energy released as waste by human activities. It is classified by the medium that carries pollutants: air, water, land and noise pollution. Pollutants move between air, water and soil, often far from their source.
focus: Meaning of environmental pollution
The four types by medium
How pollutants travel between media
remember: Pollution: release of substances and energy from human waste products harming the environment
Types by medium: air, water, land, noise
Pollutants move through air, water and soil
traps: Light pollution is not one of NCERT's four medium-based types
Pollutants do not stay where they are produced

topics.ch: India: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
topics.h: A tannery in Kanpur, a pesticide spray in Punjab, and lakhs of pilgrims at a ghat — all can pollute the same river.
p: Indiscriminate use of water by a growing population and industrial expansion has seriously degraded water quality.

Pollutants come from natural sources (erosion, landslides, decay and decomposition of plants and animals) but those from human activities are the real cause of concern; human sources are industrial, agricultural and cultural.

Industrial pollutants: industrial wastes, polluted waste water, poisonous gases, chemical residues, heavy metals, dust and smoke; most industrial waste is dumped into running water or lakes. Leather, pulp and paper, textiles and chemicals are major polluting industries.
Agricultural sources: inorganic fertilisers, pesticides and herbicides are washed into rivers, lakes and tanks, and seep into groundwater.
Cultural activities like pilgrimages, religious fairs and tourism also pollute water (e.g. bathing, immersion of idols, offerings, waste left by crowds).

ex.q: Classify these sources: tannery effluent, fertiliser runoff, waste after a religious fair, landslide debris.
st: Tannery effluent → industrial (human).
Fertiliser runoff → agricultural (human).
Fair waste → cultural (human).
Landslide debris → natural.
ex.a: Industrial, agricultural, cultural, natural

topics.rl: Eco-friendly clay idols and artificial immersion ponds during Ganesh Chaturthi in Mumbai and Pune reduce cultural water pollution.

rv.summary: Population growth and industrial expansion have degraded India's water. Human sources are the real concern: industrial (leather, paper, textiles, chemicals), agricultural (fertilisers, pesticides) and cultural (fairs, pilgrimages).
focus: Natural vs human sources of water pollution
Industrial, agricultural and cultural sources
How farm chemicals reach groundwater
remember: Natural: erosion, landslides, decay of plants and animals
Industrial: leather, pulp and paper, textiles, chemicals; most waste dumped into rivers and lakes
Agricultural: inorganic fertilisers, pesticides, herbicides; cultural: pilgrimages, fairs, tourism
traps: Natural sources are not the main cause of concern — human sources are
Organic farming is not a source of chemical pollution

topics.ch: India: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
topics.t: Effects of water pollution, the Ganga and Namami Gange
topics.h: About one in four communicable diseases in India spreads through water. Clean rivers mean healthy people.
p: Polluted water causes water-borne diseases such as diarrhoea, intestinal worms and hepatitis; about one-fourth of communicable diseases in India are water-borne.

The Ganga has highly polluted stretches near cities like Kanpur, Allahabad (Prayagraj), Varanasi, Patna and Kolkata (industrial and urban effluents); the Yamuna is badly polluted around Delhi, Mathura and Agra.

The Namami Gange Programme (2014), under the National Mission for Clean Ganga, includes: sewerage treatment systems in towns, monitoring of industrial effluents, river-front development, afforestation along the banks, cleaning of the river surface, developing 'Ganga Grams' in Uttarakhand, UP, Bihar, Jharkhand and West Bengal, and public awareness to avoid adding pollutants even through rituals.
Activity: survey a local river or pond and list its pollution sources — sewage outfalls, factory drains, farm runoff, solid waste, washing and bathing.

ex.q: A student surveys a local pond and sees a drain from houses, plastic waste, washing of clothes and cattle bathing. List the pollution sources and one solution for each.
st: Household drain → sewage: divert to treatment.
Plastic waste → solid waste: collection and ban on dumping.
Washing clothes (detergents) → separate washing area.
Cattle bathing → separate cattle trough.
ex.a: Sewage, solid waste, detergents, animal waste — with treatment, collection and separation

topics.rl: Under Namami Gange, sewage treatment plants and river-front ghats have been built in Varanasi, Kanpur and Patna.

rv.summary: Polluted water causes diseases like diarrhoea, intestinal worms and hepatitis; about one-fourth of communicable diseases in India are water-borne. The Ganga is polluted near Kanpur, Prayagraj, Varanasi, Patna and Kolkata.
focus: Health effects of water pollution
Polluted stretches of the Ganga and Yamuna
Components of Namami Gange
remember: About one-fourth of communicable diseases are water-borne; diarrhoea, intestinal worms, hepatitis
Ganga polluted near Kanpur, Prayagraj, Varanasi, Patna, Kolkata; Yamuna near Delhi, Mathura, Agra
Namami Gange 2014: sewerage, effluent monitoring, river-front, afforestation, surface cleaning, Ganga Grams, awareness
traps: Namami Gange is not only surface cleaning
The upper Ganga at Gangotri or Rishikesh is not the polluted stretch

topics.ch: India: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
topics.h: Every winter, Delhi's air turns grey and schools sometimes shut. What is in that smog?
p: Air pollution is the addition of contaminants like dust, fumes, gas, fog, odour, smoke or vapour to the air in substantial proportion and duration that may be harmful to flora, fauna and property.
Main sources: combustion of fossil fuels, mining and industries; they release oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, hydrocarbons, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, lead and asbestos.
Effects: air pollution causes diseases of the respiratory, nervous and circulatory systems.
Smoky fog over cities, called urban smog, is caused by atmospheric pollution and is very harmful to health; air pollution can also cause acid rain.
Many Indian cities, including Delhi, have high air pollution; the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP, 2019) aims to reduce particulate pollution in non-attainment cities.

ex.q: Why does Delhi's winter smog often get worse than its summer air?
st: In winter, cool still air and low wind trap pollutants near the ground.
Emissions from vehicles, industry, construction dust and crop-residue burning add up.
Fog mixes with smoke to form smog.
ex.a: Still, cold air traps pollutants, and smoke and fog combine

topics.rl: CNG buses, BS-VI fuel standards and the Graded Response Action Plan are steps to fight air pollution in Delhi-NCR.

rv.summary: Air pollution is the addition of dust, fumes, gases, smoke and similar contaminants in amounts harmful to flora, fauna and property. Fossil fuels, mining and industry are the main sources, causing breathing diseases, smog and acid rain.
focus: Definition and sources of air pollution
Health effects, urban smog and acid rain
National Clean Air Programme
remember: Sources: combustion of fossil fuels, mining, industries
Pollutants: oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, hydrocarbons, CO₂, CO, lead, asbestos
Effects: respiratory, nervous, circulatory diseases; urban smog; acid rain; NCAP launched 2019
traps: Mining does contribute to air pollution
Solar panels are not a source of air pollution

topics.ch: India: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
topics.h: A pressure horn can blast over 100 decibels — loud enough to damage hearing over time.
p: Noise pollution is the state of unbearable and uncomfortable noise caused by various sources.
Sources: factories, mechanised construction and demolition works, automobiles and aircraft, sirens, loudspeakers and noise during festivals.

Noise is measured in decibels (dB). The biggest nuisance is traffic noise, whose intensity depends on the type of vehicle, aircraft or train and the condition of roads and vehicles; in sea traffic, noise is confined to harbours.

Effects: hearing impairment, stress, irritation and sleep disturbance. Noise pollution is location-specific: its intensity declines with distance from the source, and it is hazardous in metropolitan and big cities, industrial areas and along transport routes.
Activity: survey noise at a hospital zone, a market and a highway at different times and compare decibel readings.

ex.q: A sound level metre reads 45 dB near a library and 85 dB at a traffic junction. Which is more harmful, and why?
st: Higher decibel = louder noise.
85 dB at the junction is much louder than 45 dB.
Long exposure to such noise can damage hearing and cause stress.
ex.a: The traffic junction (85 dB) — loud noise harms hearing and causes stress

topics.rl: Many Indian cities declare 'silence zones' around hospitals and schools and restrict loudspeakers at night.

rv.summary: Noise pollution is unbearable, uncomfortable noise from factories, construction, vehicles, aircraft, sirens, loudspeakers and festivals, measured in decibels. Traffic is the biggest nuisance.
focus: Sources and measurement of noise
Effects of noise pollution
Why noise is location-specific
remember: Measured in decibels (dB); traffic is the biggest nuisance
Effects: hearing impairment, stress, irritation, sleep disturbance
Intensity declines with distance; worst in metros, industrial areas, along transport routes; sea noise confined to harbours
traps: Noise does not increase with distance from the source
Festivals and loudspeakers do cause noise pollution

topics.ch: India: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
topics.t: Urban waste disposal: sources and problems
topics.h: Mountains of garbage like Delhi's Ghazipur landfill rise as tall as some buildings. Where does all that waste come from?
p: Urban areas are marked by overcrowding, congestion and inadequate facilities to support fast-growing populations, leading to poor sanitation and foul air — serious environmental and health problems.

Solid wastes are old and used articles (rusted metal, broken glass, plastic containers, polythene bags, ashes, paper, food waste etc.) from two main sources: household or domestic establishments, and industrial or commercial establishments.
Household waste is often dumped on public land or private contractors' sites; industrial solid waste is disposed of in low-lying public grounds (landfills).

Problems: foul smell, and flies and rodents that carry diseases like typhoid, diphtheria, diarrhoea, malaria and cholera; carelessly handled waste is spread by wind and washed by rainwater, causing nuisance.

ex.q: Name two diseases spread by flies and rodents breeding in garbage dumps, and one way to reduce them.
st: Flies and rodents carry diseases like typhoid and cholera (also diarrhoea, diphtheria, malaria).
Regular collection and covered disposal remove breeding grounds.
ex.a: Typhoid and cholera; regular collection and safe disposal

topics.rl: Indore, repeatedly rated India's cleanest city under Swachh Survekshan, segregates waste at source and processes it.

rv.summary: Overcrowded cities with weak facilities face poor sanitation and foul air. Solid waste comes from households and industrial or commercial establishments; it is dumped on open land or in landfills. Garbage breeds flies and rodents that spread typhoid, diphtheria, diarrhoea, malaria and cholera.
focus: Sources of urban solid waste
How waste is disposed of
Health problems from garbage
remember: Sources: household/domestic and industrial/commercial establishments
Industrial solid waste goes to low-lying public grounds (landfills)
Flies and rodents spread typhoid, diphtheria, diarrhoea, malaria, cholera; wind and rain spread waste
traps: Urban waste does not come only from factories
Waste does not stay in place — wind and rain spread it

topics.ch: India: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
topics.t: Urban waste disposal: pollution and solutions
topics.h: If every home in India separated wet and dry waste, compost and recycling could handle most city garbage. It starts at your kitchen bin!
p: Industrial solid waste and untreated urban sewage are dumped into rivers, contaminating them; many towns lack sewage treatment facilities.
A large share of urban waste remains uncollected or is not processed, so collection and management systems need to be improved.
Waste can be treated as a resource: biodegradable waste can be composted or used to generate energy (biogas, waste-to-energy plants); recyclable waste can be recovered.
Segregation at source (wet and dry waste), recycling, reducing plastic use and community participation are key solutions.
The Swachh Bharat Mission (launched in 2014) promotes cleanliness, solid waste management and toilets in cities and villages.

ex.q: Sort household waste into wet and dry: vegetable peels, newspaper, plastic bottle, tea leaves, glass jar.
st: Wet (biodegradable): vegetable peels, tea leaves → compost.
Dry (recyclable): newspaper, plastic bottle, glass jar → recycling.
ex.a: Wet: peels, tea leaves; dry: newspaper, plastic bottle, glass jar

topics.rl: Ragpickers and kabadiwalas form an informal recycling network in Indian cities; cooperatives like SWaCH in Pune work with municipalities.

rv.summary: Untreated sewage and industrial waste pollute rivers, and much urban waste is never collected or processed. Waste can be a resource: compost or energy from biodegradable waste and recycling of dry waste.
focus: Pollution from untreated urban waste
Waste as a resource: compost, energy, recycling
Segregation and the Swachh Bharat Mission
remember: Biodegradable waste → compost, biogas, waste-to-energy
Segregate wet and dry waste at source; recycle dry waste
Swachh Bharat Mission launched in 2014
traps: Waste-to-energy plants reduce, not increase, the waste problem
Open burning and dumping in rivers are not solutions

topics.ch: India: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
topics.h: Ramesh left his village to work as a welder in a big city, sending money home every month. His story is the story of millions.
p: Rural-urban migration results from high demand for labour in urban areas, low job opportunities and low wages in rural areas, and the unbalanced pattern of development between villages and cities.
Most migrants are unskilled or semi-skilled; many settle in slums and squatter settlements, putting pressure on urban infrastructure — housing, water, sanitation and transport.
Migration is often male-selective: men migrate alone, leaving women, children and the elderly in villages, which increases the burden of work and responsibility on women.

NCERT's narrative of Ramesh, a rural migrant working as a welder in a city, shows push factors (poverty, lack of work), pull factors (jobs, better wages), informal employment with little security, and remittances sent home to support his family.

ex.q: Identify the push and pull factors and one effect in this case: A young man leaves a drought-hit village with no jobs and moves to a city factory paying higher wages, sending money home.
st: Push: drought, lack of jobs in the village.
Pull: factory job and higher wages in the city.
Effect: remittances support his family; city slums and services face more pressure.
ex.a: Push: drought, unemployment; pull: jobs, wages; effect: remittances and urban pressure

topics.rl: Remittances from migrant workers in cities and abroad support lakhs of families in states like Bihar, UP and Kerala.

rv.summary: Rural-urban migration comes from high urban labour demand, few jobs and low wages in villages, and unbalanced development. Most migrants are unskilled or semi-skilled and live in slums, straining city services; male-selective migration burdens rural women.
focus: Causes of rural-urban migration
Effects on cities and on villages
The Ramesh case study
remember: Causes: high labour demand in cities, low jobs and wages in villages, unbalanced development
Most migrants unskilled or semi-skilled; slums strain housing, water, sanitation, transport
Male-selective migration; remittances support families; Ramesh worked as a welder (informal sector)
traps: Migration increases, not reduces, pressure on urban infrastructure
Male-selective means men migrate alone, not women

topics.ch: India: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
topics.h: Dharavi in Mumbai is one of Asia's largest slums — yet inside its narrow lanes, potters, leather workers and recyclers run a busy economy.
p: Indian cities show a dualistic picture: well-developed planned colonies on one side and slums, jhuggi-jhopri clusters and shanty towns on the other.

Slums are the least preferred residential areas: dilapidated houses, poor hygiene and ventilation, and lack of basic amenities like drinking water, light and toilets; they are overcrowded with narrow lanes and are prone to serious fire hazards.

Most slum dwellers work in low-paid, high-risk jobs in the unorganised sector; many are undernourished, prone to illness and unable to afford proper education for their children; poverty makes them vulnerable to drug abuse, alcoholism, crime and social exclusion.

Case study — Dharavi (Mumbai): one of Asia's largest slums, with narrow lanes, congested houses, poor drainage and sanitation; yet it has a large informal economy — pottery, leather goods, garments, recycling — and a hard-working, resilient community.
Solutions include slum upgradation and rehabilitation: in-situ redevelopment, affordable housing (e.g. PMAY-Urban), and providing water, sanitation, electricity and secure tenure.

ex.q: List three problems faced by slum dwellers and one solution for each.
st: Lack of toilets and clean water → provide community toilets and piped water.
Fire hazards in congested lanes → wider lanes, safer materials, fire services.
Low-paid insecure jobs → skill training and access to social security.
ex.a: Poor amenities, fire risk, insecure work — with services, safer planning and skills

topics.rl: Dharavi's recycling units process large amounts of Mumbai's plastic and metal waste — showing the economic energy of slum communities.

rv.summary: Indian cities are dualistic — planned colonies beside slums. Slums have dilapidated, crowded housing, narrow lanes, fire risk and no water, light or toilets; residents work in low-paid, risky unorganised jobs and fall ill often.
focus: Features and problems of slums
Dharavi case study
Solutions: upgradation, housing, services
remember: Slums: least preferred residential areas, dilapidated houses, poor hygiene, lack of water, light, toilets
Residents: low-paid, high-risk unorganised jobs; vulnerable to illness and social exclusion
Dharavi, Mumbai: pottery, leather, garments, recycling; solutions: in-situ redevelopment, PMAY-Urban, secure tenure
traps: Indian cities do not have uniform, well-developed housing everywhere
Slum dwellers mostly work in the unorganised sector, not senior posts

topics.ch: India: Geographical Perspective on Selected Issues and Problems
topics.h: In Madhya Pradesh's Jhabua district, Bhil communities turned bare, eroded hills green again through watershed work.
p: Land degradation is the temporary or permanent decline in the productive capacity of land due to natural and human causes.
Limited availability of agricultural land increases pressure on it; degraded land is often called wasteland.
Naturally created wastelands: gullied or ravinous land, desertic or coastal sands, barren rocky areas, steep sloping land and glacial areas.
Human-induced wastelands: waterlogged and marshy areas, land affected by salinity and alkalinity, degraded forests, degraded pastures and grazing land, and mining and industrial wastelands.

Measures: afforestation, check dams and contour bunding, soil conservation, controlled grazing and watershed management with people's participation (e.g. Jhabua, MP). Exam focus: pollution types and sources, Namami Gange, urban waste, slums, migration and land degradation.

ex.q: Classify these degraded lands as natural or human-induced: Chambal ravines, waterlogged canal land, abandoned mine, coastal sand.
st: Chambal ravines → natural (gullied/ravinous).
Waterlogged canal land → human-induced.
Abandoned mine → human-induced (mining wasteland).
Coastal sand → natural.
ex.a: Natural: ravines, coastal sand; human-induced: waterlogged land, mine wasteland

topics.rl: The Chambal ravines are being reclaimed through afforestation and bunding, while mined lands in Jharkhand are being restored with grass and trees.

rv.summary: Land degradation is a temporary or permanent fall in land's productive capacity from natural or human causes. Natural wastelands include ravines, sands, rocky, steep and glacial areas; human-induced ones include waterlogged, saline-alkaline, degraded forest and pasture, and mining lands.
focus: Meaning of land degradation
Natural vs human-induced wastelands
Remedies and the Jhabua example
remember: Land degradation: temporary or permanent decline in productive capacity
Natural: gullied/ravinous, desertic or coastal sands, barren rocky, steep slopes, glacial
Human-induced: waterlogged, saline-alkaline, degraded forests and pastures, mining and industrial wastelands
traps: Land degradation is not always permanent — it can be reversed
Salinity from irrigation is human-induced, not natural

qa.q: Geography as a field of study is best described as:
qa.e: Geography integrates knowledge from many fields, is grounded in observation (empirical) and is applied to real problems (practical).

qa.q: Human geography studies the interrelationship between:
qa.a: The physical environment and the socio-cultural environment created by humans
qa.e: Human geography looks at how people and their cultural creations interact with the physical environment.

qa.q: Which of these is a branch of physical geography?
qa.e: Biogeography studies the distribution of plants and animals, so it belongs to physical geography; the others are human geography fields.

qa.q: The 'dualism' in geography refers to the division between:
qa.e: Since early times geography has been split into two main branches: physical and human.

qa.q: A geographer maps where cholera cases cluster in a city in 2020 and again in 2025. Which core idea of geography does this show?
qa.a: Phenomena vary over space and time
qa.e: Mapping the same phenomenon at two places in time shows variation over space and time, the core concern of geography.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Human geography is closely tied to physical geography. Reason (R): The physical environment and the human-made socio-cultural environment interact with each other constantly.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true. Because humans and nature interact all the time, human geography cannot be separated from physical geography.

qa.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
qa.e: Climatology (weather and climate) is physical geography. Soil geography and geomorphology are also physical; settlement geography is human.

qa.q: Describing a mountain's 'foot' or a river's 'mouth' shows that geographers:
qa.a: Use human terms to describe nature, showing the close link between the two
qa.e: Using words like 'foot', 'mouth' or 'face' for natural features shows how closely human and physical ideas are woven together.

qa.q: 'Human geography is the synthetic study of relationship between human societies and earth's surface.' Who gave this definition?
qa.e: This is Friedrich Ratzel's definition, stressing synthesis.

qa.q: Ellen C. Semple described human geography as the study of the changing relationship between:
qa.e: Semple's famous phrase is 'unresting man and unstable earth'.

qa.q: Which scholar's definition refers to 'physical laws governing our earth' and 'living beings which inhabit it'?
qa.e: Vidal de la Blache, the French geographer, linked physical laws with the relations between living beings.

qa.q: What is the common idea in all three definitions of human geography?
qa.a: The relationship between humans and environment is dynamic
qa.e: All three treat the human–environment relationship as interactive and changing.

qa.q: Which key word in Ratzel's definition shows that human geography combines many elements?
qa.e: 'Synthetic' means putting together — Ratzel saw human geography as a synthesis.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Semple's definition stresses the dynamic nature of human geography. Reason (R): She described both man as 'unresting' and the earth as 'unstable'.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; calling both humans and earth restless and changing is exactly what makes her definition dynamic.

qa.q: A student writes: 'Human geography is the study of the changing relationship between human societies and physical laws.' Which correction is best?
qa.a: Semple's phrase is 'unresting man and unstable earth'
qa.e: The student has blended Semple's 'changing relationship' with Vidal de la Blache's 'physical laws'. Semple's exact idea is unresting man and unstable earth.

qa.q: Paul Vidal de la Blache belonged to which country's school of geography?
qa.e: Vidal de la Blache was a French geographer, often called a father of French human geography (possibilism).

qa.q: Which of these is an element of the cultural landscape?
qa.e: Ports are built by humans; soils, landforms and natural vegetation are part of the physical environment.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT an element of the physical environment?
qa.e: Roads are built by people, so they belong to the cultural landscape.

qa.q: According to human geography, technology indicates:
qa.a: The level of cultural development of a society
qa.e: The kind of technology a society uses reflects its level of cultural development.

qa.q: Understanding of which natural concept helped humans develop faster aeroplanes?
qa.e: Knowledge of aerodynamics allowed faster aircraft; DNA knowledge helped against diseases and friction-heat knowledge led to fire.

qa.q: Human beings created the cultural landscape by using:
qa.a: The stage provided by the physical environment
qa.e: Humans build their houses, farms and cities on and from the physical environment, which acts as the stage.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Farms and ports are part of the cultural landscape. Reason (R): They are created by human beings using the stage provided by the physical environment.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; anything humans build on nature's stage belongs to the cultural landscape, so R explains A.

qa.q: In a hill town, a student lists: pine forests, a hydroelectric dam, terraced fields and a glacier. How many are part of the cultural landscape?
qa.e: The dam and terraced fields are human-made (2). Pine forests and the glacier are natural.

qa.q: Which statement best describes how the cultural landscape forms?
qa.a: Human activities modify and build upon the physical environment
qa.e: The cultural landscape is the imprint of human activity laid over the physical environment.

qa.q: The direct dependence of primitive societies on nature is called:
qa.e: When humans adapt to and depend on nature directly, it is the naturalisation of humans.

qa.q: Benda, from NCERT's example of environmental determinism, lives in:
qa.e: Benda lives in the Abujh Marh forest area of central India.

qa.q: In the stage of environmental determinism, nature was viewed as:
qa.a: Mother Nature — feared, worshipped and revered
qa.e: Early societies treated nature as a powerful force and revered it.

qa.q: Which condition is the main reason for environmental determinism in early societies?
qa.e: With little technology, people had to adapt to what nature allowed.

qa.q: Which of these activities best fits a society living under environmental determinism?
qa.a: Gathering forest produce and hunting for food
qa.e: Gathering and hunting depend directly on nature; the others need advanced technology.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Primitive societies are said to show naturalisation of humans. Reason (R): They had low technology and depended directly on the physical environment.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; low technology forced direct dependence, which is why they are 'naturalised'.

qa.q: Which statement about environmental determinism is correct?
qa.a: Humans adapt to the dictates of nature
qa.e: In determinism, nature dictates and humans adapt.

qa.q: Benda's community gathers mahua and medicinal herbs and cultivates a forest patch, then moves on. Their dependence for livelihood is mainly on:
qa.e: Their food, medicine and livelihood come directly from the forest.

qa.q: Who introduced the concept of neo-determinism?
qa.e: Griffith Taylor proposed neo-determinism, also called stop and go determinism.

qa.q: Neo-determinism is also known as:
qa.e: Griffith Taylor's idea is called stop and go determinism, compared to obeying traffic lights.

qa.q: The NCERT example of Trondheim, Norway, illustrates:
qa.e: In Trondheim people overcome a harsh winter using technology — nature is humanised.

qa.q: Which of these is an imprint of humans on nature listed in human geography?
qa.e: Satellites, ports, oceanic routes, health resorts and urban sprawls are human imprints; the rest are natural.

qa.q: Neo-determinism argues that:
qa.a: Humans can conquer nature by obeying it
qa.e: It is a middle path: develop, but respect the limits (red signals) of nature.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Neo-determinism says humans must develop within the limits set by nature. Reason (R): The free run taken by developed economies has led to problems such as global warming, ozone depletion and degraded lands.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true. Griffith Taylor's middle path is a response to the damage caused when humans ignored nature's limits, so R explains A.

qa.q: Which pair of school and idea is correctly matched?
qa.a: Possibilism — nature provides opportunities and humans use them
qa.e: Possibilism is about humans making use of opportunities. Benda is determinism; neo-determinism is a middle path.

qa.q: In the traffic-light analogy of neo-determinism, a 'red signal' means:
qa.a: Nature's limit — stop or slow down modification
qa.e: Red means respect nature's limits; humans may proceed when nature permits modification.

qa.q: The quantitative revolution in human geography took place during:
qa.e: The spatial organisation phase, using computers and statistics, was the late 1950s to late 1960s.

qa.q: Which stage focused on identifying the uniqueness of a region and how it differs from others?
qa.e: Areal differentiation (1930s inter-war period) asked why and how regions differ.

qa.q: In which period was the thrust of human geography 'exploration and description'?
qa.e: Imperial and trade interests in the early colonial period led to exploration and descriptive accounts.

qa.q: 'All regions are parts of a whole; understanding parts in totality leads to understanding the whole.' This idea belongs to:
qa.e: Regional analysis (later colonial period) described all aspects of each region as part of the earth as a whole.

qa.q: Which tool is most closely linked with the spatial organisation phase?
qa.e: This phase used computers and statistics and applied laws of physics to human phenomena.

qa.q: What prompted the discovery and exploration of new areas in the early colonial period?
qa.e: Colonial powers wanted new lands and trade, so exploration grew.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The late 1950s to late 1960s phase is called the quantitative revolution. Reason (R): It made heavy use of computers and statistical tools, applying physical laws to human phenomena.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the heavy use of numbers and computers is exactly why it is called 'quantitative'.

qa.q: Which sequence of stages is correct?
qa.a: Exploration and description → Regional analysis → Areal differentiation → Spatial organisation
qa.e: The chronological order runs from early colonial exploration to later colonial regional analysis, then 1930s areal differentiation and 1950s–60s spatial organisation.

qa.q: Which school of human geography employed Marxian theory to explain poverty and deprivation?
qa.e: The radical school used Marxian theory, linking poverty and inequality to capitalism.

qa.q: The emphasis on human awareness, agency, consciousness and creativity belongs to:
qa.e: Humanistic geography puts the active human being at the centre.

qa.q: Which school emphasises lived experience and perception of space by ethnicity, race and religion?
qa.e: The behavioural school focuses on perception and lived experience of social categories.

qa.q: Post-modernism in geography (1990s) is known for:
qa.a: Questioning grand generalisations and stressing local context
qa.e: It doubted universal theories and stressed understanding each local context.

qa.q: Why did humanistic, radical and behavioural schools emerge in the 1970s?
qa.e: Many felt the quantitative revolution ignored human, social and cultural aspects.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The radical school relates contemporary social problems to the development of capitalism. Reason (R): It uses Marxian theory to explain poverty, deprivation and social inequality.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; Marxian theory explains inequality through capitalism, so R explains A.

qa.q: A study argues that a 'universal' model of urban growth fails for Varanasi and must be replaced by a study of its unique local context. This reflects:
qa.e: Rejecting universal models in favour of local context is the post-modern approach.

qa.q: NCERT's welfare or humanistic school of thought was mainly concerned with:
qa.a: Social well-being such as housing, health and education
qa.e: The welfare or humanistic school focused on aspects of people's social well-being.

qa.q: Electoral geography is linked with which sister discipline?
qa.e: Psephology is the study of elections and voting, the sister of electoral geography.

qa.q: Medical geography is closely linked with:
qa.e: Epidemiology studies the spread of diseases, the sister of medical geography.

qa.q: Behavioural geography is a sub-field of social geography linked with:
qa.e: Behaviour and perception connect to psychology.

qa.q: Cultural geography draws mainly on:
qa.e: Anthropology studies cultures, the sister of cultural geography.

qa.q: Gender geography is linked with which group of disciplines?
qa.e: NCERT links gender geography with sociology, anthropology and women's studies.

qa.q: Military geography is a sub-field of:
qa.e: Political geography includes electoral and military geography.

qa.q: Geography of social well-being is linked with:
qa.e: Well-being connects with welfare economics.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Human geography is called an interdisciplinary subject. Reason (R): It has close links with sister disciplines like sociology, economics, political science and history.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; its links with many social sciences are exactly what makes it interdisciplinary.

qa.q: Population geography is linked with which sister discipline?
qa.e: Demography is the statistical study of populations.

qa.q: Settlement geography is linked with:
qa.e: Settlement geography informs the planning of villages and towns.

qa.q: Geography of agriculture is linked with:
qa.e: Farming geography draws on agricultural sciences.

qa.q: Geography of industries is linked with:
qa.e: Location and growth of industries connects to industrial economics.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a sub-field of economic geography?
qa.e: Electoral geography belongs to political geography.

qa.q: Geography of marketing is linked with:
qa.e: Marketing draws on business studies, economics and commerce.

qa.q: 'Humans adapt to nature' vs 'humans modify nature with technology'. These describe, respectively:
qa.a: Naturalisation of humans; humanisation of nature
qa.e: Adapting to nature is naturalisation of humans; modifying it with technology is humanisation of nature.

qa.q: Geography of resources is the sister field of:
qa.e: The study of resources links with resource economics.

qa.q: Why are the people of a country called its real wealth?
qa.a: They use its resources and make its policies
qa.e: People turn resources into wealth and shape decisions, so they are the real wealth.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the four aspects in which population is usually studied?
qa.e: Population is studied by distribution, density, growth and composition. Altitude is a physical feature.

qa.q: 'The way people are spaced over the earth's surface' defines:
qa.e: Distribution is about pattern of spacing; density is a ratio of people to area.

qa.q: World population crossed which mark in November 2022, according to the UN?
qa.e: The UN announced the world reached 8 billion on 15 November 2022.

qa.q: Which statement about historical world population growth is correct?
qa.a: It was slow for a long time and became very rapid in recent centuries
qa.e: Growth was slow in early periods and speeded up after the Industrial Revolution.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A country is ultimately known by its people. Reason (R): People use the country's resources and decide its policies.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because people are the users of resources and makers of policy, a country is identified by them.

qa.q: Which pair is correct for the study of population?
qa.a: Distribution — spacing of people; Density — people per unit area
qa.e: Distribution = pattern of spacing; density = ratio of people to land area.

qa.q: A map shows dots crowded along the Ganga valley and few dots in the Thar desert. This map mainly shows population:
qa.e: A dot map showing where people live shows distribution.

qa.q: About what share of the world's population lives in about 10 per cent of its land area?
qa.e: Population is very unevenly spread: about 90% live on about 10% of land.

qa.q: The 10 most populous countries together contribute about what share of world population?
qa.e: NCERT notes the top 10 countries contribute about 60%.

qa.q: How many of the 10 most populous countries are located in Asia?
qa.e: Six of the ten most populous countries are in Asia.

qa.q: If the world has 8 billion people, roughly how many billion people live in the 10 most populous countries (about 60%)?
qa.e: 60% of 8 billion = 0.6 × 8 = 4.8 billion.

qa.q: On a world population map, which area would appear sparsely populated?
qa.e: Hot deserts like the Sahara have very few people.

qa.q: Which continent has the largest number of the world's most populous countries?
qa.e: Asia has 6 of the top 10.

qa.q: Assertion (A): World population distribution is highly uneven. Reason (R): About 90 per cent of people live in about 10 per cent of the land area.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true, and R is the data that shows A.

qa.q: Which country became the world's most populous in 2023, according to UN estimates?
qa.e: UN estimates showed India overtaking China in 2023.

qa.q: Density of population is expressed as:
qa.e: Density is a ratio of people to land area, so the unit is persons per sq km.

qa.q: A region has an area of 100 sq km and a population of 1,50,000. What is its density (persons per sq km)?
qa.e: Density = 1,50,000 ÷ 100 = 1,500 persons per sq km.

qa.q: A taluka of 250 sq km has a density of 600 persons per sq km. What is its population?
qa.e: Population = density × area = 600 × 250 = 1,50,000.

qa.q: Which of these is a medium density region of the world?
qa.e: NCERT lists western China, southern India, Norway and Sweden as medium density.

qa.q: Which is NOT a sparsely populated region?
qa.e: North-western Europe is densely populated; the others are sparse.

qa.q: Town P: 6,00,000 people on 200 sq km. Town Q: 8,00,000 people on 400 sq km. By how many persons per sq km is P's density greater than Q's?
qa.e: P = 3,000 and Q = 2,000 persons per sq km, so P is denser by 1,000.

qa.q: Assertion (A): High rainfall zones near the equator are sparsely populated. Reason (R): Dense forests, heat and humidity make settlement and farming difficult there.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the harsh conditions of equatorial rainforests explain the sparse population.

qa.q: Which region is among the most densely populated in the world?
qa.e: South, South-east and East Asia are among the most densely populated regions.

qa.q: Which geographical factor explains why river valleys are among the most densely populated areas?
qa.e: Fresh water for drinking, farming and transport draws people to river valleys.

qa.q: Why are the Himalayas, Andes and Alps sparsely populated?
qa.a: Rugged landforms make farming, transport and settlement difficult
qa.e: Steep slopes and harsh terrain discourage settlement.

qa.q: Which plains are cited for fertile loamy soils and dense population?
qa.a: Nile, Ganga, Hwang-He and Chang Jiang
qa.e: These alluvial river plains support intensive farming.

qa.q: Which climate type has historically attracted people due to its pleasantness?
qa.e: The comfortable Mediterranean climate attracted people from early times.

qa.q: A region is flat, has fertile alluvium and a perennial river, but is in a cold desert. Which factor would most limit its population?
qa.e: All other factors are favourable; the extreme cold climate is the limiting factor.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Plains are preferred for human settlement. Reason (R): They are suitable for agriculture, construction of roads and industries.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the ease of farming and building on flat land explains the preference.

qa.q: Which of these is a geographical (not economic or social) factor of population distribution?
qa.e: Water, landforms, climate and soils are geographical factors.

qa.q: Which pairing correctly explains low population in the Thar desert?
qa.e: The Thar has a hot, dry climate and scarce water.

qa.q: The Kobe-Osaka region of Japan is densely populated mainly due to:
qa.e: NCERT cites Kobe-Osaka as an industrial belt that attracts large numbers of people.

qa.q: Which is an example of a mineral-rich area attracting population?
qa.e: Mining and associated industry in the copper belt attract workers.

qa.q: Varanasi, Jerusalem and Vatican City attract people mainly because of:
qa.e: These are religious and cultural centres.

qa.q: Industrial belts attract not only factory workers but also:
qa.a: Transport operators, shopkeepers, bank employees, doctors and teachers
qa.e: Industries generate many service jobs too.

qa.q: Social and political unrest in a region usually leads to:
qa.a: People moving out of the region
qa.e: Unrest is a push factor causing outmigration.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Cities attract large numbers of rural migrants. Reason (R): Cities offer better civic amenities, employment, education and medical facilities.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these attractions explain the rural-urban migration.

qa.q: Which of these is an economic factor influencing population distribution?
qa.e: Minerals, urbanisation and industrialisation are economic factors.

qa.q: A new steel plant opens near an iron ore mine in a forested area. Over 20 years the area's population will most likely:
qa.a: Increase, as jobs attract workers and service providers
qa.e: Mining and industry create jobs, attracting people — as in Jamshedpur or Bhilai.

qa.q: A district's population rose from 8,00,000 in 2011 to 9,20,000 in 2021. What is the growth of population?
qa.e: Growth in absolute numbers = 9,20,000 − 8,00,000 = 1,20,000.

qa.q: For the same district (8,00,000 → 9,20,000), what is the growth rate?
A hill town shrank from 25,000 to 20,000 people. What is its growth rate?
The difference between population figures at two points of time, in absolute numbers, is called:
qa.e: Growth = absolute change; growth rate = percentage change.

qa.q: Population change expressed as a percentage is called:
qa.e: The growth rate expresses change in per cent.

qa.q: Village A grew from 1,000 to 1,200; city B from 10,00,000 to 11,00,000. Which grew at a faster rate?
qa.e: A: 200 ÷ 1,000 = 20%; B: 1,00,000 ÷ 10,00,000 = 10%. The rate, not the absolute number, decides.
