qa.q: Assertion (A): Growth rate is more useful than absolute growth for comparing places. Reason (R): Growth rate expresses change relative to the base population.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because the rate is relative to the base, it allows fair comparison of places of different sizes.

qa.q: A state's population was 5 crore in 2011. With a growth rate of 12% by 2021, what would its 2021 population be (in crore)?
qa.e: New population = 5 × 1.12 = 5.6 crore.

qa.q: Natural growth of population is the difference between:
qa.e: Natural growth considers only births and deaths.

qa.q: Which formula gives the actual growth of population?
qa.e: Actual growth adds net migration to natural growth.

qa.q: A region has 12,000 births, 4,000 deaths, 3,000 in-migrants and 9,000 out-migrants. What is its actual growth?
For the same region (12,000 births, 4,000 deaths), what is the natural growth?
When does a country show negative growth of population?
qa.a: When population decreases between two points of time
qa.e: Negative growth means the number of people falls.

qa.q: Which situation can produce positive growth even if births equal deaths?
qa.e: With natural growth zero, net in-migration still adds people.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A region can have positive natural growth but negative actual growth. Reason (R): Out-migration from the region may exceed natural increase plus in-migration.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; heavy out-migration can outweigh natural increase, making actual growth negative.

qa.q: A hill district has 2,000 births, 1,500 deaths, 200 in-migrants and 1,200 out-migrants. Its actual growth is:
qa.e: 2,000 − 1,500 + 200 − 1,200 = −500, so the district shrinks despite natural growth of +500.

qa.q: A city with a mid-year population of 5,00,000 records 12,500 live births in a year. What is its CBR (per thousand)?
A district of 8,00,000 people records 5,600 deaths in a year. What is its CDR (per thousand)?
In the CBR formula, 'P' stands for:
qa.e: CBR uses live births in the year divided by the mid-year population.

qa.q: Which are the three components of population change?
qa.e: Only births, deaths and migration change the number of people.

qa.q: A town has CBR 28 and CDR 9 per thousand. What is its natural growth rate per thousand?
qa.e: Natural growth rate = CBR − CDR = 28 − 9 = 19 per thousand.

qa.q: Mortality rates are affected by a region's:
qa.a: Demographic structure, social advancement and economic development
qa.e: NCERT lists these three influences on death rates.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Crude birth rate is expressed per thousand of population. Reason (R): CBR is calculated as live births in a year divided by mid-year population, multiplied by 1000.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; multiplying by 1000 is what makes the rate 'per thousand'.

qa.q: Village X (population 4,000) had 120 births; village Y (population 10,000) had 250 births. Which has the higher CBR?
Which of the following is a pull factor of migration?
qa.e: Security attracts people to a destination; the others push people out.

qa.q: Which of the following is a push factor?
qa.e: Backwardness drives people away from their place of origin.

qa.q: Migrants who move into a new place are called:
qa.e: Immigrants come in; emigrants go out.

qa.q: At the place of origin, migration causes the population to:
qa.e: People leaving the place of origin reduce its population.

qa.q: A software engineer moves from Kolkata to Bengaluru. This is which stream of migration?
qa.e: Both are cities, so it is urban-urban migration.

qa.q: Labourers from Bihar move to Punjab for the wheat harvest and return home after it. This is:
qa.e: They move for a season and return, so it is seasonal; it is mostly rural-rural.

qa.q: Assertion (A): People migrate from rural to urban areas in large numbers in developing countries. Reason (R): Unemployment and poor living conditions push people out of villages, while better jobs pull them to cities.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; push and pull factors together explain rural-urban migration.

qa.q: A family leaves a flood-prone coastal village for a hill town with a cooler, safer climate. Which pair of factors is at work?
qa.a: Push: natural disaster; Pull: pleasant climate
qa.e: Floods push them from the origin; the pleasant, safe climate pulls them to the destination.

qa.q: World population reached 1,000 million in 1850 and 2,000 million in 1930. What was the doubling time?
World population grew rapidly mainly after:
qa.e: Technological advances after about 1750 cut death rates and sped up growth.

qa.q: Which factor did NOT contribute to rapid population growth after 1750?
qa.a: Rising death rates due to famines
qa.e: Death rates fell, not rose; that decline drove rapid growth.

qa.q: How long did it take for world population to rise from 5 billion to 6 billion?
qa.e: NCERT notes it took only 12 years.

qa.q: World population in the first century AD was about:
qa.e: It was below 300 million (0.3 billion) in the first century AD.

qa.q: The doubling time of world population has, over the last few centuries:
qa.e: From 200 to 80 to 45 years — it kept shrinking as growth sped up.

qa.q: Assertion (A): World population growth became very rapid after the Industrial Revolution. Reason (R): Better food supply and medical facilities reduced death rates while birth rates stayed high.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; falling deaths with high births caused the rapid increase.

qa.q: If doubling time fell from 80 years to 45 years, by how many years did it shorten?
Which statement best describes the spatial pattern of population growth?
qa.a: Developed countries grow slowly; developing countries grow faster
qa.e: Growth is generally negatively correlated with economic development.

qa.q: Which is described as the most serious problem of rapid population growth?
qa.e: Fast growth uses up resources faster than they can be replaced.

qa.q: A small increase in population is considered:
qa.e: Some growth supplies workers and consumers; problems arise only beyond a point.

qa.q: Which of these is a concern of population decline?
qa.e: Fewer births mean fewer young workers and more elderly.

qa.q: Population growth and economic development are generally:
qa.e: As development rises, growth tends to fall.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Population decline is a matter of concern. Reason (R): It indicates that resources that supported a former population are now insufficient to maintain it.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; NCERT explains the concern this way.

qa.q: A city's population doubles in 20 years while water supply stays the same. Water available per person will:
qa.e: Same water shared by twice the people gives half per person.

qa.q: Which pair is correct?
qa.e: Rapid growth brings joblessness; decline brings ageing.

qa.q: According to demographic transition theory, population changes from:
qa.a: High births and high deaths to low births and low deaths
qa.e: As societies modernise, both rates fall from high to low.

qa.q: In which stage does population increase the most rapidly?
qa.e: Deaths fall while births remain high, so the gap is widest in Stage II.

qa.q: Stage I of demographic transition is characterised by:
qa.a: High fertility, high mortality and slow growth
qa.e: In Stage I both rates are high and cancel out, so growth is slow.

qa.q: What mainly causes mortality to decline in Stage II?
qa.a: Improvements in sanitation and health conditions
qa.e: Better sanitation and health reduce death rates.

qa.q: A society that is urbanised, literate and deliberately limits family size is in:
qa.e: These are features of Stage III.

qa.q: On a demographic transition diagram, which curve falls first?
qa.e: Death rate drops first (Stage II); birth rate falls later.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Population grows slowly in Stage III. Reason (R): Both fertility and mortality have declined considerably.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; with both rates low, the gap is small and growth slow.

qa.q: A country has CBR 15 and CDR 8 per thousand, high literacy and mostly urban living. Its natural growth rate and likely stage are:
qa.e: 15 − 8 = 7 per thousand; low rates with urban literate society indicate Stage III.

qa.q: Malthus put forward his population theory in:
qa.e: Thomas Malthus published his essay on population in 1798.

qa.q: According to Malthus, population grows faster than:
qa.e: He argued numbers would outpace food production.

qa.q: Which is a natural (physical) check on population according to Malthus?
qa.e: Famine, disease and war are natural checks.

qa.q: Which of these is a government measure for population control mentioned in NCERT?
qa.e: Propaganda, free contraceptives and tax disincentives are measures.

qa.q: Family planning is defined as:
qa.a: The spacing or preventing of the birth of children
qa.e: Family planning involves spacing or preventing births.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Malthus believed preventive checks are better than physical checks. Reason (R): Physical checks like famine, disease and war cause great human suffering.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the suffering caused by physical checks is why preventive checks are preferred.

qa.q: Access to family planning services helps in:
qa.a: Limiting population growth and improving women's health
qa.e: It reduces unwanted births and protects women's health.

qa.q: A government runs TV campaigns on small families, distributes contraceptives free and taxes very large families more. These measures together aim to:
qa.e: All three discourage large families, lowering births.

qa.q: Growth is best described as:
qa.e: Growth is a change in size or quantity and can be either positive or negative.

qa.q: Development is:
qa.e: Development means improvement in quality and is always positive.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of negative growth?
qa.a: A city's population falls from 5 lakh to 4.5 lakh
qa.e: A decrease in number is negative growth; growth can go either way.

qa.q: Until recently, the development of a country was measured mainly by:
qa.e: Economic growth (like GNP and per capita income) was the main yardstick.

qa.q: Development occurs when:
qa.a: There is positive growth along with a positive change in quality
qa.e: Development = positive growth + qualitative improvement.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A country can have high economic growth but poor human development. Reason (R): Growth is quantitative while development is qualitative and value positive.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because growth measures only quantity, it can rise without improving the quality of people's lives.

qa.q: Country P's income doubled in 10 years, but child malnutrition and illiteracy stayed high. This shows:
qa.a: Economic growth without matching human development
qa.e: Income grew (growth) but quality of life did not improve (no development).

qa.q: Assertion (A): Development is value neutral. Reason (R): Development is a qualitative change that is always value positive.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it is growth that is value neutral. R is true: development is always value positive.

qa.q: Who introduced the concept of human development?
qa.e: Mahbub-ul-Haq, a Pakistani economist, introduced the concept and designed the HDI.

qa.q: Prof. Amartya Sen saw the main objective of development as:
qa.a: An increase in freedom (decrease in unfreedom)
qa.e: Sen's view is development as freedom.

qa.q: The Human Development Report has been published by UNDP since:
qa.e: The first HDR came out in 1990.

qa.q: According to Haq, development is about:
qa.a: Enlarging people's choices and improving their lives
qa.e: People and their choices are at the centre of human development.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the most important aspects of human development?
qa.e: The three core aspects are health, knowledge and a decent standard of living.

qa.q: Which organisation publishes the Human Development Report?
qa.e: The United Nations Development Programme publishes it.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Human Development Report is published by the UNDP. Reason (R): Dr Mahbub-ul-Haq introduced the concept of human development.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both are true, but Haq introducing the concept does not explain why the UNDP is the publisher.

qa.q: According to Sen, what plays an important role in increasing freedom?
qa.a: Social and political institutions and processes
qa.e: Sen stresses institutions and processes in expanding freedom.

qa.q: Which are the four pillars of human development?
qa.e: These four ideas support human development; the others are approaches or indicators.

qa.q: Equity refers to:
qa.a: Making equal access to opportunities available to everybody
qa.e: Equity means equal access to opportunities irrespective of gender, race, income or caste.

qa.q: Sustainability in human development means:
qa.a: Continuity in the availability of opportunities for every generation
qa.e: Each generation must have the same opportunities.

qa.q: High school dropout rates among women and socially and economically backward groups in India point to a lack of:
qa.e: Unequal access to education is an equity issue.

qa.q: Which action threatens the sustainability pillar?
qa.e: Misusing environmental, financial and human resources reduces future opportunities.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Not sending girl children to school reduces their future opportunities. Reason (R): Sustainability requires that opportunities remain available over time.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; lost schooling today means lost opportunities later, which is what sustainability is about.

qa.q: Equity in the Indian case also means equal access irrespective of:
qa.e: NCERT adds caste to gender, race and income for India.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Sustainability is about continuity in the availability of opportunities. Reason (R): Equity is about leaving the same opportunities to future generations.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: that describes sustainability, not equity.

qa.q: Productivity, as a pillar of human development, refers to:
qa.a: Human labour productivity enriched by building people's capabilities
qa.e: It is about human work efficiency, improved by investing in people.

qa.q: Empowerment means:
qa.a: Having the power to make choices
qa.e: Empowerment is the power to make choices, from increased freedom and capability.

qa.q: Which is required for empowering people according to NCERT?
qa.e: Governance and people-centred policies enable empowerment.

qa.q: Better health facilities and education lead to:
qa.e: Healthy, knowledgeable people work more efficiently.

qa.q: Why are people called the 'real wealth of nations' in the context of productivity?
qa.a: Investment in their capabilities increases a nation's productivity
qa.e: Enriching people's capabilities boosts productivity and development.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Empowerment means having the power to make choices. Reason (R): Empowerment depends only on a person's income.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: empowerment comes from increasing freedom and capability, supported by good governance, not income alone.

qa.q: A government programme trains landless labourers as electricians. Which pillar does it mainly target?
qa.e: Building skills enriches capabilities and work efficiency.

qa.q: A panchayat reserves seats for women, who then decide village spending. This mainly reflects:
qa.e: Giving people the power to make choices is empowerment.

qa.q: The basic needs approach was initially proposed by:
qa.e: The ILO first proposed the basic needs approach.

qa.q: Which approach is associated with Prof. Amartya Sen?
qa.e: Sen's capability approach focuses on building health, education and access to resources.

qa.q: Which is the oldest approach to human development?
qa.e: The income approach is one of the oldest.

qa.q: In the welfare approach, people are seen as:
qa.a: Beneficiaries or targets — passive recipients of development
qa.e: Government spends on welfare, but people are not participants.

qa.q: How many basic needs are identified in the basic needs approach?
qa.e: Health, education, food, water supply, sanitation and housing — six.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the six basic needs?
qa.e: The six are health, education, food, water supply, sanitation and housing.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The basic needs approach ignores the question of human choices. Reason (R): It emphasises providing basic needs to defined sections of society.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; by focusing only on supplying needs, it leaves out people's choices.

qa.q: A policy argues: 'The government should spend more on education, health, social security and amenities.' This reflects the:
qa.e: Higher government expenditure on welfare is the welfare approach.

qa.q: The HDI score of a country lies between:
qa.e: HDI is a score from 0 to 1; closer to 1 means higher development.

qa.q: Which indicator is used to assess health in the HDI?
qa.e: Life expectancy at birth measures the chance of a long and healthy life.

qa.q: Access to resources in the HDI is measured in terms of:
qa.e: GNI per capita in purchasing power parity terms, in US dollars.

qa.q: What weightage does each of the three dimensions of HDI get?
qa.e: Each of health, education and access to resources gets 1/3.

qa.q: Using equal weights of 1/3, a country has indices: health 0.84, education 0.66, income 0.75. What is its HDI?
Which is currently used to measure education in the HDI?
qa.a: Mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling
qa.e: Education is measured by mean and expected years of schooling (earlier, adult literacy and gross enrolment ratio).

qa.q: Assertion (A): A country with an HDI of 0.95 has higher human development than one with 0.55. Reason (R): The closer the HDI score is to 1, the greater the level of human development.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; since closeness to 1 indicates higher development, 0.95 is higher than 0.55.

qa.q: Country X has HDI 0.62 and Country Y has HDI 0.81. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: Y has higher human development than X
qa.e: Higher score (closer to 1) means higher human development; HDI is used to rank countries.

qa.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes HDI and HPI?
qa.a: HDI measures attainment; HPI measures shortfall
qa.e: HDI shows achievement; HPI shows deprivation.

qa.q: Which of these is an indicator of the Human Poverty Index?
qa.a: Probability of not surviving till age 40
qa.e: HPI uses non-income deprivation indicators such as not surviving to 40.

qa.q: Gross National Happiness is officially used by:
qa.e: Bhutan is the only country that officially measures progress through GNH.

qa.q: The HPI is described as a:
qa.e: It looks at deprivations, not income.

qa.q: GNH emphasises which aspects of development?
qa.e: GNH values happiness and non-material well-being.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A country could have a reasonable HDI but still a high HPI. Reason (R): HDI measures attainment while HPI measures shortfall among the deprived.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; average attainment can hide large groups who are deprived, which the HPI captures.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT an HPI indicator?
qa.e: Life expectancy at birth is an HDI indicator; HPI uses probability of not surviving to 40.

qa.q: A country's development policy says: 'Material progress must not harm our environment, culture and spiritual life.' Which idea is this closest to?
qa.e: This reflects Bhutan's GNH philosophy.

qa.q: A country has an HDI score of 0.77. In which category is it?
qa.e: 0.700–0.799 is the high category.

qa.q: A country has an HDI score of 0.60. In which category is it?
qa.e: 0.550–0.699 is the medium category.

qa.q: In which HDI category is India placed?
qa.e: India is in the medium human development category.

qa.q: Which statement about size, income and human development is correct?
qa.a: They are not directly related; small countries can have high human development
qa.e: NCERT stresses that territory size and per capita income are not directly linked to human development.

qa.q: Low HDI countries are mostly characterised by:
qa.a: Political turmoil, civil war, famine or high incidence of diseases
qa.e: Instability and crises keep human development low.

qa.q: Which country is a typical example of very high human development?
qa.e: Norway is consistently near the top; the others are in the low category.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Size of territory is not directly related to human development. Reason (R): Larger countries always have a higher HDI than smaller ones.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false — many small countries rank above much larger ones.

qa.q: Many medium HDI countries:
qa.a: Emerged after the colonial period and are trying to become more people-oriented
qa.e: Most medium group countries gained independence after World War II.

qa.q: Which region has the largest concentration of low HDI countries?
qa.e: Most low HDI countries are in sub-Saharan Africa.

qa.q: Which factor most explains why a country with moderate income can achieve high human development?
qa.a: High investment in the social sector and good governance
qa.e: Spending on health and education and good governance improve HDI.

qa.q: Which pair of pillars of human development is correctly described?
qa.a: Equity — equal access; Empowerment — power to make choices
qa.e: Equity is equal access; empowerment is the power to make choices.

qa.q: Which of the following best explains 'key areas of human development'?
qa.a: Health, education and access to resources
qa.e: These three key areas define human development.

qa.q: On a world HDI map, Japan would be shown in which category?
qa.e: Japan is in the very high human development group.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Low HDI countries often face civil war and famine. Reason (R): Political turmoil and social instability reduce investment in health and education.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; instability diverts resources from the social sector, keeping HDI low.

qa.q: A question asks you to 'differentiate between growth and development'. Which pair of points is most relevant?
qa.a: Quantitative and value neutral vs qualitative and value positive
qa.e: That is the core distinction.

qa.q: A country spends little on schools and clinics, faces frequent coups and has a falling life expectancy. Its HDI category is most likely:
qa.e: Political turmoil and poor social spending typify low HDI countries.

qa.q: People engaged in primary activities are called:
qa.e: Their outdoor work earns them the name red-collar workers.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a primary activity?
qa.e: Manufacturing transforms raw materials — a secondary activity.

qa.q: Primary activities are those that:
qa.e: They use earth's resources directly.

qa.q: Why are primary activity workers called red-collar workers?
qa.a: Because of the outdoor nature of their work
qa.e: The name reflects working outdoors in sun and soil.

qa.q: As a country's economy develops, the proportion of workers in primary activities generally:
qa.e: Workers shift to secondary and tertiary sectors with development.

qa.q: Which list contains only primary activities?
qa.e: Gathering, fishing and quarrying all extract resources directly.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Agriculture is a primary activity. Reason (R): It depends directly on land, water and climate.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; direct dependence on environmental resources is what makes it primary.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In highly developed economies, most workers are in primary activities. Reason (R): As economies develop, workers shift from primary to secondary and tertiary activities.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: developed economies have only a small share in primary work. R is true.

qa.q: Chicle, used for making chewing gum, is obtained from:
qa.a: The milk of the Zapota tree
qa.e: Chicle is made from the milky sap of the Zapota tree.

qa.q: Which of these is a high-latitude zone of gathering?
qa.e: Northern Canada, northern Eurasia and southern Chile are high-latitude gathering zones.

qa.q: Which is NOT a feature of gathering?
qa.e: Gathering produces little or no surplus.

qa.q: Bark of trees gathered in modern times is used for:
qa.e: Bark yields quinine, tannin and cork; fibres give thatch and cloth.

qa.q: Early hunters made their tools from:
qa.e: Primitive tools were made of natural materials.

qa.q: On a world map of subsistence gathering, which region would be marked?
qa.e: The Amazon basin is a major low-latitude gathering zone.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Gathering is unlikely to become important at the global level. Reason (R): Many gathered products face competition from cheaper and better-quality synthetic substitutes.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; synthetic products have replaced many gathered ones, limiting gathering's global role.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Gatherers today often sell valuable plant products in markets. Reason (R): Modern gathering is purely for self-consumption.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: modern gathering is partly market-oriented.

qa.q: Which animal is most important for nomadic herders in the Arctic and sub-Arctic regions?
qa.e: Reindeer are herded in the Arctic and sub-Arctic.

qa.q: Llamas are the main herded animals in the:
qa.e: Llamas belong to the Andes; yak to Tibet.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the three main regions of nomadic herding?
qa.e: The Pampas is known for extensive grain farming and commercial livestock ranching, not nomadic herding.

qa.q: Gujjars, Bakarwals, Gaddis and Bhotiyas are examples of communities practising:
qa.e: They migrate seasonally between plains and Himalayan pastures.

qa.q: In transhumance in the Himalayas, herders move to the mountains in:
qa.e: In summer they go up to high pastures; in winter they come down.

qa.q: In tundra regions, nomadic herders move:
qa.a: South to north in summer, north to south in winter
qa.e: They follow the summer thaw northwards and retreat south in winter.

qa.q: Pastoral nomadism has declined mainly because of:
qa.a: Imposition of political boundaries and new settlement plans
qa.e: Borders and government settlement schemes restrict free movement.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Pastoral nomads depend on animals for food, clothing, shelter, tools and transport. Reason (R): Nomadic herding is a primitive subsistence activity.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; being a subsistence activity, herders meet almost all their needs from their animals.

qa.q: Commercial livestock rearing is practised on:
qa.e: It is organised on large, permanent ranches.

qa.q: Which country is NOT listed among important countries for commercial livestock rearing?
qa.e: Mongolia is known for nomadic herding; the others have commercial ranching.

qa.q: Why are ranches divided into fenced parcels?
qa.a: To regulate grazing and rotate animals between parcels
qa.e: Fencing allows rotational grazing within carrying capacity.

qa.q: Commercial livestock rearing is a specialised activity because:
qa.a: Only one type of animal is reared
qa.e: Ranches specialise in one animal like sheep or cattle.

qa.q: Which practice is emphasised in commercial livestock rearing?
qa.a: Breeding, genetic improvement, disease control and health care
qa.e: Scientific management of animals is central.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Commercial livestock rearing is capital intensive. Reason (R): It needs fencing, scientific breeding, veterinary care and processing facilities.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these costly inputs are why it is capital intensive.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Commercial livestock rearing is associated mainly with subsistence cultures. Reason (R): Its products are processed, packed and exported to world markets.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it is associated with western commercial cultures. R is true.

qa.q: Which pair about the two types of pastoralism is correct?
qa.a: Nomadic herding — subsistence; Commercial rearing — market-oriented
qa.e: Nomadic herding meets subsistence needs; commercial rearing serves markets.

qa.q: Shifting cultivation in north-eastern India is called:
qa.e: Jhuming is the Indian name; Milpa is Central American and Ladang is Indonesian/Malaysian.

qa.q: Ladang is the name for shifting cultivation in:
qa.e: Ladang is used in Indonesia and Malaysia.

qa.q: Why is shifting cultivation also called 'slash and burn' agriculture?
qa.a: Vegetation is cut and burnt, and the ashes add to soil fertility
qa.e: Clearing by cutting and fire gives the name.

qa.q: After how many years does a shifting cultivator usually abandon a plot?
qa.e: The soil loses fertility in about 3 to 5 years.

qa.q: Subsistence agriculture means:
qa.a: Farmers consume all or nearly all of the produce locally
qa.e: Subsistence farming feeds the farming family or community.

qa.q: Primitive subsistence agriculture is widely practised by tribes in:
qa.a: Tropical Africa, South and Central America and South-east Asia
qa.e: It is a tropical practice.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The cycle of jhum is becoming shorter. Reason (R): Loss of soil fertility and growing population force farmers to return to plots sooner.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; shorter fallow periods result from these pressures.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Patches are small and farmers use primitive tools like sticks and hoes. Reason (R): Shifting cultivation uses advanced machinery.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false — shifting cultivators use simple tools.

qa.q: Intensive subsistence agriculture is largely found in:
qa.e: High population and monsoon climate favour intensive subsistence farming.

qa.q: In wet-paddy intensive subsistence agriculture, which is true?
qa.a: Yield per unit area is high but labour productivity is low
qa.e: Many workers on small plots give high yield per hectare but low output per worker.

qa.q: Which crops dominate intensive subsistence agriculture in northern China, Manchuria, North Korea and North Japan?
qa.e: Where paddy is unsuitable, these crops are grown.

qa.q: Fertility of soil in wet-paddy farming is mainly maintained by:
qa.e: Farmyard manure is used to keep soil fertile.

qa.q: Why are land holdings very small in intensive subsistence agriculture?
qa.e: Many people share limited land.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In intensive subsistence agriculture, use of machinery is limited. Reason (R): Holdings are small and abundant family labour is available.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; small plots and plentiful labour make machinery less necessary.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Paddy can be grown everywhere in monsoon Asia. Reason (R): Differences in relief, climate and soil make paddy impractical in many parts of monsoon Asia.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true — that's why other crops dominate in some areas.

qa.q: In India, under intensive subsistence agriculture other than paddy, millets are grown in:
qa.a: Dry parts of western and southern India
qa.e: Millets suit drier areas of western and southern India.

qa.q: Plantation agriculture was introduced by:
qa.e: Europeans set up plantations in tropical colonies.

qa.q: Which is NOT a plantation crop?
qa.e: Wheat is a grain crop of extensive farming; the others are plantation crops.

qa.q: Which colonial power set up cocoa and coffee plantations in West Africa?
qa.e: The French established these in West Africa.

qa.q: The Dutch once had a monopoly over sugarcane plantations in:
qa.e: Indonesia was a Dutch colony with sugarcane monopoly.

qa.q: Rubber plantations in Malaysia were set up by the:
qa.e: The British established rubber estates in Malaysia.

qa.q: Which feature is essential for plantations to sell their produce abroad?
qa.a: A good transport system linking estates, factories and ports
qa.e: Plantations are export-oriented and need efficient transport.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Plantations need a good transport system linking estates, factories and markets. Reason (R): Plantation produce is meant only for local consumption by the workers.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: plantations are export-oriented, which is exactly why they need good transport.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ownership of most plantations has passed to governments or nationals of the countries concerned. Reason (R): Today most plantations are still owned by European colonial companies.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false — ownership has largely moved to local hands.

qa.q: Extensive commercial grain cultivation is practised in:
qa.a: Interior semi-arid lands of the mid-latitudes
qa.e: It is found in the semi-arid grasslands of the mid-latitudes.

qa.q: The principal crop of extensive commercial grain cultivation is:
qa.e: Wheat dominates.

qa.q: Pampas are the grasslands of:
qa.e: Pampas belong to Argentina; Velds to South Africa; Downs to Australia.

qa.q: Velds, a region of extensive grain farming, are in:
qa.e: The Velds are in South Africa.

qa.q: In extensive commercial grain cultivation, there is:
qa.a: Low yield per acre but high yield per person
qa.e: Huge mechanised farms with few workers give this pattern.

qa.q: On a world map, which region would NOT be shaded for extensive commercial grain farming?
qa.e: The Ganga plains have intensive subsistence agriculture.

qa.q: Assertion (A): All operations from ploughing to harvesting are mechanised in extensive grain farming. Reason (R): The size of the farms is very large.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; huge farms can only be worked efficiently with machines.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Extensive grain farming gives high yield per person. Reason (R): Very few workers handle very large areas using machines.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; machines let few people produce a lot.

qa.q: Mixed farming is found mainly in:
qa.a: Highly developed parts of the world like north-western Europe and eastern North America
qa.e: It is a feature of developed temperate regions.

qa.q: Which is an important component of mixed farming?
qa.e: Fodder crops feed livestock.

qa.q: In mixed farming, soil fertility is maintained mainly by:
qa.e: Rotation and intercropping keep soils productive.

qa.q: In mixed farming, emphasis is laid on:
qa.a: Both crop cultivation and animal husbandry equally
qa.e: Equal emphasis on crops and animals is its defining feature.

qa.q: Which is a feature of mixed farming?
qa.a: High capital expenditure on machinery and buildings
qa.e: Mixed farms are capital intensive and use fertilisers and green manures.

qa.q: Which animals provide the main income along with crops in mixed farming?
qa.e: These are typical mixed-farm livestock.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mixed farming depends on the skill and expertise of farmers. Reason (R): It combines crops, fodder, livestock, rotation and machinery on one farm.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; managing many linked activities needs skill and expertise.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mixed farms are usually very large, like grain farms of the Prairies. Reason (R): Mixed farms are moderate in size.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true — mixed farms are moderate-sized.

qa.q: Which is the largest region of commercial dairy farming?
qa.e: North-western Europe is the largest; Canada is second; south-eastern Australia, New Zealand and Tasmania is third.

qa.q: Dairy farming is highly labour intensive because:
qa.a: It needs rigorous care in feeding and milking every day
qa.e: Daily feeding and milking require constant labour.

qa.q: Why is there no off-season in dairy farming?
qa.a: Animals need feeding and milking throughout the year
qa.e: Unlike crops, milch animals need year-round care.

qa.q: Dairy farming is generally practised near:
qa.e: Cities provide a ready market for fresh milk.

qa.q: Which development increased the storage duration of dairy products?
qa.e: Preservation technologies extend shelf life.

qa.q: Which of these is the third main dairy region?
qa.a: South-eastern Australia, New Zealand and Tasmania
qa.e: These form the third belt of commercial dairy farming.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Dairy farming is highly capital intensive. Reason (R): It requires sheds, fodder storage, feeding and milking machines and veterinary services.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these costly facilities make it capital intensive.

qa.q: Assertion (A): It is described as the most advanced and efficient type of rearing milch animals. Reason (R): Dairy farming is the least efficient way of rearing milch animals.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: Viticulture is the cultivation of:
qa.e: Viticulture is grape cultivation.

qa.q: Inferior quality grapes in the Mediterranean region are:
qa.e: Best grapes make wine; inferior ones become raisins and currants.

qa.q: Which region does NOT practise Mediterranean agriculture?
qa.e: The Pampas is an extensive grain and livestock region.

qa.q: The Mediterranean region is an important supplier of:
qa.e: Citrus fruits are a major product.

qa.q: What is the main advantage of Mediterranean agriculture for world markets?
qa.a: It supplies fruits and vegetables in winter when demand is high in Europe and North America
qa.e: Winter supply to cold regions is its big advantage.

qa.q: Besides grapes and citrus, which crops are associated with the Mediterranean region?
qa.e: Olives and figs are typical Mediterranean crops.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mediterranean agriculture is highly specialised commercial agriculture. Reason (R): The region specialises in high-value crops like grapes, citrus, olives and figs for markets.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; specialisation in high-value market crops is what makes it specialised commercial farming.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mediterranean agriculture is found only in Europe. Reason (R): It is also practised in California, central Chile, south-western South Africa and south-western Australia.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true — it occurs wherever Mediterranean climate is found.

qa.q: Market gardening specialises in:
qa.a: High-value crops like vegetables, fruits and flowers for urban markets
qa.e: It grows high-value perishables for cities.

qa.q: The distance of truck farms from the market is governed by:
qa.a: The distance a truck can cover overnight
qa.e: Hence the name truck farming.

qa.q: The Netherlands specialises in growing:
qa.e: Dutch tulips are flown to major European cities.

qa.q: Factory farming is a modern development in:
qa.a: Industrial regions of Western Europe and North America
qa.e: It developed in industrialised regions.

qa.q: In factory farming, livestock are:
qa.a: Reared in stalls and pens and fed manufactured feedstuff
qa.e: Animals are kept indoors and fed manufactured feed.

qa.q: Market gardening farms are located where:
qa.a: There are good transport links to urban centres with high-income consumers
qa.e: Quick access to rich urban buyers is key.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Market gardening uses greenhouses and artificial heating in colder regions. Reason (R): It is a capital-intensive form of farming producing high-value crops.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; high-value crops justify heavy investment like greenhouses and heating.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In truck farming, farmers specialise in vegetables only. Reason (R): Truck farmers grow mainly cereals like wheat.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false — truck farms grow vegetables.

qa.q: Kolkhoz refers to:
qa.a: Collective farming in the erstwhile Soviet Union
qa.e: Kolkhoz was the Soviet collective farm.

qa.q: In which country is practically every farmer a member of a cooperative?
qa.e: Denmark's cooperative movement is very successful.

qa.q: Cooperative farming is based on:
qa.a: Voluntary pooling of resources by farmers who keep their farms intact
qa.e: In cooperatives, farmers pool voluntarily but retain individual farms.

qa.q: Collective farming is based on:
qa.a: Social ownership of the means of production and collective labour
qa.e: Kolkhoz farms were socially owned and worked collectively.

qa.q: In a kolkhoz, the produce up to the government target was:
qa.a: Sold to the state at fixed prices
qa.e: Targets were bought by the state at fixed prices; surplus went to members or market.

qa.q: Which is NOT a function of a farmers' cooperative society?
qa.a: Fixing yearly production targets and buying at state-fixed prices
qa.e: Targets and fixed prices were features of Soviet collective farms, not cooperatives.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Collective farms allowed members to retain very small plots. Reason (R): Farmers needed to grow crops for their daily requirements.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the small plots were allowed so that members could meet daily needs.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The cooperative movement was a failure in western Europe. Reason (R): Cooperative farming has been successful in Denmark, the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden and Italy.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Which is the easiest and cheapest method of mining minerals close to the surface?
qa.e: Surface or open-cast mining is cheapest for near-surface deposits.

qa.q: Which of these is a physical factor affecting mining?
qa.e: Size, grade and mode of occurrence are physical factors.

qa.q: Which of these is an economic factor affecting mining?
qa.e: Demand, technology, capital, labour and transport costs are economic factors.

qa.q: Underground mining is risky because of:
qa.a: Poisonous gases, fires, floods and caving in
qa.e: These hazards cause fatal accidents in shaft mines.

qa.q: Why are developed economies retreating from mining, processing and refining?
qa.e: High labour costs make these stages costly in developed countries.

qa.q: The Copper Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age show:
qa.a: The importance of minerals in human history
qa.e: Eras named after metals show how minerals shaped development.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Open-cast mining gives large and rapid output. Reason (R): Minerals are close to the surface and overhead costs like safety equipment are relatively low.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; easy access and low overheads explain the quick, large output.

qa.q: Which statement best differentiates nomadic herding from commercial livestock rearing?
qa.a: Nomadic herding is subsistence-based and mobile; commercial rearing is market-oriented on permanent ranches
qa.e: This is a common board question: subsistence/mobile vs commercial/ranch-based.

qa.q: Secondary activities are those that:
qa.a: Add value to natural resources by transforming raw materials
qa.e: They convert raw materials into more valuable products.

qa.q: Which of these is a secondary activity?
qa.e: Converting ore to steel is manufacturing.

qa.q: Which of these groups are included in secondary activities?
qa.e: Secondary activities cover manufacturing, processing and construction industries.

qa.q: Why does iron ore gain value after being converted into steel?
qa.a: It can now be used to make machines, tools and structures
qa.e: Steel is usable for many products, so its value rises.

qa.q: Building highways and dams belongs to which category of secondary activities?
qa.e: Construction industries are part of secondary activities.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Secondary activities add value to natural resources. Reason (R): Secondary activities involve only the extraction of raw materials from the earth.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: extraction is a primary activity; secondary activities transform raw materials.

qa.q: A canning factory in Ratnagiri turns fresh mangoes into mango pulp. This activity is:
qa.e: Processing raw fruit into pulp adds value — secondary.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Secondary activities transform raw materials into more valuable products. Reason (R): Mining coal is a secondary activity.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: mining extracts raw materials and is primary.

qa.q: The literal meaning of 'manufacturing' is:
qa.e: It comes from 'make by hand'; today it includes machine-made goods.

qa.q: Which is NOT a common characteristic of modern manufacturing?
qa.a: Production only for the household's own use
qa.e: Household-only production describes cottage industry, not modern manufacturing.

qa.q: Which statement about 'industry' and 'manufacturing' is correct?
qa.a: Industry is a broader term; manufacturing is a part of it
qa.e: We speak of the tourism industry, which does not manufacture goods.

qa.q: Workers engaged in factory production are usually called:
qa.e: Blue-collar = manufacturing; red-collar = primary; white-collar = office/knowledge.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of manufacturing?
qa.e: Assembling components produces goods.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Modern manufacturing produces standardised commodities. Reason (R): It uses mass production of identical products with specialised labour.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; mass production of identical items is what gives standardised goods.

qa.q: The 'tourism industry' is called an industry, but it is not manufacturing because:
qa.a: It provides services rather than producing goods from raw materials
qa.e: Manufacturing makes goods; tourism sells services.

qa.q: Which range best describes manufacturing?
qa.e: Manufacturing spans simple handicrafts to complex aerospace goods.

qa.q: Automation is described as:
qa.a: The advanced stage of mechanisation, without human thinking during manufacturing
qa.e: Automation runs processes through feedback and closed-loop control.

qa.q: Under mass production:
qa.a: Large quantities of standardised parts are made with each worker doing one task
qa.e: Mass production relies on standard parts and division of labour.

qa.q: R&D in modern manufacturing is used for:
qa.a: Quality control, eliminating waste and combating pollution
qa.e: Technological innovation through R&D improves quality and efficiency.

qa.q: Major concentrations of modern manufacturing cover about how much of the world's land area?
qa.e: They are concentrated in a few places covering under 10% of land.

qa.q: Which is NOT a feature of the organisational structure of modern manufacturing?
qa.e: Household labour with simple tools describes cottage industry.

qa.q: Closed-loop computer control systems are linked with which characteristic?
qa.e: They enable machines to 'think' — automation.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Automation is the advanced stage of mechanisation. Reason (R): In automation, no machines are used at all.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: automation uses machines that run without human thinking during manufacturing.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The craft method has low costs per piece. Reason (R): The craft method produces only a few made-to-order pieces.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: making few custom pieces raises cost per piece. R is true.

qa.q: Which is described as the most important factor in the location of industries?
qa.e: Without a market for goods, no industry can survive.

qa.q: Industries that use heavy, cheap, weight-losing raw materials are located:
qa.a: Close to the sources of raw material
qa.e: Locating near the source avoids transporting waste weight.

qa.q: The aluminium industry is usually located near:
qa.e: Aluminium smelting needs huge amounts of electricity.

qa.q: Dairy processing units are located close to milk-producing areas because milk is:
qa.e: Perishable raw materials must be processed quickly near the source.

qa.q: Which industries are said to have a global market?
qa.e: NCERT notes aircraft and arms industries serve global markets.

qa.q: Industries locate where production costs are lowest because they aim to:
qa.e: Profit maximisation drives location choice.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Iron and steel, cement and sugar industries are usually located near raw material sources. Reason (R): Their raw materials are bulky and weight-losing.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; carrying bulky, weight-losing material over long distances is costly, so these industries stay near the source.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mechanisation and automation have reduced dependence on labour. Reason (R): Modern industries no longer need any labour.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false — some industries still need skilled labour.

qa.q: Benefits that industries get from being close to a leader industry and other industries are called:
qa.e: These savings from clustering are agglomeration economies.

qa.q: Why do governments adopt regional policies for industrial location?
qa.e: Regional policies spread industry to backward areas.

qa.q: Which regions have historically attracted industries because of highly developed transport systems?
qa.a: Western Europe and eastern North America
qa.e: Dense transport networks encouraged industrial concentration there.

qa.q: Speedy and efficient transport is important to industries because it:
qa.a: Carries raw materials to factories and finished goods to markets
qa.e: Transport links inputs and outputs.

qa.q: A state offers cheap land, tax holidays and power subsidies to firms setting up in a backward district. This is an example of:
qa.e: Incentives from government guide location.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Many industries cluster near a leader industry. Reason (R): They gain agglomeration economies from nearness to it and to other industries.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; agglomeration benefits explain clustering.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Communication has no role in the location of industries. Reason (R): Industries need communication for the exchange and management of information.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true — communication is part of the transport and communication factor.

qa.q: Which factor would most explain a cluster of IT firms in one technology park?
qa.e: Firms benefit from shared talent, services and links — agglomeration.

qa.q: Footloose industries are:
qa.a: Not dependent on any specific raw material and can locate in many places
qa.e: They use components available anywhere, so location is flexible.

qa.q: The most important factor in the location of footloose industries is:
qa.e: Road access matters most for them.

qa.q: Which of these is a footloose industry?
qa.e: Diamonds are light, valuable and processed anywhere.

qa.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of footloose industries?
qa.e: Footloose industries are generally non-polluting.

qa.q: Footloose industries largely depend on:
qa.a: Component parts that can be obtained anywhere
qa.e: Components can be sourced from many places.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Footloose industries can be located in a wide variety of places. Reason (R): They are not dependent on any specific raw material.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; freedom from a specific raw material is what lets them locate anywhere.

qa.q: Assertion (A): They produce in small quantities. Reason (R): Footloose industries employ huge labour forces.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: footloose industries employ small labour forces.

qa.q: A firm makes small, light, high-value electronic sensors from imported chips and needs a highway nearby. It is best described as:
qa.e: Light components, small output and road dependence are footloose traits.

qa.q: Which is the smallest manufacturing unit?
qa.e: Cottage industry is the smallest, run by artisans at home.

qa.q: Small-scale manufacturing differs from household industry mainly in:
qa.a: Production techniques and place of manufacture (a workshop outside the home)
qa.e: Small-scale units use simple power-driven machines in a workshop.

qa.q: Why have India, China, Indonesia and Brazil developed labour-intensive small-scale manufacturing?
qa.a: To provide employment to their large populations
qa.e: Small-scale industries generate jobs and raise local income.

qa.q: Which is NOT a feature of large-scale manufacturing?
qa.e: Locally devised simple tools are a feature of cottage industry.

qa.q: Which of these is a traditional large-scale manufacturing region?
qa.a: Great Lakes region of the USA
qa.e: The Great Lakes region is a classic industrial belt.

qa.q: In household industry, capital and transportation have little influence because:
qa.a: It has low commercial significance and tools are locally devised
qa.e: Production is small and local, so capital and transport matter little.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Small-scale manufacturing raises local purchasing power. Reason (R): It provides employment to local people.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; jobs give people income, raising purchasing power.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Large-scale manufacturing uses little energy. Reason (R): Large-scale manufacturing involves a large market and assembly-line mass production.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false: it needs enormous energy. R is true.

qa.q: Which of these is an agro-based industry?
qa.e: Cotton comes from farms.

qa.q: Agri-business refers to:
qa.a: Commercial farming on an industrial scale, often financed by non-farm businesses
qa.e: It is large-scale, business-financed commercial farming.

qa.q: Cement is classified as which type of industry?
qa.e: Cement uses non-metallic minerals like limestone.

qa.q: Aluminium and copper industries are based on:
qa.e: They do not contain iron — non-ferrous.

qa.q: Which industry uses mineral oil (petroleum) as raw material?
qa.e: Petroleum is the base of petrochemicals.

qa.q: Lac and paper are products of which type of industry?
qa.e: Both come from forest raw materials.

qa.q: Which is NOT a part of food processing as listed in NCERT?
qa.e: Smelting is a metallurgical process.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ivory is a raw material for animal-based industries. Reason (R): Ivory is obtained from elephant tusks.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; since ivory comes from an animal, it belongs to animal-based industries (its trade is now strictly restricted to protect elephants).

qa.q: Industries whose products are used to make other goods are called:
qa.e: Basic industries supply inputs to other industries.

qa.q: Which is an example of a consumer goods industry?
qa.e: Soaps are used directly by consumers.

qa.q: Public sector industries are:
qa.e: Governments own public sector enterprises.

qa.q: Industries managed by joint stock companies or by public and private sectors together are:
qa.e: Joint sector combines public and private participation.

qa.q: Capitalist countries generally have mostly:
qa.e: In capitalist economies, private ownership dominates.

qa.q: Mixed economies like India have:
qa.a: Both public and private sector enterprises
qa.e: A mixed economy combines both.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Iron and steel is a basic industry. Reason (R): Its products are used as raw materials by many other industries.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; supplying other industries is what makes it basic.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Consumer goods industries produce goods that are consumed directly. Reason (R): Bread and biscuit industries are basic industries.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false — they are consumer goods industries.

qa.q: High-technology industry is best understood as:
qa.a: Application of intensive R&D to make advanced scientific and engineering products
qa.e: Intensive R&D leading to advanced products defines high-tech.

qa.q: Silicon Valley, an example of a technopolis, is located near:
qa.e: Silicon Valley is near San Francisco; Silicon Forest is near Seattle.

qa.q: In high-tech industries, the largest share of the workforce is made up of:
qa.e: Skilled professionals outnumber production workers.

qa.q: Which is an example of high-tech industry?
qa.e: Robotics is high-tech; the others are traditional.

qa.q: A 'technopolis' refers to:
qa.a: Regionally concentrated, self-sustained, highly specialised high-tech industries
qa.e: Technopolis is a cluster of high-tech activity.

qa.q: The landscape of high-tech industry is characterised by:
qa.a: Neatly spaced, low, modern, dispersed office-plant-lab buildings
qa.e: High-tech areas look like campuses, not heavy industrial zones.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Planned business parks for start-ups are part of regional development schemes. Reason (R): High-tech industries benefit from concentrated, specialised clusters.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because clustering helps high-tech firms, governments plan business parks.

qa.q: Which list contains important manufacturing industries that contribute significantly to the world economy?
qa.a: Iron and steel, textiles, automobiles, petrochemicals and electronics
qa.e: These are major manufacturing industries.

qa.q: Tertiary activities are mainly related to:
qa.e: They provide services rather than goods.

qa.q: The main difference between secondary and tertiary activities is that tertiary expertise relies more on:
qa.a: Specialised skills, experience and knowledge of workers
qa.e: Services depend on human skill and knowledge; manufacturing on machines and processes.

qa.q: Which of these is a tertiary activity?
qa.e: Medical care is a service.

qa.q: Tertiary activities involve:
qa.a: Commercial output of services rather than tangible goods
qa.e: They are not directly involved in processing raw materials.

qa.q: In developed countries, the majority of workers are employed in the:
qa.e: Services dominate employment in developed economies.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Manpower is an important component of the service sector. Reason (R): Tertiary activities depend on the skills, experience and knowledge of workers.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; since services rely on human skills, manpower is central.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Tertiary activities are directly involved in processing raw materials. Reason (R): Tertiary activities produce services rather than tangible goods.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: A publisher, a cashier and a launderer are all examples of workers in:
qa.e: They all provide services.

qa.q: Which of these is a low-order service?
qa.e: Grocery shops are common and widespread — low-order.

qa.q: High-order services are:
qa.e: Specialised services are fewer and concentrated in larger centres.

qa.q: The transport system is an example of a service geared to:
qa.e: Transport serves both industries (goods) and people (passengers).

qa.q: Which is NOT a broad type of tertiary activity?
qa.e: Manufacturing is secondary.

qa.q: Why are low-order services more widespread than high-order services?
qa.a: They are needed frequently by many people and need a small market
qa.e: Frequent, everyday needs can be met with a small catchment.

qa.q: Assertion (A): High-order services are found mostly in large towns and cities. Reason (R): Specialised services need a large number of customers to be viable.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the large threshold population needed for specialised services explains their location in big centres.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Trade, transport, communication and services are all tertiary activities. Reason (R): Tertiary activities produce tangible goods in factories.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true; R is false — tertiary activities provide services, not goods.

qa.q: A small town has 40 grocery shops but only 2 chartered accountants. This illustrates that:
qa.a: Low-order services are more common than high-order services
qa.e: Everyday low-order services far outnumber specialised ones.

qa.q: Trade is essentially:
qa.a: Buying and selling of items produced elsewhere
qa.e: Traders buy and sell goods made by others.

qa.q: Rural marketing centres are described as:
qa.a: Quasi-urban centres of the most rudimentary type
qa.e: They are basic trading centres serving nearby villages.

qa.q: Periodic markets are held:
qa.a: At fixed intervals like weekly or bi-weekly
qa.e: They meet on specified days at regular intervals.

qa.q: Where are periodic markets mainly found?
qa.a: In rural areas without regular markets
qa.e: They serve rural areas lacking permanent markets.

qa.q: Which is true of rural marketing centres?
qa.a: Personal and professional services are not well developed
qa.e: They are rudimentary centres with limited services.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Shopkeepers in a periodic market system remain busy throughout the week. Reason (R): Periodic markets move from one place to another on specified dates.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; moving between villages on different days keeps traders busy all week.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Rural marketing centres act as local collecting and distributing centres. Reason (R): Rural marketing centres do not perform any collecting or distributing function.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: A village of 2,000 people cannot support a daily cloth shop. What arrangement best meets its demand?
qa.e: A periodic market serves demand accumulated over a week.

qa.q: Retail trading is:
qa.a: Sale of goods directly to consumers
qa.e: Retail = directly to the consumer.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT an example of non-store retail trading?
qa.e: A departmental store is a fixed store.

qa.q: Which were the first to introduce large-scale innovations in retailing?
qa.e: NCERT credits consumer cooperatives.

qa.q: Wholesale trading is carried out through:
qa.a: Numerous intermediary merchants and supply houses
qa.e: Wholesale is bulk trade via intermediaries.

qa.q: Wholesalers often help retailers by:
qa.e: Retailers may operate largely on the wholesaler's capital.

qa.q: Which service is typically available in urban but not rudimentary rural marketing centres?
qa.e: Urban centres offer specialised professional services.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Chain stores can purchase merchandise very economically. Reason (R): They often have goods manufactured to their own specifications in bulk.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; bulk orders made to their specifications explain their economical buying.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Departmental stores are a form of non-store retail trading. Reason (R): In departmental stores, departmental heads handle purchasing and sales in different sections.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false — departmental stores are fixed stores. R is true.

qa.q: In a transport network, the meeting point of two or more routes is called a:
qa.e: Nodes are junctions; links join nodes.

qa.q: Every road that joins two nodes is called a:
qa.e: A link connects two nodes.

qa.q: 'Time distance' refers to:
qa.a: The time taken to travel on a route
qa.e: Time distance measures travel time.

qa.q: In selecting the mode of transport, the determining factor is usually distance in terms of:
qa.e: People choose based on time and cost.

qa.q: Demand for transport is influenced mainly by:
qa.e: More people means more demand.

qa.q: A network with 6 nodes is upgraded from 6 links to 10 links. What happens?
qa.e: More links improve connectivity.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Transport is called an organised industry. Reason (R): It was created to satisfy the basic human need of mobility.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; organising transport as an industry meets the need to move people and goods.

qa.q: Which of these does NOT affect the routes of transport?
qa.e: Routes depend on settlements, raw materials, trade, landscape, climate and funds.

qa.q: Communication services involve:
qa.a: Transmission of words, messages, facts and ideas
qa.e: Communication is about transmitting information.

qa.q: Radio and television are called mass media because they:
qa.e: They relay news and entertainment to huge numbers of people.

qa.q: Which invention made messages permanent and dependent on means of transport?
qa.e: Written messages had to be carried by hand, animal, boat or vehicle.

qa.q: Which technology allows almost instantaneous transmission of large volumes of data across continents?
qa.e: Modern telecom uses optical fibres and satellites.

qa.q: Mass media are vital for:
qa.e: Radio and TV support advertising and entertainment.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Telecommunications have shrunk time and distance. Reason (R): They allow messages to be transmitted almost instantly across the world.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; instant transmission is what shrinks effective distance.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Early communication relied on drums, smoke signals, runners and animals. Reason (R): Early communication was mostly instantaneous.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false — early methods were slow.

qa.q: A newspaper reports events from around the world each morning. It is an example of:
qa.e: Newspapers reach mass audiences.

qa.q: Which of these is a business service?
qa.e: Advertising, legal services, PR and consultancy are business services.

qa.q: Housekeepers, cooks and gardeners are examples of:
qa.e: They provide personal services, mostly in the unorganised sector.

qa.q: Which is a public utility?
qa.e: Water and electricity are public utilities.

qa.q: Rural migrants working in personal services in cities are usually:
qa.a: Unskilled, poorly paid and in the unorganised sector
qa.e: NCERT describes them as unskilled and in the unorganised sector.

qa.q: In the USA, roughly what share of workers is engaged in services?
qa.e: Services employ over 75% of US workers.

qa.q: Health care, engineering, law and management are examples of:
qa.e: These need high skills and training.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Personal service workers are poorly paid. Reason (R): Many of them are unskilled migrants working in the unorganised sector.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; lack of skills and the unorganised nature of the work explain low pay.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The share of workers in services is falling in developing countries. Reason (R): The share of service workers is rising in developing countries too.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Tourism is defined as travel undertaken for:
qa.e: Tourism means recreational travel.

qa.q: Tourism is the world's single largest tertiary activity in terms of:
qa.a: Total registered jobs and total revenue
qa.e: It leads in jobs (about 250 million) and revenue.

qa.q: Approximately how many registered jobs does tourism account for worldwide, according to NCERT?
qa.e: NCERT gives about 250 million jobs.

qa.q: Which attraction is mainly responsible for winter sports tourism?
qa.e: Winter sports need snow, a climatic factor.

qa.q: Home-stays in Coorg and heritage homes in Goa reflect which tourist attraction?
qa.e: Local customs and home-stays fall under culture and economy.

qa.q: Which is NOT listed as an industry fostered by tourism?
qa.e: Tourism boosts infrastructure, retail and crafts, not steel making.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Tourism has grown rapidly in the last century. Reason (R): Rising standards of living, more leisure time and better transport have increased tourism.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; higher demand and improved transport explain tourism's growth.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Many regions attract visitors throughout the year. Reason (R): Tourism is always seasonal everywhere.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false — some places attract tourists all year.

qa.q: Quaternary activities involve:
qa.a: Collection, production and dissemination of information
qa.e: They are knowledge-based activities.

qa.q: Which is an example of a quaternary activity?
qa.e: Software development is knowledge-based.

qa.q: Quaternary activities are:
qa.a: Not tied to resources or necessarily localised by market
qa.e: They are footloose in nature and can be outsourced.

qa.q: Workers in the quaternary sector are often called:
qa.e: They work with information and knowledge.

qa.q: Quaternary activities are seen as an advanced form of services involving:
qa.e: They demand specialised knowledge and technical skills.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Quaternary activities can be outsourced to other countries. Reason (R): They are not tied to resources or necessarily localised by market.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; since they are not bound to resources or markets, the work can be done anywhere.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Primary and secondary employment form the main basis of economic growth in developed economies today. Reason (R): The quaternary and tertiary sectors have replaced most primary and secondary employment as the basis for growth.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Over the history of a developed economy, the share of the workforce has generally shifted:
qa.a: From primary towards tertiary and quaternary activities
qa.e: Development moves workers from farms to services and knowledge work.

qa.q: Quinary activities are performed by:
qa.a: The highest level of decision makers or policy makers
qa.e: Quinary work is top-level decision making.

qa.q: Quinary activities are often referred to as:
qa.e: They are called gold-collar professions.

qa.q: Which of these is a quinary worker?
qa.e: Senior executives make high-level decisions.

qa.q: Quinary services focus on:
qa.a: Creation, rearrangement and interpretation of new and existing ideas
qa.e: They deal with ideas, data interpretation and evaluation of technologies.

qa.q: The importance of quinary activities in advanced economies:
qa.e: Few people but very high impact.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Quinary professionals are highly paid. Reason (R): They possess special skills and take top-level decisions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; rare skills and decision-making power explain the high pay.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Quinary activities are subtly different from the knowledge-based quaternary sector. Reason (R): Quinary activities are the same as quaternary activities.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false — quinary is a subdivision focused on top decisions.

qa.q: Which worker–sector pair is correctly matched?
qa.e: Top research scientists and policy makers are quinary.

qa.q: Outsourcing is done mainly to:
qa.e: Firms outsource to cut costs and gain efficiency.

qa.q: When outsourcing involves transferring work to overseas locations, it is called:
qa.e: Offshoring = outsourcing abroad.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of KPO rather than BPO?
qa.e: KPO involves highly skilled knowledge work like IP research.

qa.q: KPO differs from BPO because it:
qa.a: Involves highly skilled, information-driven knowledge work
qa.e: KPO relies on high skills and knowledge.

qa.q: Which country is NOT mentioned among major BPO destinations?
qa.e: India, China, Eastern Europe, Israel, Philippines and Costa Rica are listed; Antarctica has no BPO industry.

qa.q: Interpretation of MRIs and ultrasound tests sent from abroad to India is an example of:
qa.e: Hospitals outsource reading of medical images.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India has emerged as a leading country for medical tourism. Reason (R): World-class hospitals in Indian metros offer quality treatment to patients from many countries.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; quality treatment at Indian hospitals attracts foreign patients.

qa.q: Assertion (A): BPO and KPO require exactly the same level of skill. Reason (R): KPO involves highly skilled workers, unlike most BPO work.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: The digital divide refers to:
qa.a: Unequal access to information and communication technology
qa.e: It is the gap in access to ICT and its opportunities.

qa.q: Which example shows a digital divide within a country?
qa.a: Metros with high-speed internet vs remote villages with poor connectivity
qa.e: Within-country divides exist between metropolitan and peripheral areas.

qa.q: Home-shoring is best described as:
qa.a: Keeping or bringing work back within the home country instead of sending it abroad
qa.e: It is an alternative to offshoring.

qa.q: Which is a concern linked with outsourcing for developing countries?
qa.a: Dependence on foreign clients and need for a steady supply of skilled labour
qa.e: Over-dependence and skill needs are concerns.

qa.q: Which of these is a benefit of outsourcing for India?
qa.e: Outsourcing created many jobs and earns foreign exchange.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A digital divide exists within large countries like India. Reason (R): Metropolitan centres have better connectivity and access to the digital world than peripheral rural areas.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the metro-rural connectivity gap is the within-country divide.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Developed countries in general have surged forward in using ICT opportunities. Reason (R): Developing countries have surged ahead of developed countries in ICT access.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false — developing countries have generally lagged.

qa.q: Which statement correctly differentiates secondary and tertiary activities?
qa.a: Secondary produce goods using machines and processes; tertiary provide services using skills and knowledge
qa.e: This is the core distinction asked in exams.

qa.q: Transport and communication help to:
qa.a: Bridge the gap between places of production and consumption
qa.e: They connect producers and consumers across space.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the three basic modes of transport?
qa.e: Land, water and air are the basic modes; pipelines are a special means.

qa.q: Which mode is best suited for bulky goods over long distances between continents?
qa.e: Ships carry large, heavy cargo cheaply over long distances.

qa.q: High-value, light and perishable goods are usually moved by:
qa.e: Air is fast, so it suits light, valuable, perishable goods.

qa.q: Which mode is the most economical for short distances and offers door-to-door service?
qa.e: Roads are flexible and serve short distances best.

qa.q: Integrating different modes so goods move smoothly in standard boxes is called:
qa.e: Containers move between ship, rail and truck without repacking.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Human porters are still used in some hilly regions. Reason (R): Roads and vehicles cannot easily reach all steep and rugged terrain.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; rugged terrain limits vehicles, so people still carry loads.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The choice of transport mode depends only on distance. Reason (R): The type of goods, cost and urgency also influence the choice of mode.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Why is freight transport by road gaining importance?
qa.e: Door-to-door delivery is road transport's big advantage.

qa.q: The total motorable road length of the world is about:
qa.e: NCERT gives about 15 million km.

qa.q: Which continent has the highest road density and the highest number of vehicles?
qa.e: North America leads in road density and vehicles.

qa.q: North America accounts for about what share of the world's motorable roads?
qa.e: About 33 per cent of world roads are in North America.

qa.q: Unmetalled roads are a problem because they:
qa.a: Become unmotorable during the rainy season
qa.e: Kutcha roads turn muddy in rain.

qa.q: Peaks of traffic on city roads usually occur:
qa.a: During rush hours before and after work
qa.e: Commuter rush creates peaks.

qa.q: Assertion (A): City roads suffer from chronic congestion. Reason (R): Road networks often cannot cope with rapidly growing traffic.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; traffic outgrowing road capacity causes congestion.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Road transport is most economical for short distances. Reason (R): Roads are the most economical mode for very long-distance bulk freight.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false — rail and sea are cheaper for long-distance bulk.

qa.q: The Alaskan Highway links:
qa.e: Alaskan Highway connects Edmonton (Canada) with Anchorage (Alaska).

qa.q: The Trans-Continental Stuart Highway connects:
qa.e: It runs north–south in Australia via Tennant Creek and Alice Springs.

qa.q: The Trans-Canadian Highway links Vancouver with:
qa.e: It joins the west and east coasts of Canada.

qa.q: Which highway will connect South America, Central America and USA-Canada?
qa.e: The Pan-American Highway runs through the Americas.

qa.q: Border roads mainly help to:
qa.a: Integrate remote border areas with major cities and support defence
qa.e: They link border villages and military camps.

qa.q: Which organisation builds border roads in India?
qa.e: BRO builds and maintains roads in border areas.

qa.q: Assertion (A): North America has a very high density of highways. Reason (R): In North America, every place is within about 20 km of a highway.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; being within 20 km everywhere reflects the high density.

qa.q: The Golden Quadrilateral connects which four metros?
qa.e: GQ links the four major metros.

qa.q: The width of the standard gauge is:
qa.e: Standard gauge = 1.44 m; broad gauge is more than 1.5 m; metre gauge 1 m.

qa.q: About how much railway length is open to traffic in the world?
qa.e: About 13 lakh (1.3 million) km.

qa.q: Which continent has one of the densest rail networks in the world?
qa.e: Europe's network is very dense.

qa.q: Railways are most suitable for:
