qa.a: Bulky goods and passengers over long distances
qa.e: Rail suits heavy loads over land for long distances.

qa.q: Trans-continental railways are those that:
qa.a: Run across a continent linking its two ends
qa.e: They cross the continent end to end.

qa.q: Underground railways are especially important in:
qa.e: Big cities like London and Paris rely on metros.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Railways account for about 90 per cent of Russia's total transport. Reason (R): Russia's vast geographical area makes railways more important than highways there.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; long distances across Russia make railways the backbone of transport.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Broad gauge is narrower than metre gauge. Reason (R): Broad gauge is more than 1.5 m wide, while metre gauge is 1 m wide.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true — broad gauge is wider.

qa.q: The Trans-Siberian Railway runs from St Petersburg to:
qa.e: Its eastern terminal is Vladivostok on the Pacific coast.

qa.q: What is the length of the Trans-Siberian Railway?
qa.e: It is 9,332 km long; 7,050 km is the Trans-Canadian.

qa.q: The Trans-Canadian Railway connects Halifax in the east with:
qa.e: Its western terminal is Vancouver on the Pacific.

qa.q: The Trans-Canadian Railway is called the economic artery of Canada because it:
qa.a: Links the Quebec-Montreal industrial region with the Prairie wheat belt and coniferous forests
qa.e: It joins complementary regions, boosting the economy.

qa.q: Which is the most important rail route in Asia?
qa.e: The Trans-Siberian is Asia's most important route.

qa.q: The Trans-Canadian Railway was constructed in:
qa.e: It was built in 1886; 1869 is the Suez Canal year.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Trans-Siberian Railway helped open up Asiatic Russia to West European markets. Reason (R): It links St Petersburg in the west with Vladivostok in the east.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; connecting west and east let goods from Asiatic Russia reach European markets.

qa.q: On a map, the Trans-Siberian crosses which mountain range and rivers?
qa.a: Ural Mountains; Ob and Yenisei rivers
qa.e: It crosses the Urals and the Ob and Yenisei.

qa.q: The Union and Pacific Railway connects New York with:
qa.e: It links the Atlantic coast (New York) to the Pacific coast (San Francisco).

qa.q: The Australian Trans-continental Railway runs from Perth to:
qa.e: It runs west–east from Perth to Sydney.

qa.q: The Orient Express runs between:
qa.e: It connects Paris with Istanbul.

qa.q: Which city is NOT on the Orient Express route?
qa.e: The route passes Strasbourg, Munich, Vienna, Budapest and Belgrade, not Rome.

qa.q: The journey from London to Istanbul by the Orient Express takes about 96 hours. How many days is that?
The proposed Trans-Asiatic Railway would link Istanbul with:
qa.e: It would run via Iran, Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and Myanmar to Bangkok.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Australian Trans-continental Railway crosses the Nullarbor Plain. Reason (R): It runs west–east across the southern part of Australia.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; its west–east route across southern Australia takes it over the Nullarbor Plain.

qa.q: Which city lies on the Union and Pacific route?
qa.e: Cleveland, Chicago, Omaha, Evans, Ogden and Sacramento lie on it; the others are on the Canadian line.

qa.q: The Northern Atlantic sea route is also called:
qa.e: Being the busiest route, it is the Big Trunk Route.

qa.q: About what share of the world's foreign trade moves on the Northern Atlantic sea route?
qa.e: About 25% of world foreign trade uses this route.

qa.q: The Northern Atlantic sea route links:
qa.e: It connects two highly industrialised regions.

qa.q: Which sea route serves more countries and people than any other?
qa.e: It passes through the heart of the Old World.

qa.q: Why is water transport cheaper than land transport?
qa.a: Friction of water is far less than that of land
qa.e: Lower friction means lower energy cost.

qa.q: Which is NOT a port on the Mediterranean–Indian Ocean route?
qa.e: Rotterdam is on the North Sea; the others are on this route.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Northern Atlantic route is the busiest sea route in the world. Reason (R): It links two of the world's most industrially developed regions.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; huge industrial output on both sides generates the heavy traffic.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Oceans are linked and only port facilities are needed at the two ends. Reason (R): Water transport requires costly construction of routes on the ocean.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: The North Pacific sea route links the west coast of North America with:
qa.e: It connects ports like Vancouver and Los Angeles with Yokohama, Shanghai and Singapore.

qa.q: The South Pacific sea route passes through which canal?
qa.e: It links Western Europe and North America with Australia via Panama.

qa.q: Which is an important port of call on the Pacific routes?
qa.e: Honolulu lies mid-Pacific.

qa.q: Why is there little traffic between Rio de Janeiro and Cape Town?
qa.a: Both South America and Africa have similar products and resources
qa.e: Similar products leave little to trade.

qa.q: Which country is NOT linked by the Cape of Good Hope route to Western Europe and West Africa?
qa.e: The route links them with Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay.

qa.q: The distance between Panama and Sydney on the South Pacific route is about:
qa.e: NCERT gives about 12,000 km.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Coastal shipping is convenient for India. Reason (R): India has a long coastline.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; a long coastline makes coastal shipping practical.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Traffic on the Cape of Good Hope route is very heavy. Reason (R): South America and Africa have limited development and population along this route.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false — traffic is far less; R is true and explains why traffic is low.

qa.q: The Suez Canal links:
qa.a: The Mediterranean Sea and the Red Sea
qa.e: It joins the Mediterranean with the Red Sea.

qa.q: In which year was the Suez Canal constructed?
qa.e: Suez opened in 1869.

qa.q: Which canal is a sea-level canal without locks?
qa.e: Suez has no locks; Panama uses locks.

qa.q: The Panama Canal has how many lock systems?
qa.e: It has a six-lock system.

qa.q: By how much does the Panama Canal shorten the sea distance between New York and San Francisco?
qa.e: It shortens the distance by 13,000 km.

qa.q: The Panama Canal was constructed by:
qa.e: The US government built it and controlled the Canal Zone.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Some ships prefer the longer Cape of Good Hope route to the Suez Canal. Reason (R): Tolls on the Suez Canal are very heavy.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; when delay doesn't matter, avoiding heavy tolls makes the longer route cheaper.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The economic significance of the Panama Canal is greater than that of the Suez Canal. Reason (R): The Panama Canal is vital to the economies of Latin America.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false — Panama's significance is relatively less than Suez's. R is true.

qa.q: The Rhine is navigable from Rotterdam to:
qa.e: It is navigable for 700 km from Rotterdam to Basel.

qa.q: For how many km is the Rhine navigable?
qa.e: About 700 km.

qa.q: Which is the world's most heavily used inland waterway?
qa.e: The Rhine carries the most traffic.

qa.q: The Danube rises in the:
qa.e: It rises in the Black Forest and flows east.

qa.q: Which are the chief exports along the Danube waterway?
qa.e: NCERT lists wheat, maize, timber and machinery.

qa.q: Which is NOT a factor in the development of inland waterways?
qa.e: Physical channel conditions and technology matter.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Rhine basin has become a prosperous manufacturing area. Reason (R): The Ruhr river, joining the Rhine, flows through a rich coalfield.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; coal from the Ruhr fuelled industries in the basin.

qa.q: The Danube waterway is navigable up to:
qa.e: NCERT gives Taurna Severin as the limit.

qa.q: The Volga provides a navigable waterway of about:
qa.e: The Volga's navigable network is 11,200 km.

qa.q: The Volga drains into the:
qa.e: It flows into the Caspian; the Volga–Don Canal links it to the Black Sea.

qa.q: Which canals connect the Great Lakes to form an inland waterway?
qa.e: Soo and Welland canals connect the lakes.

qa.q: Large steamers on the Mississippi can go up to:
qa.e: Minneapolis is the upstream limit for large steamers.

qa.q: Why are goods trans-shipped to smaller vessels at Montreal?
qa.a: Because of rapids in the St Lawrence
qa.e: Rapids block large vessels; canals 4.5 m deep bypass them.

qa.q: Duluth and Buffalo are important ports on the:
qa.e: They lie on the Great Lakes.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Ocean-going vessels can travel deep inside North America. Reason (R): The Great Lakes are connected by canals and linked to the St Lawrence estuary.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the canal-linked lakes and estuary let large ships go far inland.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Mississippi–Ohio waterway connects the interior with the Gulf of Mexico. Reason (R): The Mississippi waterway connects the interior of the USA with the Pacific Ocean.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: Air transport is best suited for:
qa.a: Light, high-value and perishable goods over long distances
qa.e: Speed suits light, valuable, perishable cargo.

qa.q: The USA alone accounts for about what share of the world's airways?
qa.e: About 60 per cent.

qa.q: Which region has a dense network of air routes?
qa.e: Eastern USA, Western Europe and South-east Asia have dense networks.

qa.q: Why are air services limited in the Southern Hemisphere?
qa.a: Sparse population, limited landmass and economic development
qa.e: These factors reduce traffic.

qa.q: Which city is a nodal point from which air routes radiate to all continents?
qa.e: New York, London, Paris, Amsterdam and Chicago are nodal points.

qa.q: Why is air transport often the only option in the Himalayas during certain seasons?
qa.a: Roads get blocked by landslides, avalanches or heavy snow
qa.e: Blocked roads leave air travel as the alternative.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Air transport requires huge investment. Reason (R): It needs hangars, landing, fuelling and maintenance facilities, and expensive airports.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; elaborate infrastructure explains the high investment.

qa.q: On a map of intercontinental air routes, the densest belt in the Northern Hemisphere runs:
qa.e: There is a distinct east–west belt.

qa.q: The Big Inch pipeline carries petroleum from the Gulf of Mexico to:
qa.a: The north-eastern states of the USA
qa.e: It links Gulf oil wells with the north-east.

qa.q: In which country is milk supplied through pipelines from farms to factories?
qa.e: NCERT cites New Zealand.

qa.q: Which is an advantage of pipelines?
qa.a: Continuous, uninterrupted supply with low running cost
qa.e: Pipelines give steady flow cheaply once built.

qa.q: Which is a disadvantage of pipelines?
qa.a: Leakages are difficult to detect and repair
qa.e: Underground leaks are hard to find.

qa.q: About what share of all freight per tonne-km in the USA moves through pipelines?
qa.e: About 17 per cent.

qa.q: Pipelines are mainly used to transport:
qa.a: Liquids and gases like water, petroleum and natural gas
qa.e: They carry fluids.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Pipelines have low running costs. Reason (R): Once laid, pipelines move fluids continuously with little labour and little loss.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; continuous, low-labour flow keeps running costs low.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Pipelines are cheap to build in any terrain. Reason (R): Pipelines can carry liquefied coal as well as oil and gas.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false — construction costs are high. R is true.

qa.q: Satellite communication makes the unit cost and time of communication:
qa.e: It costs the same to communicate over 500 km as over 5,000 km.

qa.q: India's first satellite was:
qa.e: Aryabhata, launched in 1975, was India's first satellite.

qa.q: Cyberspace refers to:
qa.a: The electronic digital world of computer networks
qa.e: Cyberspace is the networked digital world of the Internet.

qa.q: Optical fibre cables are preferred because they:
qa.a: Carry large quantities of data rapidly, securely and almost error-free
qa.e: That is their key advantage.

qa.q: Satellite communication emerged as a new area in the:
qa.e: After the USA and USSR pioneered space research, satellite communication grew in the 1970s.

qa.q: Which of these is an application of the Internet in governance?
qa.e: Delivering government services online is e-governance.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The Internet is called the information superhighway. Reason (R): It allows vast amounts of information to be accessed and exchanged rapidly across the world.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the fast global flow of information gives it the name.

qa.q: Assertion (A): There were under 50 million users in 1995 and over 1 billion by 2005. Reason (R): Internet users declined between 1995 and 2005.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false — users grew enormously.

qa.q: Trade is defined as:
qa.a: The voluntary exchange of goods and services
qa.e: Trade is voluntary and mutually beneficial.

qa.q: International trade means exchange of goods and services:
qa.e: It crosses national borders.

qa.q: Why do countries need to trade?
qa.a: They cannot produce everything they need, or can buy some things cheaper elsewhere
qa.e: Unequal resources and costs make trade useful.

qa.q: How many parties are required for trade to take place?
qa.e: At least two: a seller and a buyer.

qa.q: Trade between two parties is generally:
qa.e: Both parties gain from a voluntary exchange.

qa.q: Assertion (A): International trade encourages specialisation. Reason (R): Countries cannot produce all commodities efficiently on their own.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; because no country can make everything efficiently, each specialises and trades.

qa.q: Assertion (A): International trade is exchange within a country's own states. Reason (R): International trade is exchange across national boundaries.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Japan has little iron ore but makes excellent cars; Australia has lots of iron ore. What is the likely trade pattern?
qa.a: Australia exports iron ore to Japan; Japan exports cars to Australia
qa.e: Each specialises according to its resources and skills.

qa.q: Direct exchange of goods without the use of money is called:
qa.e: Barter is goods-for-goods exchange.

qa.q: The Jon Beel Mela, where barter is still practised, is held at:
qa.e: It takes place at Jagiroad, about 35 km from Guwahati.

qa.q: The difficulties of the barter system were overcome by:
qa.e: Money became a common medium of exchange.

qa.q: Which of these was used as money in olden times?
qa.e: Cowrie shells were a common early currency.

qa.q: The Jon Beel Mela takes place:
qa.a: Every year after the harvest season
qa.e: It is an annual post-harvest fair.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Barter trade is difficult. Reason (R): It requires a double coincidence of wants between the two parties.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; needing both sides to want each other's goods makes barter hard.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Money serves as a common medium of exchange accepted by all. Reason (R): Money increased the difficulties of trade.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: The Jon Beel Mela is about how far from Guwahati?
qa.e: NCERT gives about 35 km.

qa.q: The Silk Route connected:
qa.e: It linked Rome with China across about 6,000 km.

qa.q: The approximate length of the Silk Route was:
qa.e: About 6,000 km.

qa.q: Which goods moved along the Silk Route?
qa.a: Chinese silk, Roman wool and precious metals
qa.e: High-value goods like silk, wool and precious metals moved along it.

qa.q: The slave trade was abolished in Great Britain in:
qa.e: Denmark 1792, Great Britain 1807, USA 1808.

qa.q: Which country abolished the slave trade first?
qa.e: Denmark abolished it in 1792.

qa.q: Enslaved Africans were forcibly taken to the Americas mainly to work on:
qa.e: They were forced to labour on plantations.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Trade between Europe and Asia grew in the 12th and 13th centuries. Reason (R): Ocean-going warships were developed during this period.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; ships capable of long voyages made the trade growth possible.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The slave trade was a short-lived business that lasted only a few years. Reason (R): The slave trade continued for more than two hundred years until its abolition.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: After the Industrial Revolution, industrialised nations mainly:
qa.a: Imported raw materials and exported finished goods
qa.e: They used colonial raw materials and sold back manufactures.

qa.q: Trade taxes and quantitative restrictions were imposed for the first time during:
qa.e: War conditions led countries to restrict trade.

qa.q: Which organisation helped reduce tariffs after the World Wars and later became the WTO?
qa.e: GATT was transformed into the WTO.

qa.q: After the Industrial Revolution, the monetary value of raw materials:
qa.e: Value addition made manufactures more valuable.

qa.q: In the later half of the 19th century, industrial nations became:
qa.e: Industrial countries traded heavily with one another.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Non-industrialised colonies earned relatively less from trade. Reason (R): They exported low-value raw materials and imported high-value manufactured goods.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the value gap explains their lower earnings.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Colonialism and globalisation have shaped trade patterns. Reason (R): World trade patterns have been shaped only by geography.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: history and policy also shaped trade.

qa.q: Which sequence is correct?
qa.a: Industrial Revolution → World Wars restrictions → GATT
qa.e: The Industrial Revolution came first, then wartime restrictions, then GATT.

qa.q: Which factor determines a country's mineral resource base?
qa.e: Geology decides which minerals occur.

qa.q: Bananas, rubber and cocoa can be grown only in:
qa.e: These crops need tropical heat and moisture.

qa.q: Wool is mainly produced in:
qa.e: Wool-bearing animals are reared in cold regions.

qa.q: Why are world resources unevenly distributed?
qa.a: Differences in geology, relief, soil and climate
qa.e: Physical differences cause uneven resources.

qa.q: Mountains often contribute to trade through:
qa.e: Mountains attract tourists.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Availability of mineral resources provides a basis for industrial development. Reason (R): Mineral resources are evenly distributed across all countries.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: minerals are unevenly distributed, which is itself a basis for trade.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Climate has no effect on the products a region trades. Reason (R): Climate influences the type of flora and fauna in a region.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true — climate shapes what can be produced and traded.

qa.q: Lowland regions generally have greater potential for:
qa.e: Flat, fertile lowlands support farming.

qa.q: Batik cloth, a product of distinctive culture, is associated with:
qa.e: Batik is Indonesian.

qa.q: Densely populated countries often have:
qa.a: Large internal trade but little external trade
qa.e: Most output is consumed locally.

qa.q: Agriculturally important countries generally:
qa.a: Export agro products and import manufactured goods
qa.e: That pattern reflects their stage of development.

qa.q: Foreign investment boosts trade in developing countries mainly in:
qa.a: Capital-intensive activities like mining, oil drilling and plantations
qa.e: These activities need capital that developing countries lack.

qa.q: Which development expanded the spatial reach of trade?
qa.a: Rail, ocean and air transport with refrigeration
qa.e: Better transport and preservation widened trade.

qa.q: Fine porcelain and brocades are traditional products of:
qa.e: China is known for porcelain and brocades.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Industrialised nations invest in mining and plantations in developing countries. Reason (R): This ensures them imports of foodstuffs and minerals and creates markets for their finished goods.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; securing supplies and markets is why they invest.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A higher standard of living increases demand for better-quality imported products. Reason (R): Standard of living has no effect on demand for imported goods.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: Since services cannot be measured in tonnage, the volume of trade is measured by:
qa.a: Total value of goods and services traded
qa.e: Value is used to include services.

qa.q: Composition of trade refers to:
qa.a: The nature of goods and services imported and exported
qa.e: Composition is about what is traded.

qa.q: Direction of trade refers to:
qa.a: The countries or regions with which trade takes place
qa.e: Direction shows trading partners.

qa.q: At the beginning of the last century, world trade was dominated by:
qa.e: Primary products dominated early on.

qa.q: Which sector currently commands the bulk of global trade?
qa.e: Manufacturing dominates, though services are rising.

qa.q: In the 19th century, which was the third most important trading country after Europe and the USA?
qa.e: NCERT names Japan as the third.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The direction of world trade changed in the second half of the 20th century. Reason (R): Europe lost its colonies and countries like India and China began competing with developed countries.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; decolonisation and new competitors changed trade directions.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Trade in services has been declining. Reason (R): Services such as travel, transportation and commercial services show an upward trend.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: A country exports goods worth ₹1,200 crore and imports goods worth ₹900 crore. What is its balance of trade (in ₹ crore)?
qa.e: Balance = 1,200 − 900 = +300 crore (favourable).

qa.q: A country exports ₹540 crore and imports ₹720 crore. What is its balance of trade (in ₹ crore)?
qa.e: 540 − 720 = −180 crore, an unfavourable balance.

qa.q: A favourable balance of trade means:
qa.e: Positive balance = more exports than imports.

qa.q: A negative balance of trade, if it continues, would ultimately lead to:
qa.a: Exhaustion of the country's financial reserves
qa.e: Spending more than earning drains reserves.

qa.q: Balance of payments differs from balance of trade because it:
qa.a: Also includes services, transfers and capital flows
qa.e: BoP is the broader account.

qa.q: A country's exports are ₹650 crore and its balance of trade is −₹150 crore. What are its imports (in ₹ crore)?
qa.e: Imports = exports − balance = 650 − (−150) = 800.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A country with imports greater than exports has an unfavourable balance of trade. Reason (R): It spends more on buying goods than it earns by selling goods.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; spending more than earning is exactly what makes the balance unfavourable.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Balance of trade records both imports and exports of a country. Reason (R): Balance of trade records only exports.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: Trade between two countries under an agreement for specified commodities is:
qa.e: Bi = two.

qa.q: Trade conducted with many trading countries is called:
qa.e: Multi = many.

qa.q: 'Most Favoured Nation' status is associated with:
qa.e: In multilateral trade, a country may grant MFN status to partners.

qa.q: Trade liberalisation is done by:
qa.a: Bringing down trade barriers like tariffs
qa.e: Free trade lowers barriers.

qa.q: Dumping refers to:
qa.a: Selling a commodity in two countries at prices differing for reasons not related to costs
qa.e: It is a pricing practice harmful to domestic producers.

qa.q: Why can free trade adversely affect developing countries?
qa.a: They may not get an equal playing field and face unfavourable conditions
qa.e: Unequal conditions can harm weaker economies.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Countries need protection against dumped goods. Reason (R): Dumped goods at cheaper prices can harm domestic producers.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the harm to domestic producers is why protection is needed.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Trade liberalisation prevents foreign goods from competing with domestic products. Reason (R): Trade liberalisation allows goods and services from everywhere to compete with domestic ones.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: The WTO was set up on:
qa.e: GATT was transformed into the WTO from 1 January 1995.

qa.q: Where are the headquarters of the WTO?
qa.e: WTO is headquartered in Geneva.

qa.q: GATT was formed in:
qa.e: GATT was formed in 1948.

qa.q: Which of these is a function of the WTO?
qa.a: Setting rules for global trade and resolving disputes between members
qa.e: The WTO makes trade rules and settles disputes.

qa.q: Besides goods, the WTO also covers:
qa.a: Trade in services and intellectual property rights
qa.e: Telecom, banking and IPR are included.

qa.q: Which is a criticism of the WTO?
qa.a: It is said to widen the gap between rich and poor
qa.e: Critics say it benefits rich countries more.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India is a founder member of the WTO. Reason (R): The WTO sets rules for the global trading system.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true, but the WTO's role of setting rules does not explain why India is a founder member.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Critics say issues of health, workers' rights, child labour and environment are ignored by the WTO. Reason (R): Influential nations in the WTO focus on their own commercial interests.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the focus on commercial interests is why critics feel such issues are neglected.

qa.q: About 120 regional trade blocs generate roughly what share of world trade?
qa.e: NCERT gives 52 per cent.

qa.q: The headquarters of ASEAN is at:
qa.e: ASEAN is headquartered in Jakarta, Indonesia.

qa.q: The headquarters of the CIS is at:
qa.e: The CIS is headquartered in Minsk, Belarus.

qa.q: The European Union originated as the European Economic Community in:
qa.e: EEC began in March 1957; it became the EU in February 1992.

qa.q: ASEAN was formed in:
qa.e: ASEAN was formed in August 1967.

qa.q: Which bloc uses a common currency, the euro?
qa.e: The EU has a single market and the euro.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Regional trade blocs have come up among countries with geographical proximity. Reason (R): Nearness, similarity and complementarity in trading items make regional cooperation easier.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these features make it natural for neighbours to form blocs.

qa.q: Assertion (A): ASEAN trades agro products such as rubber, palm oil, rice and copra. Reason (R): Copra, rubber and palm oil are important commodities of the EU.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false — they are typical of ASEAN, not the EU.

qa.q: The headquarters of OPEC is at:
qa.e: OPEC is headquartered in Vienna, Austria.

qa.q: Which countries were members of NAFTA?
qa.e: NAFTA covered North America's three countries.

qa.q: SAFTA came into effect in:
qa.e: SAFTA began in January 2006.

qa.q: The headquarters of LAIA is at:
qa.e: LAIA is based in Montevideo.

qa.q: The main commodity traded by OPEC members is:
qa.e: OPEC deals in crude oil.

qa.q: Which country is NOT a member of SAFTA?
qa.e: SAFTA covers SAARC countries; Myanmar is in ASEAN.

qa.q: Assertion (A): SAFTA aims to reduce tariffs on intra-regional trade. Reason (R): SAFTA came into effect in January 1995.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: SAFTA came into effect in January 2006 (1995 is the WTO's start).

qa.q: NAFTA was replaced in 2020 by:
qa.e: The USMCA (United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement) replaced NAFTA.

qa.q: Which is a benefit of international trade?
qa.e: Specialisation and higher output are benefits.

qa.q: Which is a harmful effect of international trade?
qa.e: Uneven development is a concern.

qa.q: How can global trade harm the environment?
qa.a: Resources get used faster than they can be replenished
qa.e: Competition to trade more increases resource use.

qa.q: Which of these is restricted even under globalisation?
qa.a: Free movement of people (labour) across borders
qa.e: Goods and capital flow freely; labour does not.

qa.q: Which sectors' multinational corporations are cited for expanding at all costs and creating pollution?
qa.a: Oil, gas, mining, pharmaceuticals and agri-business
qa.e: These large industries can harm the environment.

qa.q: Assertion (A): International trade can lead to commercial rivalry. Reason (R): Countries compete intensely for markets and resources.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; competition for markets and resources produces rivalry.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Trade has no effect on health and well-being. Reason (R): Global trade can affect the environment as well as the health and well-being of people.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: International trade is mutually beneficial when it leads to:
qa.a: Better standards of living and diffusion of knowledge
qa.e: Benefits come when trade raises welfare broadly.

qa.q: Piraeus is an example of:
qa.e: Out ports are deep-water ports built away from the parent port.

qa.q: Dover and Calais are examples of:
qa.e: They face each other across the English Channel and carry passengers and mail.

qa.q: Ports that are collection centres where goods are brought from different countries for re-export are:
qa.e: Singapore, Rotterdam and Copenhagen are entrepots.

qa.q: Which is a naval port of India?
qa.e: Kochi and Karwar are naval ports; the others are commercial ports.

qa.q: Aden, Honolulu and Singapore developed as:
qa.e: They were calling points for refuelling, water and food on main routes.

qa.q: Kolkata, on the Hooghly, is classified by location as:
qa.e: It lies away from the sea on a river.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The quantity of cargo handled by a port indicates the level of development of its hinterland. Reason (R): A port serves the area behind it, from which goods come and to which goods go.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; since the port handles its hinterland's trade, cargo volume reflects how developed that hinterland is.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Commercial ports handle general cargo and passengers, while industrial ports handle bulk cargo. Reason (R): Industrial ports mainly handle passengers and packaged goods.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: What was India's population according to Census 2011?
qa.e: Census 2011 counted about 1,210.8 million people.

qa.q: India accounts for about what percentage of the world's area?
qa.e: India has 2.4% of world area but about 17.5% of its population.

qa.q: India's share of world population in 2011 was about:
qa.e: About 17.5 per cent.

qa.q: The first census in India was conducted in:
qa.e: The first (non-synchronous) census was in 1872; the first complete one in 1881.

qa.q: The first complete census of India was held in:
qa.e: 1881 saw the first complete census.

qa.q: How often is the Census of India conducted?
qa.e: The Census is decennial.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India's large population puts pressure on its resources. Reason (R): India supports about 17.5% of world population on only 2.4% of world area.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; so many people on so little land explains the pressure.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Population is only a burden and never a resource. Reason (R): A skilled and healthy population is a valuable human resource.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Which state had the highest population in 2011?
qa.e: UP is the most populous state.

qa.q: Which state is second in population after Uttar Pradesh?
qa.e: Maharashtra is second, followed by Bihar.

qa.q: Rajasthan, the largest state by area, has what share of India's population?
qa.e: Only 5.67 per cent.

qa.q: Which type of area generally has low population?
qa.e: Rugged, cold, high areas are sparse.

qa.q: Together, UP, Maharashtra, Bihar, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh have about what share of India's population?
qa.e: These five hold about half of India's people.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India's population distribution is uneven. Reason (R): Some states like UP have huge populations while large states like Rajasthan have relatively few people.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R gives evidence for A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Arunachal Pradesh is a hilly, forested state with a small population. Reason (R): Arunachal Pradesh has a large share of India's population.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: On a population distribution map of India, which area would show the densest concentration of dots?
qa.e: The fertile northern plains are crowded.

qa.q: Which group lists physical factors affecting population distribution in India?
qa.a: Terrain, climate and availability of water
qa.e: These are physical factors.

qa.q: Which of these is a socio-economic factor of population distribution?
qa.e: Transport is a socio-economic factor.

qa.q: The North Indian plains, deltas and coastal plains have:
qa.e: Fertile soil, water and flat land support high population.

qa.q: Urban regions like Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru have high population concentration mainly due to:
qa.a: Industrial development, urbanisation and employment opportunities
qa.e: Jobs and amenities draw migrants.

qa.q: Which area has relatively low population due to physical factors?
qa.a: Southern and central Indian plateaus and the Himalayas
qa.e: Rugged or less fertile land holds fewer people.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Socio-economic and historical factors also affect population distribution. Reason (R): Settled agriculture, transport, industrialisation and urbanisation create opportunities that attract people.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R explains how these factors work.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Physical factors alone explain population distribution in India. Reason (R): Industrialisation and urbanisation have created dense population in cities like Pune and Ahmedabad.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true — socio-economic factors matter too.

qa.q: A canal-irrigated plain with good roads and markets is likely to have:
qa.e: Irrigation, transport and markets support dense settlement.

qa.q: What was India's population density in 2011 (persons per sq km)?
qa.e: 382 persons per sq km.

qa.q: Which state has the lowest population density in India?
qa.e: Arunachal Pradesh has about 17 persons per sq km.

qa.q: Which state has the highest population density among states (2011)?
qa.e: Bihar tops among states; Delhi (an NCT) is higher still.

qa.q: India's density in 1951 was 117 and in 2011 was 382. How many times did it become (to two decimal places)?
Which peninsular states have relatively high population density?
qa.e: Kerala and Tamil Nadu are densely populated in the south.

qa.q: Low population density in north-eastern hill states is mainly due to:
qa.e: Rugged terrain limits settlement.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Bihar has a very high population density. Reason (R): Bihar lies in the fertile Ganga plain with good water availability.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; fertile land and water support many people per sq km.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Mountainous terrain generally leads to low population density. Reason (R): Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand have very high population densities.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: Physiological density is calculated as:
qa.e: Physiological density relates all people to the cultivated land.

qa.q: Agricultural density is calculated as:
qa.a: Total agricultural population ÷ net cultivable area
qa.e: It relates farm population to cultivable land.

qa.q: Agricultural population includes:
qa.a: Cultivators, agricultural labourers and their family members
qa.e: It covers everyone dependent on farming.

qa.q: A state has a population of 6 crore and a net cultivated area of 1,50,000 sq km. What is its physiological density (persons per sq km)?
A region has an agricultural population of 24 lakh and net cultivable area of 8,000 sq km. What is its agricultural density (persons per sq km)?
Why are physiological and agricultural densities more useful than arithmetic density for farm planning?
qa.a: They show the pressure of population on agricultural land
qa.e: They relate people to the land that actually feeds them.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Physiological density of a hilly state can be much higher than its arithmetic density. Reason (R): Only a small part of a hilly state's area is cultivated, so dividing population by cultivated area gives a larger figure.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; a small denominator (cultivated area) makes physiological density high.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Agricultural density uses total population in the numerator. Reason (R): Agricultural density uses agricultural population divided by net cultivable area.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Induced growth of population is explained by:
qa.a: The volume of inward and outward movement of people
qa.e: Induced growth is the migration component.

qa.q: Natural growth of population is analysed by:
qa.e: Births minus deaths give natural growth.

qa.q: India's annual growth rate of population in 2011 was about:
qa.e: About 1.64 per cent per year; 17.64% is the decadal figure.

qa.q: In which decade was India's decadal growth rate negative?
qa.e: 1911–21 recorded a slight decline.

qa.q: In which decade did India record its highest decadal growth rate?
qa.e: 1961–71 recorded about 24.80%.

qa.q: India's population was 84.6 crore in 1991 and 102.9 crore in 2001. What was the decadal growth (in crore)?
Assertion (A): Population growth is expressed in both absolute numbers and percentages. Reason (R): Growth of population is the change in the number of people between two points of time.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; since it is a change in numbers, it can be stated as an absolute figure or a percentage.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Induced growth is explained by the inward and outward movement of people. Reason (R): Migration has no role in population growth.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: The period 1951–1981 is known as the period of:
qa.e: Rapid mortality decline with high fertility caused an explosion.

qa.q: Phase I (1901–1921) of India's population growth is called the:
qa.e: Growth was very low, even negative in 1911–21.

qa.q: Growth in Phase II (1921–1951) was mainly:
qa.a: Mortality induced, due to better health and sanitation
qa.e: Falling death rates with high birth rates raised growth.

qa.q: Which factor helped reduce the birth rate in Phase IV (after 1981)?
qa.a: Rise in mean age at marriage and female education
qa.e: Later marriage, better quality of life and female education lowered births.

qa.q: The average annual growth rate during Phase III was as high as:
qa.e: About 2.2 per cent per year.

qa.q: During Phase III, international migration added to population from:
qa.e: NCERT lists migration from these neighbours.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Population growth in Phase I was very low. Reason (R): Both birth rate and death rate were high during this phase.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; high deaths cancelled out high births, so growth stayed low.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The growth rate in Phase IV has been rising sharply. Reason (R): In Phase IV, the growth rate, though high, has started slowing down gradually.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Which state had the lowest decadal growth rate during 1991–2001?
qa.e: Kerala recorded about 9.4%.

qa.q: Which state had the highest decadal growth rate during 1991–2001?
qa.e: Nagaland recorded about 64.5%.

qa.q: Kerala's decadal growth rate in 1991–2001 was about:
qa.e: About 9.4 per cent.

qa.q: During 1991–2001, the southern states had growth rates:
qa.e: They had low growth, up to 20%.

qa.q: Which group of states had relatively high growth rates during 1991–2001?
qa.a: Punjab, Haryana, UP, Uttarakhand, Rajasthan and Bihar
qa.e: The north-western, northern and north-central belt grew faster.

qa.q: Compared with 1991–2001, growth rates in most states during 2001–2011:
qa.e: The slowdown spread to most states.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Southern states recorded low population growth during 1991–2001. Reason (R): Higher literacy, better health care and lower fertility helped reduce growth there.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these social factors explain the low growth.

qa.q: On a map of growth rates (1991–2001), which state would be shaded in the lowest category?
qa.e: Kerala had the lowest growth.

qa.q: Adolescents are people in which age group?
qa.e: Adolescents are 10–19 years; youth (in policy) is 15–29.

qa.q: Adolescents formed about what share of India's population in 2011?
qa.e: About 20.9 per cent.

qa.q: Which is NOT listed as a challenge faced by adolescents?
qa.e: Low female literacy is the challenge; high literacy is not.

qa.q: Which policy aims at the holistic development of youth in India?
qa.e: The National Youth Policy (2014) focuses on youth.

qa.q: Why are adolescents considered vulnerable?
qa.a: They may be misguided and face risks like early marriage, malnutrition and drug abuse
qa.e: Without proper guidance they face many risks.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Adolescents are a potential resource for India. Reason (R): They form about one-fifth of the population and will be the future workforce.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; their large number and future role make them a potential resource.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Low intake of nutrients is one of the challenges faced by adolescents. Reason (R): Adolescents in India face no nutritional problems.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: India's 2011 population was about 121 crore. How many crore were adolescents (20.9%), to two decimal places?
What percentage of India's population was rural in 2011?
qa.e: 68.8% rural and 31.2% urban.

qa.q: What percentage of India's population was urban in 2011?
qa.e: 31.2 per cent were urban.

qa.q: Which of these states has a very high share of rural population?
qa.e: Himachal Pradesh and Bihar are highly rural.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT an attribute of population composition?
qa.e: Rainfall is a climatic feature, not a population attribute.

qa.q: The urban population of India has increased due to:
qa.a: Economic development, better health and hygiene, and rural-urban migration
qa.e: These factors raise urban numbers.

qa.q: About how many villages were there in India in 2011?
qa.e: About 6,40,867 villages.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India is still predominantly rural. Reason (R): About 68.8 per cent of India's population lived in villages in 2011.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R is the evidence for A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Goa is one of India's most rural states. Reason (R): Goa is among the relatively urbanised states.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: According to Grierson's Linguistic Survey of India, how many languages were there?
qa.e: 179 languages and 544 dialects.

qa.q: How many languages are listed as scheduled languages in the Constitution?
qa.e: There are 22 scheduled languages.

qa.q: The Dravidian family is also called:
qa.e: Austric = Nishada, Sino-Tibetan = Kirata, Indo-European = Aryan.

qa.q: Munda languages belong to which family?
qa.e: Munda is part of the Austro-Asiatic branch of the Austric family.

qa.q: Which is the largest linguistic family in India by number of speakers?
qa.e: Indo-Aryan languages are spoken by the largest share.

qa.q: Sino-Tibetan languages are mainly spoken in:
qa.e: Tibeto-Myanmari languages are spoken in the Himalayan and north-eastern states.

qa.q: Sikhs are concentrated mainly in:
qa.e: NCERT notes Sikh concentration in Punjab, Haryana and Delhi.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India is described as a land of linguistic diversity. Reason (R): Grierson recorded 179 languages and 544 dialects in India.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the huge number of languages and dialects shows the diversity.

qa.q: According to the Census, a main worker works for at least how many days in a year?
qa.e: Main workers work at least 183 days (about six months).

qa.q: India's work participation rate in 2011 was about:
qa.e: About 39.8 per cent of the population were workers.

qa.q: Which is NOT one of the Census's four occupational categories?
qa.e: The fourth category is 'other workers', which includes such jobs; 'software engineers' is not a separate category.

qa.q: What share of India's workers are cultivators and agricultural labourers (2011)?
qa.e: About 54.6 per cent.

qa.q: A person who works for 100 days in a year is classified as a:
qa.e: Less than 183 days → marginal.

qa.q: Why is the work participation rate often higher in economically less developed states?
qa.a: Many manual workers are needed for subsistence activities
qa.e: Subsistence economies need many hands.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India has a large proportion of non-workers. Reason (R): Only about 39.8 per cent of the population were workers in 2011.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R shows that about 60% are non-workers.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Only about 3.8 per cent of workers are in household industries. Reason (R): Household industries employ the largest share of India's workers.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false — agriculture employs the largest share.

qa.q: Which states have a very large share of cultivators?
qa.e: NCERT names Himachal Pradesh and Nagaland.

qa.q: Which group of states has a higher proportion of agricultural labourers?
qa.e: These states have more landless labourers.

qa.q: Delhi, Chandigarh and Puducherry have a large proportion of workers in:
qa.e: Urbanised areas have more 'other workers'.

qa.q: In which sector are female workers relatively more numerous?
qa.e: Women work largely in agriculture.

qa.q: Which statement about gender and work in India is correct?
qa.a: Male workers outnumber female workers in all three sectors
qa.e: Males outnumber females in every sector.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Urbanised areas have a high share of 'other workers'. Reason (R): Cities offer jobs in trade, commerce, construction, repair and services.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; urban jobs are mostly in these non-farm categories.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Women's participation in the secondary and tertiary sectors has been declining. Reason (R): There has been some improvement in women's participation in secondary and tertiary sectors in recent years.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Which pair of density measures is used to show pressure on farmland?
qa.e: Both relate population to cultivated or cultivable land.

qa.q: A human settlement is defined as:
qa.a: A cluster of dwellings of any type or size where human beings live
qa.e: Any cluster of dwellings, small or large, temporary or permanent.

qa.q: Rural settlements are mainly engaged in:
qa.e: Agriculture, fishing and forestry dominate rural life.

qa.q: Urban settlements are generally:
qa.a: Compact and larger, engaged in non-primary activities
qa.e: Towns are compact with secondary and tertiary jobs.

qa.q: Social relations in urban areas are generally:
qa.e: Fast, complex urban life leads to formal relations.

qa.q: Which statement about settlements is correct?
qa.a: As settlements grow in size, their economic character and social structure change
qa.e: Size brings changes in economy and society.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Rural people have intimate social relations. Reason (R): Rural people are less mobile and live in small communities.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; small, stable communities create close relations.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Cities act as nodes of economic growth and exchange goods and services with rural areas. Reason (R): Cities do not depend on rural areas at all.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false — cities and villages are linked.

qa.q: Rural settlements mainly supply cities with:
qa.e: Villages supply food and raw materials.

qa.q: Types of rural settlements are determined by:
qa.a: The extent of the built-up area and inter-house distance
qa.e: Built-up extent and spacing between houses define the type.

qa.q: Clustered settlements are commonly found in:
qa.a: Fertile alluvial plains and north-eastern states
qa.e: Fertile plains support compact villages.

qa.q: In Bundelkhand and Nagaland, people live in compact villages mainly for:
qa.e: Compactness gives protection.

qa.q: In Rajasthan, compact settlements are necessary mainly because of:
qa.e: Water scarcity encourages compact living.

qa.q: Which of these is a cultural/ethnic factor influencing rural settlement type?
qa.e: Social factors are cultural/ethnic.

qa.q: Clustered settlements are also known as:
qa.e: Clustered = agglomerated = nucleated.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In clustered settlements, the living area is separated from the surrounding farms and pastures. Reason (R): Houses in clustered settlements are closely built-up in a compact area.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; houses packed together form a distinct living area apart from fields.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Clustered settlements never show any geometric pattern. Reason (R): Clustered villages may show rectangular, radial or linear patterns.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Local names like panna, para, palli, nagla and dhani refer to units of:
qa.e: These are names for the separated units of hamleted villages.

qa.q: Dispersed settlements are found in many areas of:
qa.a: Meghalaya, Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and Kerala
qa.e: Fragmented terrain causes dispersion in these states.

qa.q: Hamleted settlements are frequently found in:
qa.a: Middle and lower Ganga plain, Chhattisgarh and lower Himalayan valleys
qa.e: NCERT lists these regions.

qa.q: Semi-clustered settlements are widespread in:
qa.a: The Gujarat plain and some parts of Rajasthan
qa.e: Gujarat plain and parts of Rajasthan have them.

qa.q: Extreme dispersion of settlements is often caused by:
qa.a: Extremely fragmented terrain and land resource base
qa.e: Broken terrain allows only scattered huts.

qa.q: Segmentation of a large village into hamlets is often motivated by:
qa.e: NCERT links hamleting to social and ethnic factors.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Many areas of Meghalaya have dispersed settlements. Reason (R): The hilly, fragmented terrain allows only small, scattered patches of habitable land.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; fragmented terrain explains dispersion.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Hamleted settlements consist of physically separated units bearing a common name. Reason (R): In hamleted settlements, each unit has a completely different village name.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: According to the Census, the minimum population for a place to be classified as urban (without a municipal body) is:
qa.e: Minimum 5,000 persons.

qa.q: The minimum population density for an urban place under Census criteria is:
qa.e: At least 400 persons per sq km.

qa.q: What share of the male main working population must be in non-agricultural work for a place to be urban?
qa.e: At least 75 per cent.

qa.q: Which of these is automatically urban as per the Census?
qa.a: A place with a cantonment board
qa.e: Places with municipality, corporation, cantonment board or notified town area committee are urban.

qa.q: A town of 8,000 people covers 16 sq km and 78% of male main workers do non-farm work. What is its density, and is it urban?
qa.e: Density = 8,000 ÷ 16 = 500 ≥ 400; all three criteria are met.

qa.q: Cities are functionally linked to rural areas because:
qa.a: They exchange goods and services directly or through market towns
qa.e: Cities and villages depend on each other.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A place with 6,000 people and 90% male non-farm workers but a density of 300 per sq km is not urban by Census criteria. Reason (R): All three criteria — population, non-farm male workers and density — must be satisfied.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; failing the density test means it is not urban.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Urban centres perform only agricultural functions. Reason (R): Urban centres have a variety of non-agricultural economic and administrative functions.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Which of these is a prehistoric town of India?
qa.e: Harappa and Mohenjodaro are prehistoric (Indus) towns.

qa.q: Ancient towns in India mostly developed as:
qa.e: Varanasi, Prayag and Madurai grew as religious/cultural centres.

qa.q: Which of these is an ancient town?
qa.e: Varanasi is over 2,000 years old.

qa.q: Most medieval towns developed as:
qa.e: Medieval towns were political centres.

qa.q: Which of these is a medieval fort town built on the ruins of an ancient town?
qa.e: Delhi, Hyderabad, Jaipur, Lucknow, Agra and Nagpur are examples.

qa.q: Pataliputra is the ancient name of which present-day city?
qa.e: Pataliputra is modern Patna.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Many ancient Indian towns developed as religious and cultural centres. Reason (R): Places like Varanasi and Madurai have long been major centres of pilgrimage and culture.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; R gives examples explaining A.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Jaipur and Lucknow developed as headquarters of kingdoms in the medieval period. Reason (R): Jaipur and Lucknow are prehistoric towns.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: Which three cities did the British consolidate as their main nodes?
qa.e: Bombay, Madras and Calcutta were British nodes.

qa.q: Which of these was an early European trading port town?
qa.e: Surat, Daman, Goa and Pondicherry were trading ports.

qa.q: Jamshedpur is an example of a town that developed:
qa.a: As a modern industrial town after 1850
qa.e: It grew around the Tata steel plant.

qa.q: Which of these is a post-independence administrative headquarters?
qa.e: Gandhinagar, Chandigarh, Bhubaneswar and Dispur were built as capitals.

qa.q: Ghaziabad, Rohtak and Gurugram developed as:
qa.e: They are satellite towns of the Delhi metropolis.

qa.q: Which British contribution to Indian towns is correct?
qa.e: The British developed hill stations as summer resorts.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Durgapur, Bhilai, Sindri and Barauni developed as industrial centres after Independence. Reason (R): Industrial development was a priority in planned development after 1947.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; planned industrialisation created these towns.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Satellite towns developed around villages after Independence. Reason (R): Satellite towns developed around metropolitan cities like Delhi.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: The level of urbanisation is measured as:
qa.a: Percentage of urban population to total population
qa.e: It is the urban share of total population.

qa.q: India's level of urbanisation in 2011 was:
qa.e: 31.16 per cent.

qa.q: During the twentieth century, India's urban population increased:
qa.e: It rose about eleven times.

qa.q: India's level of urbanisation in 1901 was about:
qa.e: About 10.84 per cent.

qa.q: By how many percentage points did urbanisation rise between 2001 (27.78%) and 2011 (31.16%)?
Compared with developed countries, India's level of urbanisation is:
qa.e: About 31% is low compared with most developed countries.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India's urban population grew many times in the 20th century. Reason (R): Existing urban centres enlarged and new towns emerged.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; enlargement of towns and new towns explain the growth.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The growth rate of urbanisation has slowed down during the last two decades. Reason (R): The growth rate of urbanisation in India has been accelerating sharply in the last two decades.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: A Class I town has a population of at least:
qa.e: Class I = one lakh or more.

qa.q: Cities with a population of more than 5 million are called:
qa.e: Above 5 million → mega city; 1–5 million → metropolitan.

qa.q: Cities with a population between 1 and 5 million are called:
qa.e: 1–5 million → metropolitan.

qa.q: Which was India's largest urban agglomeration in 2011?
qa.e: Greater Mumbai (about 18.4 million).

qa.q: Which of these can be part of an urban outgrowth of a town?
qa.a: A railway colony or university campus
qa.e: Outgrowths like railway colonies, campuses, ports and cantonments adjoin towns.

qa.q: Into how many classes does the Census classify urban centres by population?
qa.e: Six classes.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Most metropolitan and mega cities are urban agglomerations. Reason (R): Large cities usually spread to include adjoining towns and outgrowths in a contiguous urban area.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; their spread over neighbouring towns and outgrowths makes them agglomerations.

qa.q: The Smart Cities Mission aims to promote cities that provide:
qa.a: Core infrastructure, decent quality of life, clean and sustainable environment and smart solutions
qa.e: That is the mission's objective.

qa.q: Which of these is an administrative town?
qa.e: Shillong is a state capital — administrative.

qa.q: Which of these is an industrial town?
qa.e: Modinagar is listed as an industrial town.

qa.q: Itarsi, Katni and Mughal Sarai are examples of:
qa.e: They are major railway junctions.

qa.q: Which of these is a port town engaged mainly in export and import?
qa.e: Kandla is a major port.

qa.q: Saharanpur and Satna are classified as:
qa.e: They specialise in trade and commerce.

qa.q: Towns are functionally classified on the basis of:
qa.e: The main function decides the class.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Jamshedpur is classified as an industrial town. Reason (R): Industries are the prime motive force of its economy.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; industry driving its economy is why it is industrial.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Agra is classified as a port town. Reason (R): Agra is a hub of inland transport.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false — Agra is inland; R is true.

qa.q: Digboi and Ankaleshwar are examples of:
qa.e: Both are associated with oil fields.

qa.q: Mhow, Babina and Udhampur are:
qa.e: They are military cantonment towns.

qa.q: Which of these is an educational town?
qa.e: Pilani is known for BITS.

qa.q: Which of these is a tourist town?
qa.e: Pachmarhi is a hill tourist town.

qa.q: Which of these is a religious and cultural town?
qa.e: Ujjain is a major religious centre.

qa.q: Udagamandalam is better known as:
qa.e: Udagamandalam = Ooty, a tourist town in the Nilgiris.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Even specialised cities become multi-functional as they grow. Reason (R): Cities are dynamic and their functions change over time.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; their dynamic nature leads to new functions as they grow.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Raniganj and Jharia developed in mineral-rich (coal) areas. Reason (R): Raniganj and Jharia are garrison towns.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false — they are mining towns.

qa.q: Land-use records in India are maintained by the:
qa.e: The land revenue department keeps land-use records.

qa.q: Which body measures the geographical area of administrative units in India?
qa.e: Survey of India measures geographical area.

qa.q: How many land-use categories are used in land revenue records?
qa.e: There are nine categories.

qa.q: The area under actual forest cover is different from the area classified as forest because:
qa.a: Classified area is what the government has demarcated for forest growth
qa.e: Demarcated area may not all have tree cover.

qa.q: Desert lands, ravines and barren hilly terrain are classified as:
qa.e: They cannot be cultivated with available technology.

qa.q: Roads, canals and settlements fall under:
qa.e: Built-up and infrastructure land is non-agricultural use.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Reporting area differs from the geographical area of India. Reason (R): Some areas of the country are unsurveyed and not reported in revenue records.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; unsurveyed areas explain the difference.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Barren and wastelands can be easily cultivated with existing technology. Reason (R): Barren and wastelands include desert lands, ravines and barren hilly terrain.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Land left uncultivated for more than five years is called:
qa.e: More than five years → culturable wasteland.

qa.q: Current fallow is land left without cultivation for:
qa.a: One or less than one agricultural year
qa.e: Current fallow ≤ one agricultural year.

qa.q: Cultivable land left uncultivated for more than one year but less than five years is:
qa.e: 1–5 years → fallow other than current fallow.

qa.q: Permanent pastures and grazing lands are mostly owned by:
qa.a: The village panchayat or the government
qa.e: Most are panchayat or government land.

qa.q: Land under orchards and fruit trees is classified as:
qa.e: Orchards are a separate category not included in net sown area.

qa.q: The physical extent of land on which crops are sown and harvested is the:
qa.e: Net area sown counts land once, however many crops are grown.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Fallowing is practised by farmers. Reason (R): Leaving land uncultivated helps it recoup lost fertility through natural processes.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; restoring fertility is why farmers leave land fallow.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Culturable wasteland can be cultivated after reclamation practices. Reason (R): Culturable wasteland can never be brought under cultivation.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: Which three factors influence changes in land use in a region?
qa.a: Size of the economy, composition of the economy and pressure of population
qa.e: These economic and demographic factors drive land-use change.

qa.q: As the composition of the economy changes, land tends to shift from:
qa.e: Growth of industry and services needs more built-up land.

qa.q: Why do marginal lands come under use as the economy grows?
qa.e: Growing demand for land pushes use onto marginal lands.

qa.q: Agriculture's share in GDP is declining. Pressure on agricultural land:
qa.a: Does not decline, as dependence on farming remains high
qa.e: Large numbers still depend on farming.

qa.q: Which sectors grow faster than agriculture as an economy develops?
qa.e: Industry and services expand faster.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Land under non-agricultural uses increases with economic growth. Reason (R): Growth of industries, services, settlements and infrastructure needs more land.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; these needs explain the increase.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Size of the economy has no effect on land use. Reason (R): As the economy grows, pressure on land increases.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: A district builds an industrial park, a highway and new housing colonies on farmland. Which factor of land-use change is mainly at work?
qa.e: Growth of industry and services shifts land to non-farm uses.

qa.q: Which land-use category recorded the highest rate of increase from 1950–51 to 2014–15?
qa.e: Non-agricultural uses grew fastest with industry, services and settlements.

qa.q: The increase in forest area is mainly due to:
qa.a: Increase in demarcated area rather than actual forest cover
qa.e: More land was demarcated as forest.

qa.q: Which of these land-use categories declined from 1950–51 to 2014–15?
qa.e: Culturable wasteland declined as it was brought under cultivation.

qa.q: The decline in permanent pastures and grazing lands is mainly due to:
qa.a: Pressure from agricultural land and illegal encroachment
qa.e: Cultivation expanded onto common pastures.

qa.q: Why does current fallow fluctuate a great deal from year to year?
qa.a: It depends on variability of rainfall and cropping cycles
qa.e: Rain-dependent farming leaves more land fallow in bad years.

qa.q: The recent increase in net area sown is due to:
qa.a: Use of culturable wasteland for agricultural purposes
qa.e: Culturable wasteland was reclaimed for farming.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Barren and wastelands have declined over the years. Reason (R): Increasing pressure on land has brought such marginal land into use.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; pressure on land explains the decline.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Growth of industries, services and settlements requires more land. Reason (R): Land under non-agricultural uses has declined since 1950–51.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false — this category increased.

qa.q: Common property resources are owned by:
qa.a: The state, for the use of the community
qa.e: CPRs are state-owned for community use.

qa.q: Which of these is a common property resource?
qa.e: Village water bodies are CPRs.

qa.q: CPRs are particularly important for:
qa.a: Landless and marginal farmers and women
qa.e: They depend on CPRs for fodder, fuel and livelihood.

qa.q: Which products do CPRs provide?
qa.a: Fodder, fuel and minor forest products like fruits, nuts and medicinal plants
qa.e: CPRs supply natural products for daily needs.

qa.q: Why are CPRs especially important to women in rural areas?
qa.a: Women mostly collect fodder and fuel from them
qa.e: Collecting fodder and fuel is largely done by women.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Landless families depend heavily on CPRs. Reason (R): They have no land of their own for fodder and fuel and rely on livestock income.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; their lack of land explains the dependence.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Every member of the community has a right of access to and use of CPRs. Reason (R): CPRs are owned by the state for the use of the community.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; being community resources owned by the state is why members have access rights.

qa.q: Encroachment on village pastures for private cultivation mainly harms:
qa.e: They lose their fodder source.

qa.q: The total stock of agricultural land is obtained by adding:
qa.a: Net sown area, all fallow lands and culturable wasteland
qa.e: That is the NCERT formula.

qa.q: A district's net sown area is 50,000 ha and gross cropped area is 80,000 ha. What is its cropping intensity (%)?
A village has NSA 400 ha, current fallow 30 ha, other fallow 20 ha and culturable wasteland 50 ha. What is its total stock of agricultural land (ha)?
Why must India raise cropping intensity and productivity to grow more food?
qa.a: The scope for bringing more land under cultivation is very limited
qa.e: Most cultivable land is already in use.

qa.q: In rural areas, land ownership provides:
qa.a: Social value and security for credit and contingencies
qa.e: Land is a source of status and security.

qa.q: A district's GCA is 1,80,000 ha and its cropping intensity is 150%. What is its net sown area (ha)?
Assertion (A): Quality of land directly affects agricultural productivity. Reason (R): Agriculture is a purely land-based activity.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; since agriculture depends entirely on land, its quality decides productivity.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Cropping intensity can never exceed 100%. Reason (R): Cropping intensity is GCA ÷ NSA × 100, and GCA exceeds NSA when land is cropped more than once a year.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false — multiple cropping makes CI above 100%. R is true.

qa.q: Which cropping season coincides with the south-west monsoon?
qa.e: Kharif crops grow with monsoon rains.

qa.q: Rabi season begins with the onset of winter in:
qa.e: Rabi starts in Oct–Nov and ends in Mar–Apr.

qa.q: Which of these is a rabi crop in northern India?
qa.e: Wheat is the main rabi crop.

qa.q: Watermelons, cucumbers and fodder on irrigated land are typical of the:
qa.e: Zaid is the short summer season.

qa.q: Why is there no distinct cropping season in southern India?
qa.a: Temperatures are high enough to grow tropical crops any time if soil moisture is available
qa.e: Warmth all year lets crops grow in any season.

qa.q: Which of these is a kharif crop?
qa.e: Tur is a kharif crop; the others are rabi.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Rabi crops are temperate and subtropical crops. Reason (R): The rabi season has low temperature conditions in winter.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; low winter temperatures suit temperate/subtropical crops like wheat.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Zaid crops are cultivated on irrigated lands during the short summer season. Reason (R): Zaid crops are mostly grown on unirrigated land.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false.

qa.q: Rainfed farming is also known as:
qa.e: Barani = rainfed.

qa.q: Dryland farming in India is largely confined to regions with annual rainfall:
qa.e: Below 75 cm.

qa.q: Which crops are typical of dryland farming?
qa.a: Ragi, bajra, moong, gram and guar
qa.e: Hardy, drought-resistant crops suit drylands.

qa.q: Wetland farming regions grow:
qa.a: Water-intensive crops like rice, jute and sugarcane
qa.e: Excess rainfall supports water-hungry crops.

qa.q: The objective of protective irrigation is to:
qa.a: Protect crops from soil moisture deficiency, supplementing rainfall
qa.e: Protective irrigation supplements rain to save crops.

qa.q: Productive irrigation differs from protective irrigation because it:
qa.a: Uses a higher water input per unit area to achieve high productivity
qa.e: It aims at high yields with more water.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Wetland farming regions may face flood and soil erosion hazards. Reason (R): In these regions, rainfall exceeds the soil moisture requirement of plants during the rainy season.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; excess rain explains floods and erosion.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Dryland farmers do not need any moisture conservation measures. Reason (R): Dryland farming regions practise soil moisture conservation and rainwater harvesting.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Aus, aman and boro are three crops of rice grown in:
qa.e: West Bengal grows three rice crops a year.

qa.q: Which is a fine grain cereal?
qa.e: Rice and wheat are fine grains.

qa.q: According to NCERT (2016 data), India's rank in world rice production was:
qa.e: NCERT ranks India second after China (2016 data). Recent estimates suggest India has now edged ahead.

qa.q: Wheat is grown in India mainly in the rabi season because:
qa.a: It is primarily a crop of the temperate zone
qa.e: A temperate crop grows in the cool winter.

qa.q: Which group lists leading wheat-producing states?
qa.a: Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh
qa.e: These five lead wheat production.

qa.q: About what share of India's wheat area lies in the north and central regions?
qa.e: About 85 per cent.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Wheat yields are very high in Punjab and Haryana. Reason (R): Wheat in these states is grown mostly under assured irrigation with modern inputs.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; irrigation and modern inputs explain the high yields.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In West Bengal, farmers grow three crops of rice — aus, aman and boro. Reason (R): Rice is grown only in the kharif season everywhere in India.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: rice is also grown in other seasons, e.g. the three West Bengal crops (aus, aman, boro).

qa.q: Which state produces more than half of India's jowar?
qa.e: Maharashtra alone produces more than half.

qa.q: Bajra is grown mainly in:
qa.a: Hot and dry north-western and western India
qa.e: It suits hot, dry conditions.

qa.q: Which crop is grown as both food and fodder over inferior soils in semi-arid conditions?
qa.e: Maize is a food and fodder crop.

qa.q: Maize is grown all over India except:
qa.e: NCERT notes this exception.

qa.q: In northern India, jowar is mostly grown as:
qa.e: In the north it is a kharif crop grown mostly for fodder.

qa.q: Why is bajra suited to dry regions?
qa.a: It is a hardy crop that resists frequent dry spells and drought
qa.e: Its hardiness suits drought-prone areas.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Jowar is sown in both kharif and rabi seasons in southern states. Reason (R): Southern India has temperatures high enough to grow crops in any season if moisture is available.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; warm temperatures allow jowar in both seasons in the south.

qa.q: On a map of leading crop-producing states, which state would be marked for coffee?
qa.e: Karnataka produces more than two-thirds of India's coffee.

qa.q: Pulses increase the natural fertility of soils by:
qa.e: Legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen.

qa.q: Gram is mostly grown as a:
qa.e: Gram is a subtropical rabi crop needing little water.

qa.q: Tur is also known as:
qa.a: Arhar, red gram or pigeon pea
qa.e: Tur = arhar = red gram = pigeon pea.

qa.q: Which state contributes about one-third of India's tur production?
qa.e: Maharashtra leads tur production.

qa.q: Which state contributes about one-third of India's rapeseed and mustard production?
qa.e: Rajasthan leads.

qa.q: Soyabean is grown mainly in:
qa.e: These two states produce most of India's soyabean.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Gram has been displaced by wheat in Haryana, Punjab and northern Rajasthan. Reason (R): After the Green Revolution, irrigated wheat became more profitable in these areas.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; profitable irrigated wheat replaced gram after the Green Revolution.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Rapeseed and mustard are frost-resistant kharif crops. Reason (R): Rapeseed and mustard are frost-sensitive rabi crops.
qa.a: A is false, but R is true
qa.e: A is false; R is true.

qa.q: Which state produces about three-fourths of India's jute?
qa.e: West Bengal dominates jute production.

qa.q: Which state produces about two-fifths of India's sugarcane?
qa.e: UP produces about two-fifths.

qa.q: Tea was introduced in India by the British in the:
qa.a: 1840s, in the Brahmaputra valley of Assam
qa.e: Tea plantations began in Assam in the 1840s.

qa.q: Which variety of coffee is mostly grown in India?
qa.e: India mostly grows superior arabica.

qa.q: Which state produces more than two-thirds of India's coffee?
qa.e: Karnataka leads coffee production.

qa.q: Long staple American cotton grown in north-western India is called:
qa.e: Narma is long staple American cotton.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Cotton needs a clear sky during its flowering stage. Reason (R): Cotton is a rabi crop grown mainly in cold regions.
qa.a: A is true, but R is false
qa.e: A is true. R is false: cotton is a tropical kharif crop of semi-arid areas.

qa.q: Assertion (A): India lost large jute-growing areas at the time of partition. Reason (R): Much of the jute-growing delta became part of East Pakistan (now Bangladesh).
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
qa.e: Both true; the delta going to East Pakistan explains the loss.

qa.q: High yielding varieties of wheat for the Green Revolution came from:
qa.e: Wheat HYVs came from Mexico; rice HYVs from the Philippines.

qa.q: High yielding varieties of rice came from:
qa.e: Rice HYVs came from the Philippines (IRRI).

qa.q: The Green Revolution was initially confined to:
qa.a: Irrigated areas like Punjab, Haryana and western UP
qa.e: It needed assured irrigation.

qa.q: What was the basic prerequisite for the success of the new agricultural technology?
qa.a: Assured supply of soil moisture through irrigation
qa.e: HYVs needed assured irrigation.

qa.q: Agro-climatic planning was initiated by the Planning Commission in:
qa.e: In 1988, to induce regionally balanced development.

qa.q: In which of these does India rank first in the world?
qa.e: India ranks first in pulses, jute, cattle and milk; it is second in rice, wheat, groundnut and sugarcane.
